title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 1: Wide receiver shuffling amidst injuries
summary: The Baltimore Ravens were victorious in the season opener yesterday, defeating the Indianapolis Colts in a 41-23 win. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense. Offense Jackson and the starting offensive line played all 68 snaps. Backup offensive tackle Carson Vinson saw seven snaps as an extra blocker […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Moore #17 of the Baltimore Ravens carries the ball against Cam Bynum #0 of the Indianapolis Colts during the third quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens were victorious in the season opener yesterday, defeating the Indianapolis Colts in a 41-23 win. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense. Offense QB: Lamar Jackson 68 RB: Derrick Henry 37, Justice Hill 31 WR: Rashod Bateman 53, Ja’Kobi Lane 27, Chris Moore 20, LaJohntay Wester 20, Zay Flowers 20 TE: Mark Andrews 49, Durham Smythe 42, Matthew Hibner 23, Josh Cuevas 6 OL: Ronnie Stanley 68, John Simpson 68, Jovaughn Gwyn 68, Vega Ioane 68, Roger Rosengarten 68, Carson Vinson 7 Jackson and the starting offensive line played all 68 snaps. Backup offensive tackle Carson Vinson saw seven snaps as an extra blocker in jumbo formations. In the backfield, Derrick Henry played just over half of the team’s offensive snaps and rushed for 144 yards with three touchdowns on 20 attempts. Justice Hill played 31 snaps and received seven touches in total. The snap counts at wide receiver are the biggest notable story. With Devontez Walker inactive due to an ankle injury, the Ravens suffered two more injuries at the position. Zay Flowers played 20 snaps in the first half before exiting with a hamstring injury, totaling 150 yards and a touchdown on five catches. Likewise, Ja’Kobi Lane was sidelined for the rest of the game after he too left early with a wrist ailment following 27 snaps. Lane’s first NFL touchdown catch was called back due to a penalty. With both players sidelined, Chris Moore and LaJohntay Wester took on elevated roles, each playing 20 offensive snaps. Moore had a long 53-yard catch and Wester caught two passes, in addition to both players’ duties as primary returners on special teams. Rashod Bateman started the game and played all but one snap, however he was targeted only once with no catches. Mark Andrews unsurprisingly led the tight end room with 49 snaps, catching four passes on six targets. Veteran Durham Smythe played 42 snaps as a primary blocker. Matthew Hibner is clearly third in the pecking order ahead of Josh Cuevas, out-snapping his fellow rookie 23 to six. Hibner caught one pass for 13 yards. Defense DL: Travis Jones 31, Calais Campbell 29, Broderick Washington 21, John Jenkins 13, Aeneas Peebles 10 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 44, Trey Hendrickson 40, Mike Green 17, Zion Young 12 ILB: Roquan Smith 54, Trenton Simpson 32 CB: Nate Wiggins 54, Marlon Humphrey 48, Keyon Martin 23, Chidobe Awuzie 6 S: Kyle Hamilton 54, Malaki Starks 54, Jaylinn Hawkins 52 All five of the Ravens’ defensive lineman saw 10+ snaps in this game as Nnami Madubuike’s return to action awaits. Travis Jones led the way with 31 snaps, closely followed by fellow veterans Calais Campbell (29) and Broderick Washington (21). John Jenkins and Aeneas Peebles combined to play 23 snaps. Tavius Robinson (44) and Trey Hendrickson (40) had a commanding snap share on the edge. Robinson had four quarterback hits and a sack, while Hendrickson was charted for eight pressures. Mike Green only played 17 snaps as the third banana, while rookie Zion Young’s debut saw him on the field for 12 defensive plays. Roquan Smith played every defensive snap and had a starring performance with an interception and team-high 11 tackles. Next to him, Trenton Simpson played 32 snaps and drew the start in the absence of Teddye Buchanan once again. Nate Wiggins did not leave the field and had a pass breakup in his 54 snaps. Marlon Humphrey’s 48 snaps were productive, as the veteran forced a fumble and had a key pass knockdown on a deep attempt in single coverage. Nickel corner Keyon Martin’s 23 snaps were third-most at the position. Surprisingly, Chidobe Awuzie only played six defensive snaps. T.J. Tampa suffered a knee injury and did not return to the game. The Ravens’ trio of safeties were on the field together for all but two plays where Jaylinn Hawkins was relieved. Hamilton and Starks each played 54 snaps. Hawkins occupying a near every-down role likely explains the lack of significant snaps for Martin and Awuzie at cornerback.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens vs. Colts: 9 Winners and 3 Losers
summary: The Baltimore Ravens opened the season on the road with a convincing 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The first game under new head coach Jesse Minter was a resounding success, but a few blemishes were apparent. Winners Lamar Jackson: The two-time MVP looked as sharp as ever against the Colts, completing 17-of-25 passes for […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Moore #17 of the Baltimore Ravens returns the ball against the Indianapolis Colts during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens opened the season on the road with a convincing 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The first game under new head coach Jesse Minter was a resounding success, but a few blemishes were apparent. Winners Lamar Jackson : The two-time MVP looked as sharp as ever against the Colts, completing 17-of-25 passes for 324 yards and a touchdown while adding another 40 yards and a score on the ground on seven rushes. After an injury-riddled season in 2025, Jackson reminded everyone what he is capable of with a Houdini-esque escape from a sack to convert a 3rd-and-16 with his legs. Zay Flowers : The Ravens’ No. 1 wide receiver showed why he deserved the $140 million extension he received this offseason with a monster first half against Indianapolis. The Colts had zero answers for Flowers as the shifty receiver racked up 150 yards and a touchdown on just five catches before unfortunately exiting the game with a hamstring injury. Flowers’ speed popped off the screen on his 54-yard catch-and-run touchdown. Derrick Henry : They say Father Time is undefeated, but it looks like he will have to wait at least another year to win his bout against Henry. The 32-year-old workhorse moved up to third in all-time rushing touchdowns with his three scores against Indianapolis to go with 144 rushing yards. A healthy Jackson and Henry in the backfield is nearly impossible to stop. Chris Moore : The 33-year-old special teams standout stepped up in a big way in his first game back with his original team, both as a returner and receiver. After Baltimore’s defense was walked down the field for a touchdown on the opening drive of the game, Moore responded with a 42-yard kick return to set the Ravens’ offense up at midfield. Moore later broke off a 49-yard return in the third quarter that was called back by a penalty. The biggest play of the day for the veteran came on offense, though, when Moore hauled in a 53-yard pass on third down. With rookie Ja’Kobi Lane set to miss time with a wrist injury and Flowers’ availability for the upcoming weeks unknown, Moore could find himself with more opportunities on offense. Tavius Robinson : Robinson started his contract year off with a strong game against the Colts. Robinson had one of the team’s two sacks on Daniel Jones and was a consistent force from the edge throughout the day with a team-high four quarterback hits. Roquan Smith : The All-Pro linebacker is looking to rebound from a down season in 2025, and Sunday was a good start towards doing so. After a poor first drive from Baltimore’s defense, which led to a touchdown, Smith quickly flipped the momentum on the next drive with an interception off of Jones. Smith led the team with 11 total tackles. Marlon Humphrey : Another player looking to bounce back after a poor season is the former All-Pro cornerback. Humphrey reminded everyone of his playmaking ability with a forced fumble on running back Jonathan Taylor and had an impressive pass breakup on a deep pass intended for Alec Pierce later in the game. The Ravens need their highly paid corner to continue to play at a high level. Tyler Loop : Perhaps the biggest concern for the Ravens entering the season was their kicking situation after a shaky preseason from Loop on the heels of his season-ending miss in Pittsburgh. While it would have been impossible to win back all of the goodwill in just one game, Loop certainly eased concern by making both of his kicks on Sunday, including a career-long 57-yarder. Declan Doyle : The praise for the first-time play-caller was sky high this offseason, and he showed exactly why in his first game. Doyle’s creativity was on full display against Indianapolis, particularly on Flowers’ 54-yard touchdown, where he started lined up next to Jackson in the backfield before running a route. Putting Jackson under center more and using play-action were both effective as well in Week 1. Baltimore may not have Doyle for long if he continues on this trajectory, so fans should enjoy the show while it lasts. Losers Offensive Line : While the offensive line’s performance was not terrible, it was the constant barrage of penalties that really held the unit back in their first outing together. Constant holding penalties and false starts killed momentum for an otherwise unstoppable Ravens’ offense. The unit combined for five penalties, two against left tackle Ronnie Stanley, one on center Jovaugn Gwyn, and two against rookie first-round guard Vega Ioane. The holding penalty against Gwyn nullified a touchdown catch for Lane, leading to a turnover on downs a few plays later instead. Penalties were to be expected in the first game of the season on the road, but Baltimore must fix the issue quickly if their offense is going to reach its true potential. Rashod Bateman : Much talk has been made this offseason about the potential for Bateman to bounce back in a new offensive system, but that was not the story on Sunday. Bateman finished the game with zero catches after his lone reception was called back due to a penalty. Following Flowers’ exit from the game, Bateman should have been the player to step up in the passing game instead of Moore. The Ravens need more from their former first-round pick if Flowers misses any games with his hamstring injury. Justice Hill : Hill did not have his best outing in Week 1, as the veteran running back had back-to-back penalties to kill a drive late in the third quarter. Hill had little success on the ground either, totaling just 18 yards on six carries, though he did add another ten yards on a catch.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 1: Encouraging start to the season as Ravens dominate all three phases
summary: The Baltimore Ravens began the 2026 season with a bang in Week 1, scoring 41 points en route to a 21-point victory over the Indianapolis Colts. While it was not a flawless performance, the Ravens never trailed after the first few minutes of the game and quickly opened up a three-possession lead, which they never […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens began the 2026 season with a bang in Week 1, scoring 41 points en route to a 21-point victory over the Indianapolis Colts. While it was not a flawless performance, the Ravens never trailed after the first few minutes of the game and quickly opened up a three-possession lead, which they never relinquished. Let’s break down how every position group fared in this week’s report card. Quarterback: A- Lamar Jackson had a strong performance to begin the season, completing 17-of-25 passes for 324 yards and a touchdown — with another 40 rushing yards and a score on the ground. Jackson connected with Zay Flowers for multiple chunk plays through the air and delivered another long 50+ yard pass in the third quarter. Jackson looked to be command of Declan Doyle’s offense and he’s clearly no longer compromised by injuries athletically. The lone blemish of Jackson’s day was a lost fumble where he was strip sacked in the Ravens’ own territory, which led to a Colts’ touchdown. Jackson was sacked almost immediately after turning around in play action, though, and fortunately the Ravens were up by three scores at the time, so it wasn’t a damaging sequence. Running Back: A It was just another day at the office for Derrick Henry in Week 1, who rushed for 144 yards on 24 carries with three touchdowns. Henry also added 19 receiving yards on a good catch-and-run reception. Henry’s longest run on the day went for 32 yards, and he grinded out chunk gains as the game progressed to help keep the Ravens’ offense on the field and put the game away. Justice Hill had 28 scrimmage yards on seven touches behind him, picking up a nice first-down gain through the air. Wide Receiver: A- Before exiting with a hamstring injury before halftime, Flowers had already set a new career-high in receiving yards with 150 on five catches. He had a long 54-yard touchdown catch and fell just a few yards short of scoring on the second drive of the game. Flowers was uncoverable and had he left the game early, there’s no telling what his final stat line may have been. His performance alone in just two quarters of action is enough to boost this position group’s grade. Chris Moore, who was a practice squad elevation, made an impact with a 54-yard reception in the third quarter. LaJohntay Wester had two catches, and Ja’Kobi Lane had one 11-yard catch before leaving the game early as well with a wrist injury. Lane would have had his first career touchdown reception, but it was called back due to a holding penalty. Surprisingly, Rashod Bateman was held to zero catches on just one target. Tight End: B – Mark Andrews’ first target resulted in a dropped pass, and he was also flagged for a false start in the red zone early in the game. That was a discouraging start, but he wound up reeling in four receptions for 49 yards overall. His six targets were tied with Flowers for most on the team. Matthew Hibner turned a short out-route pass into a 13-yard gain to help push the Ravens deeper into the red zone, setting up a score. Hibner wasn’t targeted again in the game, and rookie Josh Cuevas was not a factor in the passing game. Veteran Durham Smythe caught one pass for a short four-yard gain outside of the end zone. The Ravens’ tight ends as a whole seemed to do a good job of pass blocking and holding the edges in run blocking situations. Offensive Line: C – It was not the most encouraging start to the season for the Ravens’ new-look offensive line. While they did a good job in run blocking and held up okay for most of the game in pass protection, the penalties from this group were rough. Of the Ravens’ 10 penalties overall as a team, most of them were offensive line pre-snap calls, holding violations and in one instance a chop-blocking flag. It seemed like the Ravens were flagged for offensive line penalties on almost every drive and many times it negated a first-down gain or score. There were some instances where the Colts generated quick pressure up the middle, too, and they did get home on Jackson to force a fumble in the second quarter. Defensive Line: C+ Travis Jones was a force up front in this game with two notable tackles for loss, one of which he drove Taylor back several yards behind the line of scrimmage. Taylor was able to find running room against the Ravens’ defensive front a number of times, though, and the Ravens allowed 102 rushing yards overall and 5.2 yards per carry. Broderick Washington had a nice pass breakup early in the game that was close to being an interception, and Aaenas Peebles had a quarterback hit as well. Edge Rusher: B- Trey Hendrickson’s debut did not result in any splash plays, but he was close to getting home for a sack or possible forced fumble multiple times. Hendrickson had a handful of pressures on Jones and his presence may have helped opened things up a bit for Tavius Robinson, who had a big showing on the opposite side of the defensive front. Robinson racked up four quarterback hits with a sack and tackle for loss. In a contract year, this could be the start of a career-best season for the fourth-year edge rusher. Mike Green and Zion Young did not find their way onto the box score in this game. Linebacker: B+ Roquan Smith’s interception on the Colts’ second drive of the game was a thing of beauty, as he deceived Daniel Jones and tapped the ball to himself in the air before securing it. The Ravens added another touchdown a few plays later to open up an eight-point lead. Smith led the team in tackles with 11 and also had a quarterback hit. Next to him, Trenton Simpson had two tackles-for-loss, which was tied for the most of any defender. Cornerback: A- Marlon Humphrey had a starring performance with a forced fumble on Jonathan Taylor and third-down knockdown in coverage against Alec Pierce. Humphrey looked much more like his prime self than he did last season, which is an encouraging sign for this season. Nate Wiggins also an impressive pass breakup lined up against Pierce. Keyon Martin made a strong tackle in space against a much larger wide receiver. Overall, the Ravens’ corners did a good job limiting big plays in the passing game and were aggressive in coverage. Safety: B+ Following the defense’s first drive of the game, Kyle Hamilton began being used more as an extra pass rusher and his presence around the line of scrimmage made a noticeable impact. Hamilton finished with five tackles and a quarterback hit. Malaki Starks was victimized a few times against Taylor via a stiff arm and juke move, but also filled the stat sheet with seven tackles, a sack, two quarterback hits and one tackle for loss. Jaylinn Hawkins didn’t make any noticeable impact plays, but he appeared around the ball a few times on some positive defensive plays. The Ravens’ three safeties didn’t seem to leave the field very much at all. Special Teams: A Tyler Loop answered the bell in a big way, nailing a career-high 57-yard field goal attempt to close out the first half. That expanded the Ravens lead to three possessions, and he made a 45-yarder later in the second half, while also going perfect on all five extra points. Rookie punter Ryan Eckley’s three punts went for 140 yards, and Chris Moore had a couple long kick returns to set the Ravens up in good field position offensively. LaJohntay Wester also had a long 30-yard return on a kickoff as well and averaged 10.0 yards per punt return on three tries.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens overcome injuries, penalties in dominant Week 1 win over Colts
summary: The Baltimore Ravens throttled the Indianapolis Colts in a 41-23 victory on Sunday afternoon to get their 2026 season and the Jesse Minter era off to a 1-0 start. “It’s surreal a little bit, honestly.” Minter said after his head coaching debut. “I don’t know if it’s actually hit me yet. But it’s a blessing […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Indianapolis, Indiana, USA; Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson (8) and running back Derrick Henry (22) celebrate a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Trevor Ruszkowski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens throttled the Indianapolis Colts in a 41-23 victory on Sunday afternoon to get their 2026 season and the Jesse Minter era off to a 1-0 start. “It’s surreal a little bit, honestly.” Minter said after his head coaching debut. “I don’t know if it’s actually hit me yet. But it’s a blessing to be where I’m at – again, such appreciation for the opportunity given to me by this organization.” Led by first-time play-caller Declan Doyle and two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson, Baltimore’s offense racked up 502 yards (7.9 yards per play) despite several penalties by the offensive line. Jackson was brilliant through the air, completing 17 of his 25 passes for 324 yards and a touchdown and throwing in 40 yards and another score on the ground for good measure. He looked right at home in Doyle’s new-look, under-center heavy offense, and when the system broke down, his signature elusiveness took over. On one miraculous play, he somehow ducked under two oncoming pass rushers and scrambled 16 yards for a first down. LAMAR JACKSON, THE MAGICIAN YOU ARE 🤯🎩 (via: @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/BAOpJgeayW — B/R Gridiron (@brgridiron) September 13, 2026 When asked about his latest magic trick, Jackson said that he was “just playing football.” He also shouted out Doyle for “dialing it up” on offense and praised the team for finishing the game strong. Wide receiver Zay Flowers flew around the field for 150 receiving yards on just five catches before leaving the game late in the first half with hamstring injury. Running back Derrick Henry averaged 6.0 yards per carry and scored three times on the ground to pass Marcus Allen for third place on the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list. The Colts offense surprised Minter’s defense with seven straight passes to start the game, putting the secondary on its back foot and setting up a Jonathan Taylor touchdown. The opening possession stirred painful memories of the Zach Orr defenses that folded all too easily in the past two seasons. “Defensively, I thought I didn’t do a great job on the first drive,” Minter explained. “They had us on our heels a little bit, and then I felt like we really settled in on defense and did some good things and attacked the football well.” Baltimore responded by forced three punts and two turnovers on Indianapolis’ next five drives. Notably, those turnovers were forced by Smith and cornerback Marlon Humphrey, two veteran defenders who, by their own admission, played below their standard last year. “I feel like the start of the game kind of went against their identity, in my opinion,” linebacker Roquan Smith said. “Those guys [are] normally known for running the ball…There are highs and lows, but we took a deep breath, came to the sideline, and [said] ‘Hey, this isn’t us.’” Edge rusher Trey Hendrickson did not notch any sacks in his Ravens debut, but he consistently moved Colts quarterback Daniel Jones off his spot with eight pressures on just 26 pass rushes, per Next Gen Stats . The 31-year-old appears to be worth every penny of the massive $112 million free agent deal he signed in Baltimore this offseason. And just because John Harbaugh is no longer in Baltimore does not mean special teams are not an emphasis. In Anthony Levine’s debut as a coordinator, the Ravens consistently won the field position battle. Rookie punter Ryan Eckley landed all three of his punts inside the Colts’ 20-yard line, and returners Chris Moore and LaJohntay Wester both ripped off long returns. Second-year kicker Tyler Loop entered Week 1 under the microscope after an up-and-down preseason and the signing of former 49ers kicker Jake Moody to the practice squad. He made both of his field goal attempts and all five of his extra points. His 57-yard field goal was a career-long, while his 45-yarder effectively clinched the Ravens’ victory in the fourth quarter. “My confidence in him has never really shaken,” Minter said of his young kicker. “Obviously, you have to make kicks and things like that, and in the preseason, he had a couple of mishaps. But just the work ethic and the trust in the process in so many different things that he’s been working on, I expected nothing less. I am really happy for him that he performed that way today.” All told, the Ravens controlled the game from start to finish and more than doubled the Colts’ in yardage (506 to 251). 10 penalties for 86 yards and injuries to Flowers (hamstring) and rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane (wrist) were the only blemishes on a deeply satisfying victory for the team. Minter did not have updates on either wideout following the game. The Ravens will return to Baltimore brimming with confidence after beating a talented, well-coached Colts squad. They will take on the New Orleans Saints in their home opener next week, likely as heavy favorites. However, the Saints barely lost to the Detroit Lions in overtime on Sunday afternoon; this could be the kind of early-season trap game the Ravens have fallen into multiple times in recent years.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Roundtable Reactions: Ravens cruise to a blowout victory in Week 1
summary: To open up the 2026 regular season, the Baltimore Ravens secured a convincing 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. Here are the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reactions to the game: In a game filled with some major highs and major lows, at the end of the day, it’s just nice to start the season with a […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens scores a rushing touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images To open up the 2026 regular season, the Baltimore Ravens secured a convincing 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. Here are the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reactions to the game: In a game filled with some major highs and major lows, at the end of the day, it’s just nice to start the season with a win — something the Ravens didn’t do the last two seasons. They dominated for the most part on the way to a 41-23 win on the road. Lamar Jackson looked like Lamar Jackson, Derrick Henry looked like Derrick Henry and Zay Flowers showed why he’s a top wide receiver in the NFL, both when he was on the field and when he wasn’t. Jesse Minter’s defense showed up after a rough opening drive. Despite the dominating win, there’s going to be plenty for this team to work with, starting with double digit penalties calls in this one. The offensive line also looked rough at moments but also opened up holes in the run game and Jackson did have moments with plenty of time in the pocket, despite it being inconsistent. The offense as a whole also went from looking like a Top 10 unit in the NFL to a bottom-tier unit after Flowers left due to injury. They will need to be better at having gameplans ready in the future. Overall, despite the penalties being maddeningly frustrating and worried surrounding the offense is Flowers misses more time, it’s hard to be unhappy after a Week 1 win. — Zach Canter It’s tough to draw up a better opening performance for the new Ravens regime. The offense was simply unstoppable in the first half with Zay Flowers racking up over 150 yards and Lamar Jackson looking healthy and back to MVP form. Unfortunately, Flowers left the game with a hamstring injury that’s been nagging him since training camp. Hamstrings are particularly tricky and the Ravens might have to plan on being without their star receiver for a few games. Additionally rookie Ja’Kobi Lane left the game with a wrist injury. Defensively, the Ravens already looked greatly improved. They gave up some yards to Jonathan Taylor but Daniel Jones and the passing game were largely ineffective (I also counted about 3 holds that weren’t called on Trey Hendrickson). The addition of Nmandi Madubuike in the coming weeks will provide an additional boost. Obviously, the Flowers and Lane injuries will be ones to watch and they need to clean up some penalty issues but this was a great start to the Jesse Minter era. — Stephen Bopst It’s hard to come away from Jesse Minter’s first game as anything but impressed. Both sides of the ball were dominant with small lapses throughout the game. The main negative is of course the amount of penalties committed on offense, but I expect that to be ironed out as the starting offensive line gels. I am worried about the passing attack without Zay Flowers, so hopefully his injury will not keep him out for long. Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry look as good as usual, which makes the sky the limit for Declan Doyle’s offense, who I thought called an excellent game in his first outing. Defensively, I was impressed by the secondaries ability to keep everything in front of them. Paired with consistent pressure on Daniel Jones up front, Baltimore’s defense was as advertised through one game. Adding Madubuike to the mix is an exciting thought now. — Dustin Cox The good far outweighed the bad for the Ravens in Week 1. After a disappointing defensive opening drive, Jesse Minter’s unit settled in and helped flip the game with forced turnovers. Allowing 23 points is not the most ideal number, but the Colts racked up some points and yards with the game all but out of reach in the second half. It was refreshing to see the Ravens come up with multiple takeaways and connect on explosive plays consistently on offense. Lamar Jackson had a sharp performance, and his agility looked night and day compared to last season as he dealt with injuries. The offensive line held up pretty well in pass protection and opened up running lanes for Derrick Henry. However, the Ravens were also victimized by a number of pre-snap penalties and other offensive line violations throughout the game. Their ability to score in bunches and rip off chunk yardage helped compensate for this, but they had several positive plays called back by penalties and lost 10-20 yards at the same time. This will need to be cleaned up moving forward. The only other significant concern coming out of this game is the status of Zay Flowers (hamstring) and Ja’Kobi Lane (wrist). Flowers was halfway to 300 receiving yards in the second quarter before exiting due to injury. — Frank Platko The Ravens looked like a complete team during Sunday’s win over the Colts. Offense, defense, and special teams all played complementary football with Baltimore’s new coaching staff putting their best players in positions to shine. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle was cooking with Zay Flowers in the first half but his injury – as well as Ja’Kobi Lane’s – places a lot of pressure on the rest of receiving corps who did not show up for much of the game. But on Sunday, neither that nor way too many offensive line penalties really mattered with Lamar Jackson kicking off another MVP campaign and Derrick Henry rumbling for 6.0 yards per carry and three touchdowns. Minter’s defense was taken by surprise by the Colts’ pass-heavy opening drive, but quickly tightened up and forced two turnovers that led to touchdowns. Anthony Levine’s special teams unit contributed throughout the game with solid punt coverage and several big returns from LaJohntay Wester and Chris Moore. Outside of the injuries, it’s hard to ask for a better start to the Ravens’ new era. — Nikhil Mehta
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Instant takeaways from the Ravens’ 41-23 Week 1 win over the Colts
summary: The Baltimore Ravens throttled the Indianapolis Colts by a score of 41-23 to kick off their 2026 season. Here are the instant takeaways from Baltimore Beatdown’s staff! Explosives, explosives, explosives One positive takeaway from this game is that the Ravens’ new-look offense is clearly capable of generating explosive plays. Zay Flowers was the primary engine […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Indianapolis, Indiana, USA; Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers (4) runs with the ball against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Trevor Ruszkowski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens throttled the Indianapolis Colts by a score of 41-23 to kick off their 2026 season. Here are the instant takeaways from Baltimore Beatdown’s staff! Explosives, explosives, explosives One positive takeaway from this game is that the Ravens’ new-look offense is clearly capable of generating explosive plays. Zay Flowers was the primary engine of that in the first half, but even after he exited the game, Chris Moore and Derrick Henry added long chunk gains. With a healthier wide receiver room, the Ravens will likely be even more potent in the passing game. – Frank Platko Penalties, penalties, penalties It’s easy to come away from this game with plenty of positive takeaways, but I will point out the one glaring negative in Jesse Minter’s head coaching debut, which was the amount of penalties, particularly on the offensive line. With no preseason reps as a starting unit and on the road to start the season, some penalties were expected, but the amount of them is unacceptable. The only thing stopping Baltimore’s offense all day seemed to be ill-timed penalties, which needs to be cleaned up as the unit begins to gel together over the course of the first month. – Dustin Cox Another takeaway is that the Ravens’ offensive line is clearly not gelled together yet and will need to clean up penalties. It’s almost a miracle that the Ravens were able to score 41 points when they were victimized by what felt like at least one negative pre-snap penalty or offensive line violation on every drive. Committing this many penalties is not sustainable for offensive success moving forward. – Frank Platko Declan Doyle won’t be in Baltimore for long Declan Doyle’s resume includes apprenticeships under Sean Payton and Ben Johnson, two of the NFL’s most innovative offensive minds. Now he’s working with one of the league’s best offensive trios in Lamar Jackson, Derrick Henry, and Zay Flowers. Jackson started his third MVP campaign on Sunday afternoon, while Henry and Flowers looked like OPOY candidates with several explosive plays. If the Ravens can clean up the penalties, they could be the best offense in the league, and other teams could come calling for Doyle as early as next offseason. Zay Flowers was worth every penny… One major takeaway from this game should be that Zay Flowers is absolutely worth the contract he received this offseason. Flowers was basically uncoverable in the first half of the game, racking up 150 yards and a touchdown. His impact was felt even more when he left the game with a hamstring injury, as Baltimore’s offense struggled to sustain drives. The Ravens need a healthy Flowers going forward, even if that means sitting him for next week’s game. – Dustin Cox …but the Ravens will need a plan if he misses time My takeaway is the Ravens need to have a better game plan if Zay Flowers misses time. While most teams would struggle if their top wideout was out, the Ravens offense looked completely inept for a large portion of the game. No other pass catcher was able to take over, especially when Ja’Kobi Lane went out as well. The eyeglass is over Rashod Bateman, who needs to have a bounce back season and get back to his 2024 form, where he did take over some games and during the playoffs when Flowers missed time. – Zach Canter
author: Zach Canter

title: Ravens vs. Colts Inactives: Devontez Walker OUT, Elijah Sarratt and Emery Jones scratched
summary: With just under an hour remaining until kickoff, the Baltimore Ravens have announced their inactive player list for Week 1 against the Indianapolis Colts. Inactives: The Ravens’ wide receiver depth will be tested to begin the season with Walker out due to an ankle injury. Rookie wideout Elijah Sarratt is a healthy scratch and the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Devontez Walker #81 of the Baltimore Ravens stands during an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images With just under an hour remaining until kickoff, the Baltimore Ravens have announced their inactive player list for Week 1 against the Indianapolis Colts. Inactives: WR Devontez Walker (ankle) CB Chandler Rivers ILB Teddye Buchanan (knee) OL Emery Jones WR Elijah Sarratt DT Nnamdi Madubuike (neck) QB Joe Fagnano (3rd QB) The Ravens’ wide receiver depth will be tested to begin the season with Walker out due to an ankle injury. Rookie wideout Elijah Sarratt is a healthy scratch and the Ravens elevated Chris Moore from the practice squad to take his place on the gameday roster, likely due to his special teams abilities. The Ravens also elevated linebacker Carl Jones from the practice squad as well. In addition to Sarratt, fellow rookie Chandler Rivers is a healthy inactive at cornerback, meaning Keyon Martin will be the primary backup nickel defender. Joe Fagnano is unsurprisingly designated inactive as well as the team’s third quarterback. Buchanan and Madubuike were already pronounced as out prior to today and will aim to make their return from injuries next week. The biggest surprise from this list is Emery Jones being a healthy scratch. Jones is believed to be a primary backup offensive guard/tackle, but the Ravens are rolling with Andrew Vorhees and Carson Vinson to have on-hand instead if needed.

full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 4: Roquan Smith #0 of the Baltimore Ravens talks to teammates in a huddle prior to an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Dustin Cox I predict a low-scoring, defensive game between these two teams. The Ravens’ new-look interior offensive line will be tested immediately against DeForest Buckner. Score prediction: Ravens 23, Colts 16 Frank Platko Week 1 will present a good first test for the Ravens’ reshaped interior offensive line and young wide receivers. The Colts have a capable front seven and secondary. The Ravens are integrating three new interior starters up front. Jovaughn Gwyn and Vega Ioane’s reps against DeForest Buckner will be worth watching. X-factor: Travis Jones. Jones missed some time in training camp but will be relied upon heavily with Nnamdi Madubuike still sidelined for Week 1. Jonathan Taylor presents a difficult matchup as one of the league’s elite running backs. Jones’ ability to plug rushing lanes and get interior pressure on QB Daniel Jones will be key. Score prediction : Ravens 27, Colts 17 Zach Canter I think a lot is being made up both defenses taking charge of offenses that might not be at their best to open the season for various reasons. But not enough people have talked about how befuddled defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo has been by Lamar Jackson. During his six years as the Bengals DC, the Ravens averaged nearly 30 points a game during 12 regular season games from 2019-2024 against Anarumo’s defenses. I think Derrick Henry could feast again an unsure linebacker core for the Ravens to help control a strong interior line for the Colts. The big matchup for me is Zay Flowers. Score predictions: Ravens 28, Colts 17 Stephen Bopst My key storyline to watch today has to be the Ravens defensive line and specifically, Trey Hendrickson. The Ravens have made a few key additions this offseason but none bigger than Hendrickson. At his floor, he is statistically a top 5 pure pass rusher in the league and a continuation of that will do wonders for Jesse Minter and this revamped Ravens defense. If the Ravens can generate consistent pressure with four lineman today against a good Colts offensive line, they will win the game and give major optimism for season long success, especially with the impending return of Nmandi Madubuike. title: Buffalo Bills learn from past mistakes in victory over Houston Texans
summary: Not much had gone right for the Buffalo Bills when playing at the Houston Texans over the last twenty years. Whether it was NRG Stadium or Reliant Stadium, the Bills had a Houston problem, as they had lost six straight decisions in Houston. I fact, Buffalo had only won twice—once in the Texans’ inaugural season […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Quarterback Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills readies for a snap behind offensive tackle Spencer Brown #79 of the Buffalo Bills and guard O'Cyrus Torrence #64 of the Buffalo Bills during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Not much had gone right for the Buffalo Bills when playing at the Houston Texans over the last twenty years. Whether it was NRG Stadium or Reliant Stadium, the Bills had a Houston problem, as they had lost six straight decisions in Houston. I fact, Buffalo had only won twice—once in the Texans’ inaugural season in 2002 and then again in 2006—when playing the Texans in their home stadium. So it was especially encouraging to see the Bills emerge with a 36-31 win yesterday to open the 2026 season, slaying some demons in a house of horrors for the franchise throughout the 24-year tenure of the Houston football club. Plenty of things went Buffalo’s way on Sunday, including two offensive fumbles that were recovered by the Bills and a Josh Allen fourth-quarter chuck that Kamari Lassiter dropped in the end zone just one play before the game-winning touchdown pass. Those lucky instances are things that right, but there were plenty of things in Buffalo’s control that went right for the team, as well. One of the biggest issues the Bills had in their previous losses to the Houston was with protection—namely, they couldn’t keep Allen upright. In last year’s 23-19 loss at Houston, Allen took a career-high eight sacks. While some of those sacks were on him for holding the ball too long, there were too many instances where a four-man Houston rush easily overwhelmed a five-man Buffalo protection scheme. When that five-man look still didn’t work, the Bills offered little in the way of changing their plan throughout the contest. On Sunday, though, the protection scheme looked much different. Buffalo still stuck with some five-man looks, but they varied their protections to keep the Houston edge rushers guessing. Sometimes, they doubled Danielle Hunter and used a tight end to chip Will Anderson. Other times, they did the opposite. They even used wideouts to chip, which we saw work to success on the game’s final play. It was DJ Moore who chipped Hunter on the game’s final play, helping the keep Spencer Brown in a good position to keep Allen upright. That chip from Moore led to a delayed release into his route, which safety Calen Bullock definitely saw as he cheated just a bit to Moore’s side. That gave Allen the window to chuck a “horseshoe,” as he called it postgame, that Joshua Palmer caught for a game-winning 34-yard score. "This is not where the ball is supposed to go. We have never once repped the ball going there." Josh Allen breaks down the Josh Palmer TD, which gave the Bills the lead late in the game 🎙️: @EvanWashburn pic.twitter.com/SMxQxE7Ti4 — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) September 13, 2026 Color analyst Ross Tucker said multiple times on the broadcast that teams need to “think players, not plays” in big situations. With Houston likely following that mantra by cheating towards Moore, it gave the Bills and Josh Allen an opening to hit an unlikely hero in Palmer across the field. Had the Bills and their offensive coaching staff not made a conscious decision to change their protection scheme entering this game, giving their offensive linemen help against a ferocious Texans pass rush, that split-second might have been the difference in an incomplete pass or worse. And what we saw was the winning score. Credit to head coach Joe Brady, offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr., and offensive line coach Pat Meyer for changing their approach in Sunday’s win.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Joe Brady aced fourth-down decisions, clock management in first game as Bills head coach
summary: Buffalo Bills head coach Joe Brady had a lot on his plate in Week 1. In his first game as a head coach in the NFL, he had to call the offensive plays, manage the clock, and make critical fourth-down decision on the fly, and he handed everything outstandingly. Let’s focus on the fourth-down decisions […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Head coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills reacts after his team's touchdown against the Houston Texans in the second quarter of a game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills head coach Joe Brady had a lot on his plate in Week 1. In his first game as a head coach in the NFL, he had to call the offensive plays, manage the clock, and make critical fourth-down decision on the fly, and he handed everything outstandingly. Let’s focus on the fourth-down decisions and in-game management here, because we know the 36 points and 7.9 yards per play from his offense were outrageous accomplishments against that Texans defense. Per Adam Pensel’s DownSetDominance.com , an excellent new analytics site catered toward Bills metrics, Brady went 6-for-6 in fourth-down decisions in Houston in Week 1. From Pensel’s site: “Every Buffalo Bills fourth down against the nfl4th model: go for it, kick, or punt, judged by win probability.” Let’s run through all of those decisions, which I must add, seemed to be made without hesitation by Brady in this contest — shout out to his analytics/in-game management team in the booth led by Dennis Lock: First quarter, 11:18 left, 4th & 1, at Texans 34 — model suggested go for it, Bills went for it (did not covert) First quarter, 7:28 left, 4th & 6, at Texans 28 — model suggested “toss up”, Bills kicked field goal (coverted) Third quarter, 9:41 left, 4th & 12, at Bills 33 — model suggested punt, Bills punted Third quarter, 4:24 left, 4th & 10, at Texans 16 — model suggested field goal, Bills kicked field goal (converted) Fourth quarter, 10:31 left, 4th & 4, at Texans 14 — model suggested field goal, Bills kicked field goal (converted) Fourth quarter, 5:45 left, 4th & 12, at Bills 18 — model suggested punt, Bills punted Now, there weren’t a bevy of challenging fourth-down decisions in this game, but Brady (and his staff) made all the correct decisions. Even when the Bills were called for too many men in the huddle — which you could ding Brady for — on a 4th & 1 midway through the first quarter, the model suggested the Bills go for it, and the offense was on the field before the penalty. In a league where the margins are incredibly thin, these decisions absolutely matter. Per Pensel, and referencing the nfl4th model, Brady gave up exactly 0.0 probability points against the Texans in Week 1. That’s huge, particularly in such a tight game. Sean McDermott gradually improved his fourth-down decisions during his time as Buffalo’s head coach — he began very conservative — but based on the nfl4th model had six contests in which his decisions cost the team 2.0 or more points of win probability last season. Included in every head-coach interview for the Bills job was an in-game management quiz, and we learned Brady’s score was the best of the all of the candidates. And he aced his fourth-down decisions in his first game, a contest in which emotions could’ve gotten the best of him, particularly late. There was this too (thanks, ChuckWagon): Brady also decided to keep the foot on the gas with clock management. The Bills got the ball on their own 17 with 0:18 remaining in the first half — after a three-play, 96-yard touchdown drive on the previous possession — and Allen dropped back to pass on the first play. After it fell incomplete, Brady decided to take the 24-21 lead into halftime yet started the drive looking for more points. Every single point is at a premium in today’s NFL. Brady’s first game as the Bills head coach — and in-game manager — indicates he’s well aware of that.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: 4 takeaways from Bills win over Texans in Week 1
summary: The Buffalo Bills didn’t just exorcise demons against the Houston Texans, they sent those defensive demons to another dimension. While not a runaway victory, Josh Allen and Co. scored 36 points on the DeMeco Ryans’ vaunted unit, which tied for the most the Texans have allowed in a single game since October 2022. These were […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills warms up prior to the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills didn’t just exorcise demons against the Houston Texans, they sent those defensive demons to another dimension. While not a runaway victory, Josh Allen and Co. scored 36 points on the DeMeco Ryans’ vaunted unit, which tied for the most the Texans have allowed in a single game since October 2022. These were my four biggest takeaways from Buffalo’s thrilling victory. That was the most explosive I’ve seen the offense in a long time …especially considering the opponent. And the numbers matched the feeling while watching the game. The Bills had five 30+ yard passing plays against the Texans, more than any in a single game over the past two seasons. They had four while scoring 42 points against the Rams in 2024 and four again the following Week in a 48-42 victory over the Lions. In this contest, Buffalo forced Houston to cover the entire field, which is precisely what Josh Allen is capable of given his arm talent and accuracy, notably when he has proper weapons. Allen’s average depth of target was 12.8 yards in this game, his highest figure in a win since Week 18… of 2022. The exclamation mark of this eruption in Houston was this — last season, Allen had 25 completions on throws he made 20 or more yards down the field. He had four such completions against that Texans defense on Sunday. That is 16% of the 2025 total in 5.8% (1 of 17) of the regular season games. Goodness. Deone Walker and Ed Oliver combo was sensational Remember when there was worry about Oliver’s fit in Jim Leonhard’s scheme? Even odd-man base fronts need one-gap upfield disruptors, and Oliver was exactly as advertised in this game. Ironically, it was Oliver’s first step and lightning-quick backfield entries that allowed many of his front-seven mates to generate big plays near the line of scrimmage or pressures of C.J. Stroud throughout this contest. Many of us thought it’d be the oversized defensive linemen who’d free Oliver for one-on-one wins. His impact was huge, beyond any stat sheet. And where to begin with Walker? He looked exactly like the 2023 Kentucky version of himself that prompted me to write an article that suggested he could become the next Dexter Lawrence… or even scarier. Walker’s swim move for an enormous sack of Stroud on the final drive was outrageous. Borderline unprecedented for a man his size. He was a 6’7”, 330-pound magnet to the football against the run too, often demolished Houston’s blocking schemes on his 51 (!) snaps. The Oliver and Walker duo definitely needs a nickname. The secondary will take some time to master new scheme The Max Hairston-Dee Alford miscommunication on Houston’s final drive is fresh in my mind, but the Bills gave Texans receivers — even those not named Nico Collins — far too much room when Buffalo played zone throughout this game. Leonhard blitzed 31% of the time against Houston, which was right around the Broncos’ 2025 blitz rate, yet they weren’t very successful because of holes in coverage behind them. This new scheme is complex. Lots of moving parts — players rapidly replacing blitzers — and goes all-in much more frequently than any iteration Buffalo’s defense under Sean McDermott. The Bills secondary is filled with young players. Don’t be surprised if it takes time for this unit to gel together against the variety of offensive looks it will see early in the season. Also too… with an improved offensive line, Houston’s offense is going to be noticeably better this season, so it’s not as if the Bills defense laid an egg against a bad unit. That perspective matters. 13 personnel Buffalo utilized 11 personnel — three receivers — 45.6% of the time against the Texans. Reasonably normal. Their second-most used personnel grouping was… 13 personnel, which is three tight ends on the field at the same time, at 36.8% of the offensive snaps! That’s a huge number. Like seismic. Of course, just one game here, but for perspective, the Rams led the NFL in 13 personnel at 30.4% last season. Dalton Kincaid had the most receiving yards for a Bills tight end in a single game since 1967 and appeared on 72% of the snaps (!) while Dawson Knox played 67%. Jackson Hawes played 43%, and even Keleki Latu appeared on four snaps. These hybrid receiver-blockers make it impossible to guess run or pass, and as Kincaid demonstrated against last season’s No. 1 EPA per play and EPA per drop back defense, he can rip a secondary to shreds when he’s not blocking. The 13 personnel wrinkle — which may actually be a staple — in this offense can take the unit to new heights this season.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills TE Dalton Kincaid emerging as true X-factor for Buffalo’s offense
summary: In his first regular-season game as head coach of the Buffalo Bills, Joe Brady called a fantastic game that saw the Houston Texans unable to contain a varied and deep passing game. Entering the 2026 NFL season, tight end Dalton Kincaid was widely discussed as someone with real potential to break out like never before. […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Tight end Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills points to the crowd after getting a first down after a long reception during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In his first regular-season game as head coach of the Buffalo Bills, Joe Brady called a fantastic game that saw the Houston Texans unable to contain a varied and deep passing game. Entering the 2026 NFL season, tight end Dalton Kincaid was widely discussed as someone with real potential to break out like never before. Now healthy, Kincaid’s contributions Week 1 showed off the kind player he can be for Buffalo’s offense. A true X-factor against the Texans, Kincaid hauled in five catches on six targets for 130 yards. Kincaid’s play routinely took the top off of Houston’s vaunted defense, where no cornerback or linebacker could meaningfully cover him down the field. Time and again, the camera had to pan way downfield to focus on Kincaid as he caught a pass for another first down. Whatever Allen threw his way, Kincaid caught it with ease, even if several defenders were around or on him. Kincaid is a matchup nightmare waiting to be further unleashed in Brady’s scheme. We saw the first fruits of that on Sunday, which could be a sign of things to come as the season unfolds. Far more than a traditional tight end, even one known as a primary pass catcher, Kincaid brings a near-unparalleled skill set to the position. Finding ways to move Kincaid around on offense to create mismatches will be key, as we saw on several plays in Week 1 that featured him in a role similar to wide receiver Joshua Palmer last season. Kincaid shouldn’t be pigeon-holed into only TE-specific routes and situations. He’s talented and explosive enough to play anywhere the offense needs him. In ways, Kincaid’s play and potential on offense reminds me of retired NFL wide receiver Ed McCaffrey. The former Denver Broncos standout was often unstoppable out of the slot and catching passes deep down the middle of the field. Kincaid can play a similar role as an efficient boundary or slot receiver who proves to be a mismatch for almost every defender he faces in coverage. It’s clear that quarterback Josh Allen trust Kincaid, calling him a “stud” in his postgame press conference. Time will tell if Allen and Kincaid put together the type of QB-TE season common to quarterback Patrick Mahomes and tight end Travis Kelce. A former first-round pick with Buffalo from the 2023 NFL Draft, the Bills wisely picked up Kincaid’s fifth-year option in March of 2026. Kincaid and One Bills Drive understand what’s at stake this season, for the team and for Kincaid’s contract future. Hopefully a huge season by Kincaid leads to big things en route to a new long-term contract that keeps him catching passes from Josh Allen for years to come.
author: Matt Byham

title: Buffalo Bills’ Week 1 win over Houston Texans fueled by Greg Rousseau
summary: The Buffalo Bills are 1-0 after a thrilling Week 1 road victory over the Houston Texans. The house that Houston built has been more of a house of horrors for Buffalo and Bills Mafia in recent seasons, where prior to Sunday’s win quarterback Josh Allen and the team were 0-4 in their last four trips […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Linebacker Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills strips the ball from quarterback C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans in the final minutes of the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are 1-0 after a thrilling Week 1 road victory over the Houston Texans. The house that Houston built has been more of a house of horrors for Buffalo and Bills Mafia in recent seasons, where prior to Sunday’s win quarterback Josh Allen and the team were 0-4 in their last four trips to Reliant Stadium. Allen will garner all the headlines and much of the game’s coverage in the hours and days after this win, and it’s justified. Yet it’s anything other than given that the team wins the game without two key plays by outside linebacker Greg Rousseau. Rousseau was a man possessed at several points during Sunday’s game, playing the role of a true game-wrecker both very early and quite late. During the Texans’ first drive of the game and season, Rousseau found the express lane around the edge en route to a strip-sack of quarterback C. J. Stroud. Defensive tackle Ed Oliver was there to rub salt in wound, stealing the ball back for Josh Allen and company. In what could be viewed minimally as a six-point swing, Buffalo’s offense went on to secure a field goal and the early 3-0 lead thanks to that play. Overall it was a productive afternoon for Rousseau, but he saved the absolute best for the final play of the game when he reprised his role from the first drive. With mere seconds to play, Rousseau once again got free off the edge and slammed into Stroud for another drive-ending strip-sack and turnover to seal the 36-31 victory for the Bills. Rousseau’s work in Week 1 was the sort of effort that so many have been screaming for in recent years. Buffalo has actively sought out defenders who could take over at any moment with the game-winning plays. That’s exactly what Rousseau did on Sunday, in what may now be viewed as his signature game. Defensively, the Bills forced two turnovers, and both of those came via Rousseau’s dominating play that totaled four tackles and five quarterback hits in addition to those two strip sacks. Rousseau has the potential to act as a defensive X-factor this season, his first as a stand-up edge rusher from the outside linebacker position. It’s the first time he’s played this role in his NFL career, and the early returns are positive — including his play as a pass defender when he dropped back in coverage and used his crazy length to stretch out and break up a key pass. In prior seasons, I’ve been critical of Rousseau’s play. He’s always been a consistent player who did most of his work behind the scenes. Rousseau is the type of player begging to be featured more, which was never going to happen in prior head coach Sean McDermott’s system. Despite a solid career to this point, it’s arguable that he was miscast by McDermott as a 4-3 defensive end. Rousseau looks to be playing with a renewed energy and a level of ferocity that could make him a nightmare for NFL offenses in 2026. After his first game at outside linebacker Rousseau should find plenty of votes toward the AFC Defensive Player of Week 1.
author: Matt Byham

title: Fernando’s Notebook: Bills 36, Texans 31, NFL Week 1
summary: Joe Brady’s head coaching debut with the Buffalo Bills ended in a win, and it took quarterback Josh Allen’s 34-yard touchdown to Joshua Palmer with 1:36 left to get there. Allen finished with 334 yards passing with two passing touchdowns and two more rushing scores. Here’s everything I wrote down as it unfolded. Let’s open […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter against the Houston Texans of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images Joe Brady’s head coaching debut with the Buffalo Bills ended in a win, and it took quarterback Josh Allen’s 34-yard touchdown to Joshua Palmer with 1:36 left to get there. Allen finished with 334 yards passing with two passing touchdowns and two more rushing scores. Here’s everything I wrote down as it unfolded. Let’s open the notebook… 1st Half A lot of 3 TEs early , but some of those formations were essentially what the Bills run with 12 personnel, simply with Dalton Kincaid in Tyrell Shavers’ role as a big wide receiver. Interesting. I like Joe Brady going for it on 4th and 2. It didn’t work, but you have Josh Allen and a powerful offense. Live and die by them. Good to see a healthy Terrel Bernard flying around to start the game. Base 3-4 D did okay against the run , but when in nickel, they struggled to stop it. Man-to-man with Damar Hamlin on the field is dumb. It cost the Bills a good opportunity to leave the field on a third down. Michael Hoecht is being used as the 2nd IDL on passing downs , but he hasn’t looked close to the guy we saw for two games last year — which is normal coming back from the injury he had. Buffalo’s D needs better IDL play. Deone Walker is the only consistent good piece there. Ed Oliver must be better — credit where it’s due, he did come up with the fumble recovery that set up Tyler Bass’ first field goal, but the group needs more of that. Can’t say I expect much from Landon Jackson or DeWayne Carter. T.J. Sanders didn’t look good in preseason and is out now. Gaines was invisible. Major room for improvement there. Kincaid looks good. Awesome catch to start the 2-minute drill — he’d finish the day with five catches for 130 yards. Brady had balls to call that PA play with his back against the wall against that pass rush. Nice how Brady has used his main pass catchers in several different positions — Kincaid inside and out, Khalil Shakir outside sometimes, D.J. Moore in the slot sometimes. Move the guys around, make it tough for the D, keep them thinking. Poor Reed Blankenship. That’s Josh Allen’s ball velocity — you think you can make a play on the ball just to see it zip past you. Moore appreciates it: that’s the 43-yard touchdown that pushed it to 24-14, and he’d close out his Buffalo debut with 5 catches for 100 yards. 24 first-half points , and you thought my Madden 27 simulation wasn’t realistic, huh? What was that by the D with one minute left in the 1st half? Bernard gets caught changing the play during the snap, covers the flat, and leaves the middle wide open for a big play. Awful — that’s the drive that set up Nico Collins’ 12-yard touchdown, cutting it to 24-21 at halftime. It’s not an easy matchup for anybody , but Nico Collins is winning too much versus Christian Benford. Josh certainly isn’t afraid of targeting Moore deep , and I love it. For now, our O is the real deal, our D is a work in progress. Josh in MVP form already, BTW . 2nd Half Good to see Tyler Bass playing consistent — a perfect 2-for-2 on field goals, 46 and 33 yards. Bills need that. Good debut by rookie punter Tommy Doman Jr. as well. Ray Davis continues to be a threat on kickoffs , but quiet debut by Greg Dortch. D allowed a lot of in-break route completions. Lack of pass rush, plus loose man coverage, plus no enforcers to make people pay for those catches in the middle of the field, isn’t a good combination. 2nd half by the D was way better. Forced Houston to go for it on a couple of 4th downs to keep drives alive. Avoided the mess of the last few minutes of the 1st half. Still, it seems this D lacks talent. Deone Walker might be the only potential true game changer, and he doesn’t even play on clear passing downs (he should, going forward). Next few weeks will be interesting to see if somebody else steps up. Other than the fumble, it’s been frustrating how our D wasn’t even close to potential INTs or other forced TOs — David Montgomery still walked away with a 3-touchdown day between the ground and through the air. For all the preseason hype, C.J. Gardner-Johnson was invisible. Josh Allen threw through some really tight windows in this game. It’s gonna be a fun season. Josh wasn’t afraid of giving his guys a chance downfield by any means. I know people will say that throw to Joshua Palmer was careless, but he literally threw it up high, versus single coverage. As a receiver you gotta be able to locate that ball quickly to at least compete for it. Palmer took too long and it almost became an INT by Kamari Lassiter. Awesome throw and catch on the very next play — the 34-yard game-winner with 1:36 left. Palmer as your 4th option is ok. You don’t pay that much for 4th options, though. Can this D close the game? That’s why Jim Leonhard is there. (Yes, they could). Maxwell Hairston’s mental mistake set the Texans up for a potential game-winning TD. What a time for it. Already in a rotation, that’s how you lose your job to the new guy. Deone Walker is a beast. What a move for such a big guy. He gotta stay on the field more often, also on clear passing downs. Greg Rousseau — he flashed during this game , with two strip-sacks on the day, the second one sealing it. That’s a guy the Bills need to see making those plays more often. Oliver and Bradley Chubb are the other two. Terrel Bernard is such a ball magnet. Love to see him closing the game out with the ball in his hands — recovering Rousseau’s game-sealing strip-sack — after everything he went through last season. If he can stay healthy, he’ll have a big season. As crazy as it sounds, with all the numbers Josh has put up during his career , there were a lot of times when he didn’t play free, didn’t have the weapons, or was stuck on a ball control/run-first offense that limited his numbers. Not anymore. He’s finally freed from the get-go. It’s clearly a different Bills team. They don’t seem to care about ball possession. Josh is in full command of the offense and has the green light to go and score on any play. They aren’t worried about the D “looking bad” because of the number of points on the scoreboard, as long as they make enough plays to make sure that number is lower than the one the Bills put up. Will it always work? Obviously not. But today it did. Offense put points on the board (as they usually do), and the defense, despite its shortcomings, closed the game. That’s what really matters at the end of the day — make the plays when it’s needed. 1-0. Go Bills! Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!
author: Fernando Schmude

title: Horns Up, Horns Down for Buffalo Bills NFL Week 1
summary: What a way for the Buffalo Bills to open up the 2026 NFL season! Winning a back-and-forth affair against the Houston Texans—in Houston, no less—is a big accomplishment for a Buffalo squad looking to forge a new identity under first-year head coach Joe Brady. The Bills were able to lock in a victory for their […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter against the Houston Texans of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images What a way for the Buffalo Bills to open up the 2026 NFL season! Winning a back-and-forth affair against the Houston Texans—in Houston, no less—is a big accomplishment for a Buffalo squad looking to forge a new identity under first-year head coach Joe Brady. The Bills were able to lock in a victory for their new head coach, winning 36-31 for their first win at (now) Reliant Stadium since J.P. Losman led the team to a win back in 2006. It wasn’t all roses, though, and even if it were, Bret Michaels told us long ago that every rose does have its thorn. There were plenty of players deserving of their flowers, but there are definitely some areas for improvement after Week 1. Our Horns Up and Horns Down are below. Let us know your thoughts about who and/or what stood out, in the comment section below! _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Up: WR DJ Moore The newest addition to the Bills’ offense was as-advertised today, making big plays in tight windows to give Buffalo’s offense big yardage. Moore wasn’t targeted until Buffalo’s third possession, but he had a huge second quarter. He made his first grab on a deep post off a play-action pass, and he nearly caught his first touchdown later in the quarter on a deep ball from quarterback Josh Allen. However, safety Calen Bullock tackled Moore while the ball was in flight, and given that the foul occurred in the end zone, it gave the Bills a first down at the one-yard line. Moore eventually did catch his first touchdown later in the quarter, as Houston safety Reed Blankenship’s near-interception went into Moore’s hands instead. Some fancy footwork kept him in bounds, and there was nobody around him to prevent him from finishing the 43-yard score. Moore caught three passes for 76 yards and that touchdown in the second quarter alone en route to a five-catch day for 100 yards and the aforementioned touchdown. Moore also had a team-high eight targets on the afternoon. Horns Up: QB Josh Allen Josh Allen was exceptional in Week 1. He scored two rushing touchdowns in the first half — one was a 21-yard scramble where he rolled right, found a lane, and dodged multiple defenders inside the five on his way to paydirt. The second was quarterback sneak where tight end Dawson Knox played the role of the schnowplow. Allen also threw the aforementioned touchdown pass to DJ Moore. The game plan featured some quick-hitters, but the protection plan up front helped keep Allen out of harm’s way for most of the afternoon. Buffalo chipped Houston’s edge rushers with different players, and their varied personnel packages gave Allen clean looks against a top-line defense. Overall, it was the best day Allen’s had in his career in Houston. He was efficient, he took checkdowns, he found big plays with his arm and with his legs, and he gave the Bills’ defense a chance to win it in the end, and they obliged him. Allen completed 20-of-29 passes for 334 yards and two touchdowns, adding six carries for 23 yards and two more scores on the ground. Horns Down: Defensive Secondary Buffalo’s new-look secondary faced a strong test in trying to stop wide receiver Nico Collins, and they didn’t do a particularly great job at it. Collins killed the Bills throughout the first half, catching all three of his targets for 46 yards and a score. Additionally, the Bills were called for far too many penalties in the secondary. Safety Damar Hamlin and rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun were each called for a hold, and cornerback Christian Benford was called for pass interference. Hamlin’s penalty erased a stop on 3rd & 9 that immediately led to a touchdown by running back David Montgomery. Later, Benford’s penalty gave the Texans great field position at the end of the first half to set up a touchdown throw to Collins. Granted, they mostly stepped up when they needed to on the final drive of the game, but there were too many instances of players losing their assignment. There are going to be growing pains on defense with a new system implemented by defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, but the early returns were not great. Horns Down: Run Defense There were some encouraging early signs that the Bills would be able to bottle up David Montgomery, but unfortunately, the much-maligned Houston offensive line was able to clear space consistently on the ground. Montgomery has always been tough to get on the ground, and Buffalo’s stop unit had a tough time tackling on Sunday. Montgomery had touchdown runs of one yard and 18 yards in the first half, as he carried 13 times for 52 yards in the half. Woody Marks acted as a solid change-of-pace, as well. Montgomery had 60 rushing yards and two touchdowns, and he also added three catches for 19 yards and a receiving touchdown to his line. Marks had 36 rushing yards on eight carries, and while Houston averaged just 3.8 yards per rush on the day, it felt like they were able to gain the yards they needed in multiple clutch situations. Horns Down: Discipline and Penalties Buffalo was called for just too many flags on the afternoon. This has been a pattern so far this year, as the Bills were heavily penalized in the preseason, as well. A holding penalty on defensive back Sam Franklin Jr. wiped out a great kickoff return by running back Ray Davis at the end of the first half; Franklin Jr. was also whistled for a chop block early in the second half that negated a solid punt return from wide receiver Greg Dortch. Left tackle Dion Dawkins was whistled for holding, as was left guard Alec Anderson, and the Bills even managed to commit ineligible-man-downfield penalties on consecutive plays in the first half. There were quite a few penalties in the game, as the teams combined for 17 flags and 191 penalty yards, so maybe there’s an argument that second-year referee Alex Moore and his crew were a bit flag-happy. The fact remains, though, that Buffalo needs to be cleaner in its operations moving forward. Horns Up: TE Dalton Kincaid Buffalo’s top tight end made some big plays for his quarterback in scramble-drill action. He hauled in a 38-yard pass in spectacular fashion right before the two-minute warning in the first half. Then, he made his second grab of the day on a third-quarter scoring drive, sticking with Allen on a rollout to find a nine-yard gain between two Texans defenders. Kincaid found space for big gains on a second field goal drive in the second half, and he also made the key reception off a play-action pass to set up wide receiver Joshua Palmer’s go-ahead touchdown in the fourth quarter. Overall, Kincaid notched five catches on six targets for 130 yards in what was an incredible first game of the 2026 season for him. Horns Up: OLB Greg Rousseau The Bills forced two turnovers, and both of them came on strip-sacks of C.J. Stroud from Groot. On Houston’s first possession of the game, Rousseau came around the edge and took the ball from Stroud, forcing a fumble that defensive tackle Ed Oliver (who had a good game himself) recovered. On Houston’s final possession, Rousseau strip-sacked Stroud once again, bringing a third-down play to an end when linebacker Terrel Bernard, who also had a game-high 12 tackles on the afternoon, recovered it. Rousseau had four tackles and five quarterback hits to go with his two strip-sacks, but perhaps the most impressive play he made all afternoon came in coverage against tight end Dalton Schultz. The big tight end ran an angle route off the edge, and Rousseau, who has converted to a stand-up outside linebacker after having played defensive end for his whole career, not only stuck with Schultz, but he laid out and broke up the pass. title: Buffalo Bills HC Joe Brady joins rare list with win over Houston Texans
summary: Joe Brady’s first regular-season game as head coach of the Buffalo Bills ended the same way his tenure began — with a win. Buffalo defeated the Houston Texans 36-31 Sunday, giving Brady his first victory as an NFL head coach and putting him on a short list in Bills history.  Brady became just the fourth head coach in franchise history […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills enters the field prior to the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Joe Brady’s first regular-season game as head coach of the Buffalo Bills ended the same way his tenure began — with a win. Buffalo defeated the Houston Texans 36-31 Sunday, giving Brady his first victory as an NFL head coach and putting him on a short list in Bills history. Brady became just the fourth head coach in franchise history to win his regular-season debut with Buffalo, joining Marv Levy, Rex Ryan, and his immediate predecessor, Sean McDermott. That’s some interesting company. Levy was the first, taking over midway through the 1986 season and beating the Pittsburgh Steelers, 16-12, on November 9. He would eventually lead Buffalo to four consecutive Super Bowl appearances and earn a place in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Nearly three decades later, Ryan opened his Bills tenure with a 27-14 win over the Indianapolis Colts on September 13, 2015. McDermott followed two years later, beating the New York Jets, 21-12, on September 10, 2017. Now Brady gets to add his name to the list. The 36-year-old was promoted to head coach in January after an extensive search to replace McDermott. Brady was already a familiar face inside One Bills Drive, having joined the organization as quarterbacks coach in 2022 before taking over as offensive coordinator during the 2023 season. He held that job full time for the past two seasons before being named the 21st head coach in franchise history on Jan. 27. There are much bigger goals ahead for Brady and the Bills in 2026. But the first one is officially checked off the list. Joe Brady is 1-0, as he’ll certainly remind us soon.
