title: Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen ties Frank Gore on NFL rushing TD list
summary: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen just keeps climbing.  The dual-threat quarterback found the end zone with his legs for the second time Sunday against the Houston Texans, giving him 81 rushing touchdowns for his career and moving him into a tie with running back Frank Gore on the NFL’s all-time list.  Allen’s second score came […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 07: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates a 40-yard rushing touchdown against the Cincinnati Bengals during the fourth quarter at Highmark Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen just keeps climbing. The dual-threat quarterback found the end zone with his legs for the second time Sunday against the Houston Texans, giving him 81 rushing touchdowns for his career and moving him into a tie with running back Frank Gore on the NFL’s all-time list. Allen’s second score came in the second quarter, giving Buffalo a 17-14 lead over the Houston Texans. And, yes, we are talking about a quarterback. Allen entered the season already sitting alone atop the NFL record book for rushing touchdowns by a quarterback. His 79 were four more than Cam Newton, who finished his career with 75. Now, just two quarters into the 2026 season, Allen has moved onto another list filled almost entirely with running backs. At 81 ground scores, Allen is tied with Gore and Ottis Anderson for 20th on the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list. Gore scored his 81 rushing touchdowns over a 16-year career that included one season in Buffalo. Anderson reached the mark during a 14-year career spent with the St. Louis Cardinals and New York Giants. Allen needed considerably less time. He’s now in his ninth NFL season, and, with another rushing touchdown, both Gore and Anderson will be behind him. For now, though, Allen has 81. And another line in the record book has his name on it.

title: The Optimist: Worst Luke Kuechly tribute ever
summary: Former Carolina Panthers linebacker Luke Kuechly, who famously wore the #59 jersey for his entire career, entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame this year. He was one of the best defenders in Panthers history, famous for being a stout, athletic, and cerebral linebacker who turned the middle of the field into a nightmare for […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jimmy Horn Jr. #15 of the Carolina Panthers is tackled against the Chicago Bears during the first half of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Carolina Panthers linebacker Luke Kuechly, who famously wore the #59 jersey for his entire career, entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame this year. He was one of the best defenders in Panthers history, famous for being a stout, athletic, and cerebral linebacker who turned the middle of the field into a nightmare for opposing offenses. Yesterday, in a loving, if misguided, tribute to Luke’s absence on the field, the Carolina Panthers kept anything stout, athletic, or cerebral from touching the field on defense and allowed a symbolic 59 points to the Chicago Bears in the season opener. It was the most points allowed in franchise history and, combined with the Panthers own 37 points, the highest scoring Week 1 game in NFL history. If we told you even two days ago that Bryce Young was going to throw for 361 yards and account for four touchdowns then you would have been pretty optimistic about the Panthers chances in their season opener. Unfortunately, baffling penalties, inopportune turnovers, and an embarrassing defensive effort turned a shoot out into a firing squad. The defense It’s tough sledding when you open your season against what is expected to be one of the best offenses in the NFL and you’re starting your third string outside linebacker. You’ll be expected to struggle rushing the passer, containing scrambles, and holding the edge in the rushing game. It’s also tough when you have multiple starters and contributors on defense who were not with the team in training camp. Tough is one thing. Giving up four touchdowns, out of a total eight surrendered, on plays of twenty yards or more is another flavor of avalanche entirely. Caleb Williams averaged 6.6 yards per attempt and was the Bears least efficient rusher with more than one carry. D’Andre Swift (6.9 yards per attempt) and Kyle Monangai (10.0 yards per attempt) combined with Williams for 289 yards rushing and six touchdowns on the ground. If Ejiro Evero’s seat wasn’t hot coming into the season then it certainly is now. That said, there were flashes of pressure and good linebacker play. We know the secondary has the talent to compete. They did manage to hold expected super star tight end Colston Loveland to a whole two targets and zero catches in the game. Give these guys the Panthers’ traditional four to five weeks to pull themselves together and they could be a good unit down the stretch. Could be. I hope. Jimmy Horn, Jr That wasn’t it, Jimmy. One more week of this, at most, and the Panthers should be looking for new blood in the return game. The offense Atlanta Bryce made a rare appearance in Charlotte yesterday, blasting a mile ahead of his career average game and captaining the offense to a largely respectable showing in Brad Idzik’s debut as play caller. There are some kinks to work out and zero guarantee that they’ll look like this again before December, but you could hardly have asked for a better realistic start on offense. Jalen Coker was everything we had hoped for when Tetairoa McMillan was blanketed. McMillan still managed to find success in the second half despite an abundance of attention from the Bears secondary. And that was all with more production from the tight end position than it feels like we have ever seen in Dave Canales’ tenure. It’s funny how many yards and targets there are to go around in a 37 attempt, 361 yard day. The volume is probably exaggerated, but if that’s the gist of what we can expect in the air with Idzik calling plays then color me excited. Unfortunately, it wasn’t a balanced effort. The ground game struggled heavily. As with the defense, multiple injuries along the line depressed expectations for the rushing attack, but what we saw was still disappointing. A limited ability to gain even three yards when the chips were down hampered this offense and kept them from keeping up with the Bears. The only bright side, and I’m scared to even publish this lest it changes today, is that Jonathon Brooks escaped the game without further injury. Same as with the defense, the seeds shined through in the season opener. There is still a lot of work for them to do to prove that they can be a consistent threat to opposing teams with their offense. Well, not the same as with the defense. Maybe there is less work to do on this side of the ball. @ Atlanta There’s not much more I can say about 59 points. That’s bad. We’re not going to change schemes or onboard 11 new starters. We also, as a fan base, as promised, are not going to overreact to Week 1. Now, to overreact to Week 1, scoring 37 points a game—the Carolina Panthers current 2026 regular season average—would have seen them as a 15-2 team with at least one playoff win in 2025. That’s statistics. On the one hand, I’d expect both sides of the ball to come back to Earth over the course of September before landing on an actual identity through October. That story arc will be true for most teams in the NFL. On the other hand, the sky’s the limit if this is the team’s cold start to the 2026 season. Next week will be an interesting test against Bijan Robinson and whatever dime store quarterback the Falcons think looks healthy. Even if the defense manages to pitch a shutout, we still might not know a lot about them entering Week 3 against the Cleveland Browns. Losing a season opener is nothing new. Losing one while showing promise, sadly, is. I’ll take it for now.

title: Panthers vs. Bears Week 1: A shootout to open the season
summary: The offense looked very good, but the defense was about as bad as we’ve ever seen it as the Carolina Panthers dropped their season opener to the Chicago Bears, 59-37. First Quarter The Bears got the ball first, and on the first play D’Andre Swift ripped right through the middle of the defense for a […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers looks to pass the ball during the fourth quarter of the game against the Chicago Bears at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The offense looked very good, but the defense was about as bad as we’ve ever seen it as the Carolina Panthers dropped their season opener to the Chicago Bears, 59-37. First Quarter The Bears got the ball first, and on the first play D’Andre Swift ripped right through the middle of the defense for a big gain. However, it was called back for a holding penalty. Two plays later, two offseason acquisitions made their first impacts. Bobby Okereke punched the ball out from Luther Burden III, and rookie Will Lee IV recovered it. Bryce Young hit Tommy Tremble across the middle to get the drive started. A few plays later he found Jalen Coker deep down the right sideline, who made a spectacular toe tapping catch inside the five. The Panthers scored a couple plays later on a pass to Darren Waller, but he was called for a questionable pass interference. No matter. A couple plays later, Young eluded pressure and found Chuba Hubbard wide open for a touchdown. The Bears responded. D’Andre Swift picked up some more big chunks that weren’t called back. Caleb Williams found space with some scrambles as well. The last of those came deep in Panthers territory, and he scampered down the right sideline for a game tying touchdown. The Panthers got good field position after the kickoff missed the landing zone, but they didn’t do anything with it. Xavier Legette dropped a bubble screen then Young was sacked on third down. A short punt gave the Bears their own good field position. A couple plays into the drive Lee let Rome Odinze run free and was very lackadaisical trying to recover ground. He got mossed at the catch point, setting up 1st and goal. Two plays later, Swift punched in the Bears second touchdown. The first quarter ended with the Panthers going three and out for the second straight drive. Second Quarter A penalty on the punt gave the Bears the ball in Panthers territory to start their next drive. Kyle Monangai was wide open on a checkdown to big up a big gain. On the next play, Caleb Williams threw a dime to Cole Kmet, who pulled the ball in for the Bears’ third touchdown in as many possessions. The Panthers answered quickly. Young found Coker across the middle for a nice gain. After a short run for Hubbard, Young went deep for Coker again, and he reeled it in behind the defense for a 51 yard touchdown. The defense finally pulled their weight. They limited the Bears offense to a couple of short gains and brought up 4th and inches. The Bears went for it despite being on their own 20. The defense bowed up and stuffed the sneak. Tetairoa McMillan got his first catch of the season on the ensuing drive to take the offense inside the 10. After an exchange of penalties, Young bobbed and weaved on a scramble and weathered a big hit to tie the game up at 21. The defense once again forced a three and out after Trevis Gipson made a great backside tackle against his former team. This time the Bears punted, and Jimmy Horn Jr. completely whiffed on the punt and muffed it back to Chicago. The defense held up though and forced a field goal. Young found Jonathon Brooks up the sideline on a scramble drill for a 50 yard gain. That got the Panthers into field goal range, and that’s what they had to settle for. Ryan Fitzgerald knocked through the 44 yarder. Jaelan Phillips sacked Caleb Williams on the first play of the two minute drive, but Williams was able to make a highlight throw on 3rd and long to keep the drive alive. A few plays later, Williams broke contain and again took off down a wide open left sideline for a 29 yard touchdown. The Panthers tried to force the issue in the last 22 seconds. Young got picked off trying to make a play, but it was an inconsequential interception with just five seconds left. Third Quarter The Panthers got the ball first coming out of the half and unceremoniously went three and out. The Bears did the same thanks to a sack by Princely Umanmielen. Jimmy Horn Jr. almost fumbled again but was fortunately down before the ball came out. Chuba Hubbard was a bit more assertive running the ball and tight ends Darren Waller and Tommy Tremble had some nice catches to move the offense down the field with haste. They ended up on the doorstep of the goal line, and Hubbard was able to punch in his second touchdown of the game. The Bears marched down the field with a handful of modest games. The defense forced the Bears into a 2nd and 20 after a run stuff and a holding penalty, but Derrick Brown was called for roughing the passer to gift the Bears a first down at the 11 yard line. Three handoffs to D’Andre Swift ended with the Bears in the end zone once again. Another illegal kick gave the Panthers good field position, and another in breaker to Jalen Coker crossed midfield. The Panthers found themselves in a 4th and short and left the offense on the field, but Young overthrew McMillan on a corner route. On the first play after the turnover, Kyle Monangai ran right through the middle of the defense for a 61 yard touchdown. Fourth Quarter Young found McMillan wide open across the middle of the field for a huge gain, but he had the ball punched out when he got tackled. The defense got the Bears into a couple of third downs but they kept leaving large gaps in coverage and let the Bears pick up easy first downs. Caleb Williams ran the ball all the way down to the goal line. Bobby Brown tipped a pass to himself and picked it off, but it was called back because Derrick Brown was lined up in the neutral zone. A couple plays later, Williams found Johdae Walker uncovered in the end zone for a knockout punch touchdown. Young shoveled a ball to Hubbard under pressure for a 29 yard gain. He then completed back to back passes for McMillan for another 33 to get inside the five. He found Mitchell Evans for a touchdown, but it was called back for a pick by Jalen Coker. Coker made amends a couple plays later by shedding a tackle and waltzing in for a touchdown. The extra point was blocked just because this game was nuts. In a fitting way to close the game, the Panthers defense had the Bears in a 3rd and 2 needing a stop for one last desperation attempt to get back into the game, but Trevis Gipson jumped offsides on the hard count and gave up the first down. Two plays later, D’Andre Swift ripped right through the middle of the defense once again for yet another touchdown. The backups came in to finish the game. Overall Outlook On one hand, the offense was encouraging. Bryce Young pushed the ball down the field and was aggressive fitting the ball into windows. It was one of the better games he’s played in his career, and it was by far the best he’s played in a season opener. On the other hand, the defense was as bad as we’ve seen it. The Bears offense won what felt like 80% of the plays. They were gashed in the run game, couldn’t get Caleb Williams on the ground, and left huge openings for receivers. Compounding the problems by the defense were self inflicted mistakes by players that the Panthers are counting on. Derrick Brown committed two penalties in the red zone that gave the Bears new life after a rare defensive win and Tetairoa McMillan fumbled away a must score possession. Those have to be cleaned up, and it goes without saying that the defense has to figure something out if this team is going to compete for anything. You’re not going to win any games giving up 300 yards on the ground. The Panthers will try to tighten things up as they get ready for their first divisional game next week against the Faclons.

title: 10 Bears Takes: Run Game Dominance, Caleb Williams Improvement, History Made
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season is under way, and I’m not sure the Chicago Bears could have had a more emphatic offensive performance than they did on Sunday afternoon in Carolina. Now, it’s always important not to overreact to anything that happens in Week 1 (we’ll take more on that in a few), but the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball against Bobby Okereke #58 of the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season is under way, and I’m not sure the Chicago Bears could have had a more emphatic offensive performance than they did on Sunday afternoon in Carolina. Now, it’s always important not to overreact to anything that happens in Week 1 (we’ll take more on that in a few), but the offense did something we’ve never seen before. Without getting too much into the weeds right now, let’s dive into our first regular season edition of 10 Bears Takes for the 2026 regular season. 1. Once again, the 2026 opener continues to prove how unpredictable Week 1 can be. Man, what a weekend, huh? Once again, the NFL showed why they are king, even if the two opening games of the weekend didn’t deliver the same way many had hoped. Across the league, plenty of results didn’t match expectations, starting with Thursday’s game, where the Los Angeles Rams were run out of Australia by the San Francisco 49ers. To make matters worse, offseason prize Myles Garrett will miss at least four games after undergoing a knee scope. Surprises on Sunday included the New Orleans Saints taking the Detroit Lions down to the wire in overtime, the New York Jets dominating the Titans in Tennessee, and the Atlanta Falcons on their QB3 hanging with Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers on the road. While the results of the week make it easy to conclude, no matter how “crazy” things might feel in the moment, we should have learned to let things play out for a few months into the season. For example, the Las Vegas Raiders beat the New England Patriots 20-13. A few months later, the Patriots were in the Super Bowl, and the Raiders were firing their head coach (and staff) after a disastrous first season. Heck, even Justin Fields went off for a 9.9 yards-per-attempt average and three total touchdowns, before being benched two months later. Long story short, it’s best to hold all of our hot takes for at least a few more weeks. Even for as exciting as the Bears’ win was on Sunday, let’s see how things play out into October. 2. Don’t be fooled by last year’s results; the Carolina Panthers’ defense should be much improved. No matter the opponent, 59 points is something Bears fans have never seen this team accomplish before. Seriously, what the Bears’ offense did on Sunday is something fans have never seen their favorite team accomplish before. In total, Chicago hung 59 points, 552 yards, and 70 plays. Even more impressive, they ran for 291 yards on 39 carries for a 7.5-yard average, and six touchdowns on the ground. Through the air, they were as efficient as they have been with Caleb Williams going 21-for-29 (72.4%) for 269 passing yards and two passing touchdowns, while adding 65 yards and two touchdowns on the ground. Even more impressive, he averaged 9.3 yards per attempt. In total, the offense scored nine times on 14 drives, punting just twice. One of those drives came at the end of the half, and it was a run play. We’ll dive into more specifics on each aspect of their offensive attack here in a few, but what this group did, especially in Week 1, should not be overlooked, even if it’s unlikely to be replicated many times this season. During the offseason, head coach Ben Johnson went on record saying he wanted to have the league’s highest-scoring offense ever. While that might feel like some super lofty expectations, it’s worth noting that the team with the current record (the 2013 Denver Broncos) did not crack 59 (or more) at any point during their impressive 16-game campaign. They did, however, hang 50-plus three times, as well as 40-plus. Although lofty, the Bears are technically out-pacing the Broncos one game into the season. Even if I don’t believe they can break the record for points-per-game, it’s a great start, and again, not something we’ve ever seen a Bears offense accomplish. Buckle up, Bears fans. The defense is likely to struggle, which means these types of offensive outbursts will be musts for them to win ball games. 3. Speaking of the offense, the subtle differences in Caleb Williams’ game were noticeable and, more importantly, promising. As noted above, Williams was above the high-water mark set by his head coach, with a 72.4% completion rate. A big part of that, beyond an impressive offensive outburst, was how often he simply took the checkdown. He started five-for-five before throwing one away, and finished the first half 12-of-15 for 196 passing yards, a touchdown, and a 141.0 passer rating. For those who believe “settling” for checkdowns results in lower efficiency numbers, Sunday was his second-highest yards-per-attempt in his career, and a 15.19 total EPA (best of his career). Simply put, Williams taking what the defense gave him resulted in higher efficiency, fewer incompletions, and was a good contribution to Week 1’s highest-scoring offense. Expanding out further to the entire offense, Sunday’s game was a great example of how much opposing defenses are going to struggle to contain this group all season. Everyone, including me, agrees that tight end Colston Loveland is one of, if not the best, offensive weapons the team has. After all, he was their most dangerous pass catcher down the stretch last season. Yet, somehow, the Panthers’ defense held Loveland to no catches (or yards) on two targets, but still found a way to give up 552 yards and 59 points. In the passing game, veteran Kalif Raymond led all pass catchers with eight catches for 88 yards. Luther Burden factored in with five catches for 63 yards, and Rome Odunze had the catch of the day, mossing Carolina’s rookie cornerback. In total, the Bears had 261 total yards through the air, despite not getting Loveland or rookie Zavion Thomas involved. The only touchdown came from Jahdae Walker’s 1-yard catch to ice the game. What should scare defensive coordinators is that Johnson cannot only feature less-likely heroes like Raymond and Walker, but also bludgeon opposing defenses on the ground. We’ll get into the team’s rushing attack and D’Andre Swift’s much-deserved extension later, but hanging more rushing yards (291) than passing yards (261) shows how versatile and unpredictable this group can be. Even if fans shouldn’t expect 59 points or 500-plus yards, they can expect their head coach (and offensive play caller) to find every potential avenue to success for his offense on a weekly basis. 4. Much was made of how the Bears handled their defensive acquisition this offseason; after one week, there’s plenty to be concerned about moving forward without serious adjustments from defensive coordinator Dennis Allen. Make no mistake: there’s plenty to be excited about in 2026 for this Bears team. That said, if Sunday was any indication of how much this defense will struggle, everyone should have serious concerns moving forward. I’m not one to sit here and continue to poo-poo Bryce Young and his development heading into Year 4. In fact, I’m someone who believes the conversation for the top quarterback in the 2023 class between Young and C.J. Stroud is closer than many want to admit. That said, allowing him to go for 361 yards, a 110.3 rating, and a total EPA of (9.18) is just not going to win this unit many awards. Many, including myself, expect the Panthers’ offense to take a step forward this season, but that big of a step forward? Highly unlikely. The lack of pressure on Young was a concern, but the missed tackles and lack of gap integrity were more concerning. The open-field tackling at the second level was atrocious, and the team’s top-2 cornerbacks looked slow and overmatched. Outside of the two takeaways, there wasn’t a whole lot to like about the Bears’ defensive performance on Sunday. The…

title: Bears vs. Panthers: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and Everybody Blocks
summary: The Chicago Bears’ 59-37 win over the Carolina Panthers was a perfect way to kick off the season because, while so much went right, there’s still plenty that didn’t for head coach Ben Johnson to focus on. Most notably, the defense that allowed Carolina to get 478 yards of offense and 24 first downs. In […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after his rushing touchdown against the Carolina Panthers in the first quarter of a game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears’ 59-37 win over the Carolina Panthers was a perfect way to kick off the season because, while so much went right, there’s still plenty that didn’t for head coach Ben Johnson to focus on. Most notably, the defense that allowed Carolina to get 478 yards of offense and 24 first downs. In his postgame press conference, Johnson was asked how they can solve some of their defensive issues, and he used that as a way to discuss them getting better overall. “We talked about with the team, find a way to get to the plane with a win. And we did that,” Johnson said in his postgame press conference. “We accomplished that. Now we’re in a race to improve — in all three phases and collectively as a team. That’s what we gotta do. So we’ll take a look at the tape. What can we get better at? You know, it only gets harder from here on out. And yet, I told those guys, you’d like to think in a long season like this, we’re playing our worst football early on, and we continue to get better and better and better. That’s really the message right there. All three phases, we all got to get better each and every week.” Johnson has set a high bar for his team in 2026, and his offense’s performance will obviously make him happy. They racked up 552 yards of offense, had 26 first downs, and were 71.4% (10-14) on third-down tries. But the defense’s woes and their 12 penalties (for 57 yards) matched the 12 times his team was penalized in Week 1 last season. One aspect of the game that everyone will be pleased with is the 291 yards rushing, Chicago’s most in a game since getting 302 on September 9, 1984. Johnson acknowledged how his entire offense had a hand in it. “The story of the game ended up being the rushing and, so, the offensive line — shout out to them,” he said. “But it was collective with the tight ends, the receivers were blocking their tails off as well. And Swifty (D’Andre Swift) and (Kyle) Monangai both were able to do a great job there. Caleb added quite a bit with his feet also.” Ben gave the offensive line a game ball in his locker room speech, and their o-line spokesman, right guard Jonah Jackson, made sure to spread the love, saying, “It took all of us, tight ends, wideouts, backs, QB, and a shout out to the playcaller.” The 59-37 win was good, but the Bears are a long way from being the best. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing time breakdowns and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE Caleb Williams is just the 4th quarterback in NFL history with at least 250 passing yards, 50 rushing yards, 2 touchdown passes, 2 rushing touchdowns, and a passer rating over 120 in the same game. He also hit 70% completion for the sixth time in his NFL career, but for the first time under Ben Johnson. His 10 rushes, 65 rushing yards, and 2 rushing TDs are all career highs. Kalif Raymond’s 8 receptions are a career high, as was Kyle Monangai’s 61-yard run. Jahdae Walker only had one catch for a touchdown, but he left an impact on this game in other ways, including the final block on Monangai’s touchdown. “I saw Jahdae chasing down and making sure that wasn’t just a big play, but a touchdown,” Kalif Raymond said via the team site. “I mean, it’s a huge play for Kyle, but Jahdae’s out there taking guys to make sure it happens. I mean, it goes from a big play, a first down to a touchdown. That’s a testament to the guys blocking. I think Lu (Luther Burden III) had a big block too … so just all the stuff working together, and that’s what you want, especially for the backs we have.” Jahdae Walker combined video. Block on special teams, block on offense, and touchdown catch. pic.twitter.com/7S24DcVoIQ — ✶Ⓜ️𝕒𝕣𝕔𝕦𝕤 ▶️✶ (@_MarcusD3_) September 13, 2026 DEFENSE Tyrique Stevenson, who had a rough game in coverage, led the Bears with 9 tackles on defense. Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman had 8 tackles on defense, a QB hit, and a pass defended, plus 2 more tackles on special teams. Rookie Malik Muhammad II, who started at nickel but kicked outside to corner when Stevenson was dinged up, had 3 tackles, 2 pases defende, and an interception. Cam Lewis, who got the start at safety but also got some reps at nickel, had 6 tackles. Devin Bush has 6 tackles, a fumble recovery, and a QB hit. Jaylon Johnson had 3 tackles and a forced fumble. Montez Sweat had 2 tackles, a tackle for loss, and a sack. Kentavius Street also had 2 tackles, a tackle for loss, and a sack. SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos missed the landing zone a couple of times, drawing penalties, but he made all 8 extra points and a 40-yard field goal. Tory Taylor (2 punts for 102 yards) hit a banana ball that the Panthers muffed, leading to a Kaden Davis recovery. Raymond had a 23-yard punt return. Josh Blackwell had 4 kickoff returns and a 21.3 average. Roschon Johnson had 4 special teams tackles. Long snapper Beau Gardner had a tackle. Walker had a couple of special teams tackles. Dayo Odeyingbo blocked an extra point. What is this "banana ball" Ben Johnson is talking about? Look at the angle Tory Taylor strikes this punt. It starts outside towards the sideline, but then comes all the way back inside the hashes. Hard to track, especially with this kind of hang time. title: Bears offense shows no rust in shootout win over Panthers
summary: Going into the 2026-27 regular season, Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson indicated that his goal was for Chicago to break the NFL’s record for single-season scoring on offense. Purely based on how the team performed in Week 1 against the Panthers, it appears that it’s on its way to achieving that goal. It wasn’t […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears looks to pass against the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Going into the 2026-27 regular season, Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson indicated that his goal was for Chicago to break the NFL’s record for single-season scoring on offense. Purely based on how the team performed in Week 1 against the Panthers, it appears that it’s on its way to achieving that goal. It wasn’t always pretty on the defensive side of the ball, but the Bears started the new year with a 59-37 win over the Carolina Panthers to begin the season with a 1-0 record. The game marked the highest-scoring season debut the Bears have had in franchise history, as well as the most points they’ve scored in a single game under Johnson. To kick off the season, these are our day-after takeaways from the Bears’ victory. Caleb Williams makes it look easy Finishing out the Bears’ season opener, Caleb Williams scored four touchdowns with no interceptions, surpassing 260 passing yards and reaching a passer rating in the triple digits in an incredible performance to kick off his third year with Chicago. He looked accurate moving the ball down the field, he looked poised avoiding pressure in and out of the pocket, he knew when to throw the ball away or take off running, and his patented elastic arm was on full display, too. Any time you can lead your team to a performance scoring over 50 points, it’s worth celebrating. Williams looked the part in Week 1, showing off improved accuracy and demonstrating the poise that helped Chicago secure the NFC North crown in the second half of the season. He ended the year ranked No. 20 in the NFL in PFN QB Impact Scoring , and once the scores are solidified for the week, he’ll surely rank higher than that after Week 1. The best RB duo in the NFL? Both of the Bears’ primary running backs scored touchdowns on Sunday, as D’Andre Swift ended the game with two rushing touchdowns, and Kyle Monangai ended up with one. Both running backs had big gains against Carolina, with Swift gaining 32 yards on one run and Monangai picking up 61 yards on a touchdown run in the second half. Chicago’s offensive line continued to look the part, executing assignments up front and paving the way for its running backs to find open running lanes in between the tackles. Swift especially showed off impressive burst and a relentless demeanor on a snap-by-snap basis, while Monangai’s massive touchdown run played a big role in the Bears creating separation in an offensive shootout. As easy as it can be to be impressed with how Williams threw the ball on Sunday, the Bears’ running back tandem looked the part, as well. Defense is a major concern The Bears ultimately broke away thanks to great play from their offense, but their defense was a lot more rocky than many in the fanbase would have hoped this week. They gave up 37 points on Sunday, with the secondary giving up multiple big plays in coverage. In particular, Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson looked especially shaky throughout the course of the afternoon. It wasn’t all bad, as rookies Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad both made some nice plays. Montez Sweat and Kentavius Street both contributed sacks on Sunday. There’s a lot for defensive coordinator Dennis Allen to get locked down, and the hope is that the return of Xavier Woods at safety will free up Cam Lewis into more of a chess piece role, rather than a full-time starter. Obviously, Chicago won’t score 59 points every game, as fun as that would be. It will need to sharpen a lot of things on defense going forward. Weapons for days If you told me that the Bears would score 59 points against the Panthers without Colston Loveland tallying a single reception all afternoon, I would have thought you were crazy. That says a lot about how much other weapons stepped up for Chicago on Sunday. Kalif Raymond led the team with eight receptions for 84 yards. Luther Burden III contributed five catches on five targets for 63 yards. Rome Odunze had a stellar 47-yard jump ball grab early in the game, and both Cole Kmet and Jahdae Walker secured receiving touchdowns against Carolina’s porous defense. Ryan Poles has invested heavily in the Bears’ group of pass-catchers, and that heavy investment paid off with how many players were able to contribute in Week 1.

title: Bears and Panthers Scorigami starts 2026 with a bang
summary: The final score between the Chicago Bears and Carolina Panthers has never happened before in NFL history. When we see an unprecedented score in an NFL game, it’s called Scoigami. There haven’t been too may times where a team scored 59 points, so that’s a dead giveaway. The 59-37 final was the first time that […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Cole Kmet #85 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after a touchdown in the second quarter of a game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The final score between the Chicago Bears and Carolina Panthers has never happened before in NFL history. When we see an unprecedented score in an NFL game, it’s called Scoigami . There haven’t been too may times where a team scored 59 points, so that’s a dead giveaway. The 59-37 final was the first time that has happened in NFL history. It is the 1096th unique score in NFL history. Normally when we get a Scorigami, it’s because something weird happened in the game like going for 2 or missed extra points. This one wasn’t that. The Bears just laid the smack down. Chicago scored 14 points in the first, third, and fourth quarters along with a 17-point third quarter. Standard fare. We had a late extra point blocked, but 59-38 also has never happened. During the 2025 season we saw four Scorigamis including one in Week 1: Bills beat Ravens 41-40 Cowboys and Packers tie 40-40 Texans beat Jaguars 36-29 Bills beat Buccaneers 44-32 We can expect a few more Scorigamis in 2026, but the Bears and Panthers started the new year with a bang. While we expected more this season, we didn’t expect it so soon. The Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings’ 39-22 score had never happened before either.

title: 3 things we learned from the Bengals’ Week 1 win over the Bucs
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals held on for a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Here’s what we learned. The defense is hungry and confident After a long offseason of conjecture, we finally know what the defense can actually do. Yes, they’re still a little leaky, missing tackles. And they were flagged for being line up […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 13: Cade Otton #88 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers is tackled by Demetrius Knight Jr. #44 of the Cincinnati Bengals during the second half of the game at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals held on for a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Here’s what we learned. The defense is hungry and confident After a long offseason of conjecture, we finally know what the defense can actually do. Yes, they’re still a little leaky, missing tackles. And they were flagged for being line up offsides multiple times. But they’re bold and chomping at the bit to make a big play. It’s somewhat similar to those playmaking defenses in 2021 and 2022. Bend but don’t break, with some turnovers in between that give the offense a nice boost. The four fumbles and four sacks were a lot more than we would’ve seen out of the defenses in 2024 and 2025, and three early fumble recoveries are what gave the Bengals a nice cushion for the game. It’s not an injury thing; Joe Burrow just needs real reps to warm up For a QB with as high of a football IQ as Joe Burrow, his interception was a head scratcher. The only real explanation is that Burrow just needs some time to get back into a rhythm in the regular season. It kinda makes sense when you consider how little the seventh-year QB has played in the preseason. The good news is, he was able to do just enough to secure a victory in Week 1, so the offense should only be better from here on out. Touches on offense are going to be more evenly distributed With Ja’Marr Chase being the focus of the Bucs’ secondary and only getting four targets, Burrow looked elsewhere. Chase Brown had six targets, which was as many as Tee Higgins. But it was Mike Gesicki who led the team with seven targets. Drew Sample, Andrei Iosivas, and Samaje Perine had three targets, and Dohnte Meyers and Tanner Hudson even got a look each. And the run-to-pass ratio was solid, with 27 runs and 35 passes. There has been talk of a move to a more traditional approach on offense with Dan Pitcher more involved in play design, but now it seems to be official.

title: Bengals beating Bucs without offensive stars shining bodes well for rest of the season
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals’ 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was a fairly tightly contested affair. You can take so many things away — both positively and negatively — from this game. One thing that is a bit of both, but we will spin as a positive, was the team winning despite Ja’Marr Chase and […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 13: Bryan Cook #6 of the Cincinnati Bengals walks off the field after 33-27 win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals’ 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was a fairly tightly contested affair. You can take so many things away — both positively and negatively — from this game. One thing that is a bit of both, but we will spin as a positive, was the team winning despite Ja’Marr Chase and Joe Burrow having some issues. It used to be that if I told you Chase had 12 receiving yards and Burrow threw a pick-six, you would have been positive the team had lost. In fact, it has never happened when both players have been healthy for a game. How were they able to win? The defense, an unexpected leading receiver, and the running backs stepped up in key situations. The defense created four turnovers, which included a scoop-and-score by Demetrius Knight Jr. in the first quarter. It helped set up a short field in the first quarter as well on the very next drive, and caused a 14-point swing when (on the drive after that, if you can believe) Barrett Carter stripped Baker Mayfield as he was diving for the end zone to save a possible touchdown. Burrow and company went ahead and marched 80 yards. In all, the four fumbles resulted in 24 points. Effectively wiping out Burrow’s interception in the third quarter that made it a one-score game. The running game deserves more credit than the box score will tell you. The team had just over 100 yards in total. However, it was a rushing touchdown by Chase Brown that gave the team a 21-3 lead in the second quarter. Those short-yardage situations near the end zone proved to be an issue when attempting to pass the ball outside of Mike Gesicki’s touchdown. Speaking of, Gesicki deserves a game ball of his own. The Bucs and refs did everything they could to take away Chase. Gesicki made them pay with five receptions that resulted in a total of 78 yards and the aforementioned touchdown. Samaje Perine deserves a quick nod as well. He had a total of eight touches for 50 total yards. There were three first-down plays among those touches. Not something that will jump out at you, but he certainly made an impact. It is fairly easy to feel like, had this Bucs team played the 2025 Bengals, that it would have been a much different outcome. Not to mention how many new acquisitions popped up during turnover plays. Bryan Cook and Boye Mafe each forced a fumble and recovered a fumble on the day. Now, we just need to see this team with Burrow and Chase firing on all cylinders. But if nothing else, this type of performance shows that this team is capable of winning in more ways than one, a far cry from past years when it felt like the offense always had to win the game.

title: Amarius Mims dominated Rueben Bain Jr. in Bengals’ win over Bucs
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals offensive line got very little respect entering the 2026 season, despite returning every starter from a promising 2025 season for the unit. One analyst even had this group ranked among the five worst o-lines in the NFL. Thankfully, the unit we saw in Sunday’s 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers not […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - SEPTEMBER 13: Cincinnati Bengals offensive tackle Amarius Mims #71 in a game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Cincinnati Bengals on September 13, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Jeff Moreland/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals offensive line got very little respect entering the 2026 season, despite returning every starter from a promising 2025 season for the unit. One analyst even had this group ranked among the five worst o-lines in the NFL . Thankfully, the unit we saw in Sunday’s 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers not only looked far better than that ranking, but it looked like one with the potential to be a strength in an offense that already has plenty of strengths. Joe Burrow had a clean pocket most of the game while taking just one sack, and he needed every bit of it to help ice this win. As of Sunday evening, Pro Football Focus gave the Bengals a 76.3 pass-blocking grade for their performance vs. the Bucs. This unit had just three games with a higher grade in the entire 2025 season and just one in 2024. A big reason for the rise of the Bengals offensive line has been right tackle Amarius Mims, and that was on full display Sunday for the 18th overall pick of the 2024 NFL Draft out of Georgia. In 38 pass-blocking snaps, Mims did not allow a single pressure and earned an 84.5 pass-blocking grade from PFF. To give you an idea of how strong that is, that grade would have ranked sixth among all offensive tackles in the NFL last year over the entire season. It’s also the highest single-game grade of his career. Mims did this while mostly blocking Buccaneers first-round pick Rueben Bain Jr., a popular mock draft target for the Bengals this offseason until they traded the 10th overall pick for Dexter Lawrence. Against Mims, Bain was a ghost, finishing the game with a 40.1 PFF grade and no pressures. If Mims keeps this up, he could be in line for a monster contract next offseason when he finally becomes extension-eligible. Amarius Mims had Reuben Bain on the moon. pic.twitter.com/QeL7SHn3Kp — Goodberry (@JoeGoodberry) September 13, 2026 Be sure to download the SB Nation app on Apple and Android devices so you can come chat with us! title: Joe Burrow owns up to pick-6 vs. Bucs while giving strong praise to Bengals offensive line
summary: Joe Burrow’s first game of the 2026 season was just about what you’d expect from Joe Burrow in Week 1. There were some really good throws. There were some frustrating ones. There was a little bit of rust. There was a whole lot of “How the hell did he see that?” And then there was […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) yells out instructions to his teammates during home opener against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026. The Bengals beat the Buccaneers 27-33. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Joe Burrow’s first game of the 2026 season was just about what you’d expect from Joe Burrow in Week 1. There were some really good throws. There were some frustrating ones. There was a little bit of rust. There was a whole lot of “How the hell did he see that?” And then there was the pick-six. Let’s just get that one out of the way. With the Bengals sitting on a comfortable lead in the third quarter, Burrow tried to fit a ball into a tight window, and Tampa Bay rookie Josiah Trotter made him pay, taking the interception 38 yards to the end zone. Suddenly, a game that had been feeling pretty comfortable was a one-score affair. It was the kind of mistake that can completely change the tone of a game. Burrow knows it. And judging by the way he talked about it afterward, he’s not exactly looking for anyone to let him off the hook. “Terrible (throw) from me. I had an out route to the field. The flat defender got underneath it, so I’m trying to throw the replacement, and the guy made a good play, but I can’t make that turnover,” said Burrow. Burrow finished the afternoon completing 25/35 passes for 254 yards and a touchdown, and Cincinnati ultimately walked out of Paycor Stadium with a 33-27 win. The interception was the glaring mistake, but it was also basically the one play that everyone is going to remember from what was otherwise a pretty solid afternoon from the quarterback. Joe Burrow “If I didn't have that interception, I'm feeling great walking out of here. You can't make plays like that, so I got to get that fixed. Offensive line was pretty lights out. I thought we ran the ball, ran the ball well in spots, and you know, I got the got the ball to… pic.twitter.com/KKXqLXTTNR — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) September 13, 2026 True to his offseason messages, Burrow was critical of himself on that pick-six, saying he would “have felt great walking out of here” without it. But, as big of a perfectionist as he is, No. 9 took the onus on himself. And that’s where the offensive line deserves some credit. For all the talk about Burrow’s interception and Cincinnati’s offense leaving points on the field, the offensive line gave him a pretty clean afternoon against a Tampa Bay defense that came into this matchup with plenty of reasons to believe it could make life miserable for him. “Lights out” was how Burrow coined the offensive line’s Sunday performance, per Mike Petraglia on Twitter and other members of the Cincinnati media. Burrow was sacked just once. That’s it. A marquee matchup of Tampa Bay’s first-round pass-rusher Rueben Bain Jr. against Amarius Mims was on full display Sunday afternoon. And the Bengals’ former first-round tackle stepped up in a huge way. Amarius Mims allowed 0 pressures on 37 pass block snaps today vs. the Bucs and primarily Rueben Bain, per PFF initial charting. Would be the highest pass block grade of his career if it holds. Definitely looked like that good of a game. https://t.co/O8uOQR5BPB — Gridiron Grading (@GridironGrading) September 13, 2026 Burrow had enough time to work through progressions, finding Mike Gesicki repeatedly, hitting Tee Higgins in some big spots, and, when things broke down late, made plays with his legs. That last part mattered, too. Cincinnati needed to close this game out, and the offense was able to put together the final possession and drain the last 3:19 off the clock. That’s not something the Bengals have always been able to say when a game gets uncomfortable in the fourth quarter. The line wasn’t perfect. Nobody is going to confuse Week 1 with a finished product. But it looked like a group that can actually give Burrow a solid chance to operate. And maybe that’s the biggest takeaway here. We’ve spent so much time talking about Burrow getting hit over the years that it can be easy to miss when he’s actually standing in a clean pocket. On Sunday, he had one sack. One. Against a Tampa Bay defense that was supposed to be one of the tougher tests Cincinnati would face early in the season. That’s a pretty good place to start. The pick-six is going to get the headlines because, well, that’s what happens when the franchise quarterback throws one directly into the end zone at the other end of the field. But Burrow doesn’t need to be perfect for this team to win. That’s the interesting thing about this Bengals team. The defense forced four turnovers. Evan McPherson drilled two field goals from 55 and 58 yards. The offensive line protected its quarterback. Chase Brown found the end zone. Mike Gesicki became a much bigger part of the offense than anyone probably expected. And when Tampa Bay made the game uncomfortable, Cincinnati didn’t completely fall apart. Burrow’s interception helped make it uncomfortable in the first place. He’ll be the first person to tell you that. But the response matters, too. The Bengals didn’t need Burrow to throw for 400 yards and four touchdowns to win this one. They needed him to make enough plays, avoid turning one mistake into three, and help close the game when the Bucs inevitably made their push. He did that. The pick-six was ugly. The rest of the afternoon was a lot more encouraging. And if the offensive line really can keep giving Burrow this kind of protection, Cincinnati’s offense has a pretty good chance to look a whole lot better once the Week 1 rust finally disappears.
author: Anthony Cosenza

title: Bengals defense went nuts with 3 straight fumble recoveries vs. Bucs that effectively won the game
summary: There are probably a lot of people who had the Cincinnati Bengals‘ defense scoring the first touchdown of the 2026 season somewhere on their bingo card. Not many had Demetrius Knight Jr. doing it on a 27-yard fumble return. And absolutely nobody had the Bengals forcing three straight fumbles in one of the wildest defensive […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals safety Bryan Cook (6) celebrates after recovering a Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield (6) fumble in the second quarter of the NFL Week 1 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There are probably a lot of people who had the Cincinnati Bengals ‘ defense scoring the first touchdown of the 2026 season somewhere on their bingo card. Not many had Demetrius Knight Jr. doing it on a 27-yard fumble return. And absolutely nobody had the Bengals forcing three straight fumbles in one of the wildest defensive stretches Cincinnati has produced in a long time, and every bit of it was needed in the team’s 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . This is not the same defense we watched last year. That became pretty obvious in the first quarter against the Bucs, when Cincinnati’s revamped front started getting after Baker Mayfield and the football started flying around Paycor Stadium. The first one was the big one. Mayfield got hit, the ball came loose, and Knight scooped it up and took off. Twenty-seven yards later, the Bengals had their first touchdown of the season — and it wasn’t Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase or Tee Higgins putting points on the board. It was a linebacker running with the football. D KNIGHT SAID GIMME THAT. #TBvsCIN at 1:00 on Fox pic.twitter.com/WNSKgJ6STf — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) September 13, 2026 Then, somehow, the Bengals did it again. And then again. Three consecutive Tampa Bay possessions ended with Cincinnati recovering a fumble. That’s the kind of sequence that makes you start wondering whether somebody accidentally turned the turnover slider all the way up. That stretch effectively won the game for the Bengals, as all three turnovers were converted into touchdowns that gave the Bengals a 21-3 lead in a game they ultimately won by just six points, 33-27. And seven of those points came off a Joe Burrow pick-six. If not for that stretch of three straight fumble recoveries, we may very well be talking about a different result. The reaction from the Bengals’ sideline said plenty. This defense has spent the better part of the last few seasons begging for someone to make a play, begging for a pass rush to change a game, begging for a turnover to fall its way. On Sunday, the ball just kept finding them. There was even a moment when it looked like Cincinnati had another takeaway through the air, only for the interception to come off the board because of a penalty. It didn’t matter much in the moment because the Bengals were already creating chaos every time Tampa Bay had the ball. BRYAN COOKED. #TBvsCIN at 1:00 PM on Fox pic.twitter.com/J0ZyIeZs05 — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) September 13, 2026 And that’s the part that makes this sequence more interesting than simply looking at the turnover column. Cincinnati isn’t just recovering loose footballs. The defensive front is actually affecting the quarterback. Dexter Lawrence II, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe and the rest of the revamped defensive line were brought in for exactly this kind of thing. They also brought in a game-changing safety in former Chiefs Super Bowl-winner Bryan Cook, who recovered a fumble in the end zone after Baker Mayfield was stripped by Barrett Carter, which had to feel really good after the second-year linebacker was someone who many clamored to be benched and replaced throughout the offseason. The Bengals spent the offseason trying to fix a defense that couldn’t consistently get off the field, and against Tampa Bay, the new-look group has already shown flashes of being a completely different animal. Of course, it’s one game. It’s also Week 1. And turnovers can come in bunches before disappearing for a month. But you can’t fake the feeling of a defense that suddenly expects to make plays. Last year, a loose ball could feel like a minor miracle. Sunday, the Bengals were practically fighting over them, left and right. And, when the team needed another big play in the fourth quarter, it happened again. Boye Mafe forced a fumble on another quarterback sack of Mayfield, which Cincinnati recovered to begin to seal the game in the final half of the final period. OPEN SACK SEASON. 😤 #TBvsCIN at 1:00 PM on Fox pic.twitter.com/biYgNfO2gs — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) September 13, 2026 And if this is what Al Golden’s defense is going to look like when the pass rush gets rolling, Cincinnati may have finally found the thing it has been missing. The offense doesn’t always have to be the reason the Bengals win. Sometimes, apparently, the defense can just take the football three times in a row and score one of the touchdowns itself. Closing the door late in a contest helps, too. Honestly, after watching this defense last year, that’s about as crazy as it gets.

title: AFC North: 3 winners, but who looked good, who had injuries, and who is suspect?
summary: As Cleveland Browns fans lament another terrible start to an NFL season, the beat goes on around the AFC North. The Browns are the lone team to lose in Week 1, a drubbing handed to them by the Jacksonville Jaguars, with many turning their attention to the 2027 NFL draft to try to avoid thinking […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 4: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates with his teammate Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens after a touchdown during an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images As Cleveland Browns fans lament another terrible start to an NFL season, the beat goes on around the AFC North. The Browns are the lone team to lose in Week 1 , a drubbing handed to them by the Jacksonville Jaguars , with many turning their attention to the 2027 NFL draft to try to avoid thinking about what former Cleveland QB Baker Mayfield might do in Week 2 . As always, we still want to keep track of what is going on in the AFC North, including two big contract issues that could lead to rumors and a trade . Baker hands Bengals the game It is almost impossible to have an honest, good conversation about Baker Mayfield around Cleveland fans. For a lot of good reasons, as mentioned in The Feed . Those convesations, however, will probably never stop especially with Week 2’s matchup. In Week 1, the Cincinnati Bengals once again saw the full Baker experience. Mayfield completed 23 of 28 passes for 216 with zero touchdowns and zero interceptions. He willed the team back into the game, including five carries for 30 yards and a touchdown, while handing, almost quite literally, the game to the Bengals with three fumbles. For Cincinnati, the defense was much improved while the offense was good, not great, as they get ramped up. No one had two catches for 12 yards for Ja’Marr Chase also leading to a Bengals victory, but he we are. Steelers hold off Kevin Stefanski, 3rd-string QB Not sure what Stefanski did in a past life, but his quarterback options have been limited for quite a few years. On Sunday, that included starting third-stringer Cooper Rush , who completed just 12 of 22 passes for 143 yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions, including a back-breaking pick-6. Pittsburgh’s offense did just enough, and the defense was solid. The opponent drops the excitement level for Steelers fans, although a victory is a victory. Ravens control the game, have injury concerns coming out With four straight touchdowns between the first and second quarter, the Baltimore Ravens were in control 28-6, then 31-13 heading into halftime. While the Bengals and Steelers didn’t have huge offensive days, the Ravens saw Lamar Jackson throw for 324 yards, Derrick Henry rush for 144 yards, and Zay Flowers have 150 yards receiving. The bad news for Baltimore is Flowers’ hamstring issue popped up, which isn’t expected to be long-term but is notable for a speedster. On top of that, hotshot rookie Jakobi Lane has a fractured wrist and could miss signficant time. Overall, the Ravens looked the most dominant of the three winning AFC North teams in Week 1. title: 4 thoughts from the Browns lackluster season opener versus the Jaguars
summary: Not ideal. The 2026 Cleveland Browns season opener was a disaster in a lot of ways. It would be lazy to say that everyone expected this to happen because no one thought it would be this bad. Beating the Jacksonville Jaguars, who were in the playoffs last season and are projected to be back in […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13:Kc Concepcion #1 of the Cleveland Browns runs a route in the second half during an NFL football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Everbank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Not ideal. The 2026 Cleveland Browns season opener was a disaster in a lot of ways . It would be lazy to say that everyone expected this to happen because no one thought it would be this bad . Beating the Jacksonville Jaguars, who were in the playoffs last season and are projected to be back in the postseason again this year, was not going to be easy, but the Browns didn’t give themselves a fair chance to cause an upset . Four thoughts from Sunday’s dismal performance: 1st Down: Offense was offensive but it’s a work in progress Going into the season, expectations for the Cleveland Browns offense were low. Despite the influx of talent, from revamping the offensive line and wide receiver room it would be hard to evaluate how the offense would look because the quarterback room could be the worst in the entire league. The stats will say quarterback Deshaun Watson played fine, but the film says otherwise. He held the ball too long, wasn’t as decisive as he should and lacked drive in terms of throwing the ball. Watson will take what the defense gives him and not take deep shots down the field, which limits an offense with a low ceiling. Shedeur Sanders is someone that fans want to see because he’s popular and well-liked (something Watson isn’t), but I don’t see the offense getting any better with him either. Could Sanders provide excitement to a fanbase that needs it? Yes, but at this point this fanbase would be excited about anything. The run blocking for the offensive line isn’t where it needs to be, but to be fair, this is a group with five new starters. Rookie Denzel Boston had a nice touchdown grab when the game was out of reach. Will the offense get better? Maybe. Maybe not. Keep in mind, this is a new offensive scheme that should get better as the season progresses. Hopefully. 2nd Down: Defense has an identity issue Going into the season, the Browns defense was considered to be a strength despite losing defensive end Myles Garrett and defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz. Sunday, the defense looked anything but a strength. The pass rush was lacking, the secondary was picked apart, and they struggled to get a stop. Cornerback Tyson Campbell talked about the scheme and how defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg wanted to be more diverse: Browns CB Tyson Campbell postgame said that new DC Mike Rutenberg’s scheme is stylistically the same as last year “in some ways, but we got some more zone concepts that we run as well. So a little bit more diverse.” Per ESPN Research, the Browns played zone coverage on 67% of… — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) September 14, 2026 As mentioned, the Browns defense spent more time in zone today than they usually do, but the defense doesn’t have the players to run zone as frequently as they did. It’s not a bad thing to diversify and change your scheme, however, you have to pick and choose when to do it. This defense has blue-chip talent, and it’s clear that this unit needs to be better after having a performance like this. How do they fix it? Go back to what works, but be more diverse and not as predictable. 3rd Down: It’s Week 1. It’s fair to say out of all the Week 1 performances in the NFL, the Cleveland Browns had the worst performance. However, it’s Week 1. It’s the NFL. Week-to-week league (Insert fans “weak-to-weak” joke here). Yes, the Browns looked unprepared on both sides of the ball. The coaching wasn’t what it needed to be, and the players didn’t perform the way they were supposed to. Could things change? Absolutely. However, a performance like this didn’t do much to encourage fans, and it’s up to the team to fix it. 4th Down: Things are bad, but it doesn’t mean it will stay this way Let me get this out of the way. I grew up a Seattle Seahawks fan. My parents weren’t diehard Browns fans so it made it easier. As I scrolled through social media, I saw a post saying “Today felt like a low point in Cleveland Browns fandom.” To be honest, today wasn’t a low point. It was a bad loss, but this team has had numerous low points since they’ve come back, and today wasn’t one of those lowest points if you were a fan. That seems like an overreaction. Things will eventually get better for this team considering that this team has talent. You can choose to believe that things will get better or choose to believe things will get worse. The team has put a winning product out there before, even if it seems so long ago, so it’s not hard for the team to get back to it. Having young, talented players is always a good starting point for a team looking to turn things around, even if Week 1 was tough to watch. ( Editor’s addition : I’m a Lord of the Rings fan, and 4th down had me thinking of this clip, so it gets added.) After a night of sleep, what are some of your thoughts on Week 1? title: Assigning blame for Browns loss in Week 1: Deshaun Watson tops the list but is not alone
summary: In assessing the Cleveland Browns’ 34-10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, several factors contributed to a performance in which Cleveland was never really in the game. Deshaun Watson threw an interception on his third pass attempt of the first quarter, setting the tone for what would become a disappointing game for the Browns. Watson was […]
full_text: In assessing the Cleveland Browns’ 34-10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars , several factors contributed to a performance in which Cleveland was never really in the game. Deshaun Watson threw an interception on his third pass attempt of the first quarter, setting the tone for what would become a disappointing game for the Browns. Watson was certainly a substantial part of what went wrong for Cleveland in this matchup, but several other factors also contributed to the Browns’ struggles. The Browns’ defense did little to help give the team a chance to win. They allowed Trevor Lawrence to go 18 of 23 for 245 yards and four touchdowns. With Myles Garrett no longer leading this defense, there was plenty of uncertainty around what the unit would look like. This group’s performance did little to give anyone confidence that they could replicate the dominant defense they used to be. Some of the blame also falls on Todd Monken , who seemed unprepared with his game plan and struggled with some game management decisions throughout the matchup. It only added to the struggles the team was already having, as did the lack of a solid run game. Watson finished 16 of 22 with 205 yards, one interception, and one touchdown. This stat line is not particularly concerning; however, much of the production came at the end of the fourth quarter when the game was already out of reach. The Browns trailed 31-0 at one point, making Watson’s lack of production and inability to run the offense effectively a major factor in the team’s struggles.
