title: Detroit Lions stock report: 13 risers, 7 fallers vs. Saints
summary: After a long Detroit Lions offseason—and finding themselves on the wrong end of a 24-3 second-half run—the Lions scraped by the skin of their teeth thanks to a missed Daniel Carlson 62-yard field goal attempt at the end of regulation and defending a failed two-point conversion attempt in a 31-30 overtime victory. Not exactly how […]
full_text: After a long Detroit Lions offseason—and finding themselves on the wrong end of a 24-3 second-half run—the Lions scraped by the skin of their teeth thanks to a missed Daniel Carlson 62-yard field goal attempt at the end of regulation and defending a failed two-point conversion attempt in a 31-30 overtime victory. Not exactly how it was scripted. It was mostly a lethargic first half offensively, but after taking a 21-0 lead midway through the third quarter, there was almost a feeling that the Lions might step on the accelerator and floor it past the Saints. That made the dramatic, anxiety-ridden, thrilling finish feel a little disappointing. But survive and advance as far as Week 1 goes. It’s an oddball NFL slate that often isn’t an accurate indicator of what’s to come. Just last year, the eventual Super Bowl champion Seahawks lost 17-13 and started the season 0-2, the eventual first-overall-pick Las Vegas Raiders beat the eventual AFC champion New England Patriots, and J.J. McCarthy was NFC Offensive Player of the Week. Dan Campbell was level-headed and appreciative of the victory, showing little concern both in the locker room and during his postgame press conference. This stock report will carry a similar non-overreactionary approach. Stock up: Jahmyr Gibbs, RB Gibbs got his contract extension, and in his new “bell-cow” role, accounted for 50.4% of the Lions’ 369 total yards and 57.7% of their 26 first downs. His 183 total yards are the fourth-most by a Detroit Lions player in a season opener in franchise history. On a day when the Lions’ offense went through some lulls and wasn’t quite firing on all cylinders, Gibbs willed them down the field and into the end zone. While the offensive line and play design deserve some credit for the run game, it was truly a masterful display from Gibbs, with his vision, patience, pacing, and acceleration all fully on display to the tune of seven runs of 10-plus yards, 12 missed tackles forced, and 82 yards after contact. The team rode him when they needed it most, accounting for 35 yards on their final overtime touchdown drive. For a Saints defense that finished top-10 in the second half of last season in a number of run defense metrics, the Lions rushing attack looked more comfortable and consistent than last season. The lone negative was a fumble that was overturned on replay review, but Gibbs remains fully primed for a career season as a strong Offensive Player of the Year contender. Stock up: Derrick Barnes, LB Barnes, taking on the role of the team’s second linebacker in his sixth season, played a career-high 77 snaps while successfully filling the shoes of his long-time good friend Alex Anzalone. Barnes stepped up and was flying around like a bat out of hell in the second half and overtime. He did so while evolving beyond the SAM linebacker role on the line of scrimmage in five-down fronts that he had become accustomed to over the last two seasons, instead playing the majority of his snaps as an off-ball, stand-up linebacker next to Jack Campbell. Barnes kicked off his playmaking by jumping the route and intercepting Tyler Shough’s pass intended for Noah Fant on the first play of the Saints’ opening drive of the second half. On the next drive, he cleaned up Shough for a sack. Later, he brought down Travis Etienne at the line of scrimmage, corralled Shough on a third-down scramble, shut the door on another drive by bringing Etienne down on a third-down red-zone reception to force a field goal, and forced an incompletion along the side of the end zone in overtime. Finally, Barnes even stepped up to take away Shough’s first-read on the two-point conversion. Overall, Barnes stuffed the stat sheet with six tackles, two quarterback pressures, a sack, an interception, a pass breakup, and three run stops. He looked like the best version of himself—the player the Lions envisioned when they signed him to an extension last offseason and entrusted him with added responsibility while confidently moving on from Anzalone. Stock down: Jameson Williams, WR Williams might have had the most apparent and unexpected poor performance of the day. He had one deep pass over the middle—his original bread and butter—that was dropped, another intermediate shot over the middle that was potentially tipped by the defender and couldn’t be hauled in, and he bobbled a reverse that appeared well-designed for him to jettison his way into an explosive gain, if not a touchdown. Williams also had two other third-down targets on routes near the sideline that were almost within reach. He could’ve created more separation, the throws could’ve been better placed, or both, but Williams and Jared Goff simply couldn’t connect, with both plays resulting in punts. Williams and Goff just couldn’t get on the same page for most of the afternoon, despite Drew Petzing at least appearing to have a good idea of how to play to Williams’ strengths. A runway route at some point would’ve been nice, but the yards-after-catch opportunities just weren’t as available. Williams started the first two months of last season, outside of Week 2 against Chicago, with fairly cold and disappointing performances. There’s plenty of evidence to believe that won’t be the case again, but Sunday was still surprising after how impressive Williams looked throughout training camp, when he appeared to be the most polished and dominant version of himself. To his credit, Williams responded with an unbelievably clutch 22-yard catch on a corner route in overtime, setting up the offense at the 5-yard line. It was Goff’s only completion of the day on a pass traveling 10-plus air yards downfield and outside the numbers. Williams finished strong when the Lions needed him most, and hopefully that play is something to build on after he managed just 23 receiving yards on eight targets in regulation. Stock up: Aidan Hutchinson, DE While his presence wasn’t always felt, one of the qualities needed most from an elite-level pass rusher is getting home when his team needs him most, and Aidan Hutchinson rang the bell there against the Saints. His undressing of left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. with a timely chop-spin move to sack Tyler Shough and knock the Saints out of field goal range on their final drive of the second quarter was colossal. So was taking advantage of a one-on-one matchup against running back Kendre Miller for his second sack late in the fourth quarter when Detroit desperately needed it. It took Hutchinson almost two full quarters to really get going, but his impact extended beyond the sacks. He beat right tackle Taliese Fuaga for a pressure that led to Derrick Barnes’ sack, had another clean spin-move win against Fuaga in the red zone before the Saints’ first touchdown on a quick slant, bull-rushed his way into the pocket to force a checkdown to Travis Etienne, and blasted Shough on a twist during the Saints’ late fourth-quarter 42-yard completion to Chris Olave. Too many defensive snaps played is going to be a theme for a handful of Lions defenders from this game, but all things considered, Hutchinson playing 83.3% of the snaps (75 of 90) is an improvement from the workload he carried in the majority of his games over the last few seasons. Stock neutral: D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Avonte Maddox, and Chuck Clark, starting secondary Tyler Shough having over 60 dropbacks is going to leave some bad plays on tape for any secondary. So will playing 90 total defensive snaps—the most of the Dan Campbell era—while deploying a top-10 man coverage rate and blitz rate in Week 1. That approach also contributed to Shough having the second-fastest time to throw (2.44 seconds) of the week, especially as the Saints’ offense cranked up the pace in the second half. Add in the cornerbacks not always having safety help over the top, and this gray-beard, veteran-laden defensive back group understandably had its share of ups and downs. Each player had plenty of highlights early before the lowlights began to pile…
author: Al Karsten

title: Detroit Lions Week 1 snap counts: Several defensive rotations unveiled
summary: The Detroit Lions needed overtime to secure a 31-30 win over the New Orleans Saints in Week 1, but a win is a win in September as teams adjust to a new season. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) is sacked by Detroit Lions defensive tackle Alim McNeill (54) during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions needed overtime to secure a 31-30 win over the New Orleans Saints in Week 1, but a win is a win in September as teams adjust to a new season. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can glean moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 77 snaps (100%) Josh Dobbs: Did not play (DNP) With the Lions’ run game clicking, Goff had an average day at the office on Sunday, though the Saints’ fast tempo sped up the game and created more opportunities for both offenses. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 57 (74%) Sione Vaki: 22 (29%) — 24 special teams (71%) Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 24 (71%) We were told Gibbs would be the workhorse back, and he certainly was in the opener, carrying the ball a league-leading 29 times and rushing for a league-leading 156 yards. He also added five receptions for another 30 yards for good measure. Despite Gibbs touching the ball a ton, he was still on the field only 74% of the time, leaving 20 opportunities for Vaki and two snaps when they were on the field simultaneously. It was an up-and-down day for Vaki’s first run as RB2, showing well in pass protection and as a receiver, but in the locker room after the game, he was left frustrated with the mistakes he made. When I asked him to point out the parts of his game he was happy with, he had this to say: “To be honest, I couldn’t tell you. I feel like there’s nothing but improvement that needs to happen.” It’s worth noting that, according to PFF, 20 of Vaki’s 22 reps came on passing downs, which points to coaches’ confidence in his ability to hold up in one of the more critical components of a running back’s responsibilities. Wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown: 69 (90%) Jameson Williams: 65 (84%) Isaac TeSlaa: 52 (68%) Tay Martin: 0 (0%) — 24 (71%) Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 11 (32%) The Lions rolled with just three receivers on offense, with Martin and Kennedy taking on starting roles on special teams. Martin was fantastic as a gunner on punts and on kickoff coverage, securing a career-high three special teams tackles. “I just wanted to make sure I made Dan (Campbell) right for believing in me,” Martin said of using special teams to make the active roster. “I’ve been waiting on this chance my whole life, to go out there on the 53-man roster and make some plays.” Tight end Sam LaPorta: 62 (81%) Brock Wright: 39 (51%) — 11 (32%) Tyler Conklin: 10 (13%) Jackson Meeks: 0 (0%) — 18 (53%) No real surprises here, as the Lions were expected to utilize all three of their top tight ends, and the distribution of snaps is very similar to what we’ve seen in previous years. Offensive line LT Penei Sewell: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) C Juice Scruggs: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) RG Tate Ratledge: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) RT Blake Miller: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) G Ben Bartch: 66 (86%) — 5 (15%) LG Christian Mahogany: 11 (14%) OT Larry Borom: 9 (12%) — 5 (15%) G/T Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 5 (15%) Mahogany got the start, but an awkward injury on the 11th offensive play cost him the rest of the game. The initial scan of his knee was negative, and Mahogany was in good spirits in the locker room , suggesting it’s not a long-term injury, but on a short week, the Lions may continue to lean on Bartch to start at left guard. Borom found the field nine times in Jumbo sets, and offensive coordinator Drew Petzing was very creative in his usage, lining him up as a tight end and at left tackle. That gave the Lions the opportunity to move Sewell all over the formation, create mismatches in the run game, and was a catalyst in both of Gibbs’ rushing touchdowns. Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 83 (92%) — 5 (15%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 47 (52%) — 5 (15%) DT Tyleik Williams: 35 (39%) — 5 (15%) DL Ben Stille: 9 (10%) 3T Mekhi Wingo — INACTIVE McNeill seeing the field on 92% of defensive snaps is borderline insane for a big man. So why do it? His positional versatility and ability to impact the game from multiple spots is a massive advantage for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. With the Lions maintaining a double-digit lead for most of the game, the Saints threw the ball often. That situation led the Lions to lean on rookie Gill-Howard more than starter Williams. After the game, he talked with Pride of Detroit about his impact on the game: “I think I need to pass rush way better. There were times when I was rushing too down the middle, or I got stuck in a gap—I had a few decent rushes for sure, but I felt like the area I took a step (forward) was in the run game. I didn’t get moved (off the ball) at all.” Gill-Howard’s assessment is backed up by PFF, who assigned him a 76.8 grade for his run defense, the second-highest on the team in Week 1. EDGE EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 75 (83%) Rush End DJ Wonnum: 69 (77%) — 5 (15%) EDGE Derrick Moore: 18 (20%) Big End Tyler Lacy: 15 (17%) Rush End Eric O’Neill: 4 (4%) — 17 (50%) Big End Ahmed Hassanein — INACTIVE Like McNeill, Hutchinson played a ridiculous amount of snaps in this game, but it was surely hard to take him off the field when he was so dominant. Not only did Hutchinson secure two sacks, but he leads the NFL in pressures in both PFF (10) and NFL Pro’s (10) metrics. With the Lions electing to play more nickel defense in this game, that meant more Wonnum, and he rewarded Sheppard with his performance, forcing six pressures (tied for seventh best in the NFL, per NFL Pro) and a couple of pass breakups at the line of scrimmage. O’Neill, who was active over Hassanein, showed why with his special teams performance, securing two special teams tackles at critical moments. author: Erik Schlitt

title: Detroit Lions report card, grades: Trenches thrive, boundaries struggle vs. Saints
summary: After the Detroit Lions’ nail-biting win over the New Orleans Saints, let’s go position by position and hand out some grades for how Detroit performed in their Week 1 contest. Quarterback: B+ It was a strong day from Jared Goff, and while it was only modest statistically, it would look a lot better had he […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; d carrie the ball against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After the Detroit Lions’ nail-biting win over the New Orleans Saints, let’s go position by position and hand out some grades for how Detroit performed in their Week 1 contest. Quarterback: B+ It was a strong day from Jared Goff, and while it was only modest statistically, it would look a lot better had he not dealt with some drops. He also deserves some credit for avoiding negative plays (zero turnovers, one sack). Even his sack fumble that never was , he deserves credit for having enough grip strength to endure the hit and still begin his throwing motion, which was crucial to the official’s ruling. However, some of the aforementioned drops were also the result of less-than-ideal ball placement. Two of Jameson Williams’ “drops” were outside routes, and Goff placed the ball too high and outside for each. Those were both drive-killing third down plays. Still, hard to complain about his day. Running back: A- After a couple of plays where I thought Jahmyr Gibbs tried to do a little too much (including his fumble), I thought he was outstanding on Sunday. Whether it was his explosiveness on the outside, vision on the inside, or the 12 missed tackles he forced (career-high) , Gibbs proved fully worthy of the increased workload on Sunday. Unfortunately, it wasn’t as promising of a debut for Sione Vaki. While I thought he was fine with the ball in his hands, his pass protection—which was supposed to be his calling card—was not at its best. Wide receivers: C Let’s talk about Jameson Williams. While Goff deserves some blame for his drops, Williams deserves the bulk of the blame—particularly on the early deep shot that could’ve swung the game in Detroit’s favor early. Goff took the blame on the end around fumble, but that feels like covering for his wide receiver publicly. It was a disappointing step back for Williams after what was very clearly his best training camp. Worst of all, Williams’ mistakes seemed to happen in the worst moments. One (contested) drop set up a third-and-15, two drops happened on third down, and the fumble essentially ended that drive. But it wasn’t even all bad for Williams. He converted a third-and-8 in the red zone to set up Detroit’s first touchdown, and his 22-yard gain in overtime set up the game-winning score. Meanwhile, Amon-Ra St. Brown continued to be fantastic—10 catches on 14 targets for 67 yards and two touchdowns. His overtime touchdown was incredible, holding the ball tight through contact and bouncing off for the score. I will say I was a bit disappointed by the YAC from this group, though. The Saints deserve credit for strong tackling efforts, but St. Brown and Williams combined for just 29 yards after the catch. Tight ends: B+ Sam LaPorta put a decent showing in the passing game, hauling in five of eight targets for 48 yards. And he looked pretty impressive as a blocker, too. Just take a look at him on the goal line here: Penei Sewell is a grown man. pic.twitter.com/qOjCXtVQPd — Coach Dan Casey (@CoachDanCasey) September 13, 2026 It was a pretty ho-hum day beyond that, which is certainly not a bad thing. Offensive line: A- The Lions produced a 51.5% rushing success rate, which was second-best in the NFL in Week 1. The Lions also averaged 2.18 yards before contact (seventh-best), showing that the offensive line was producing a ton of holes for Gibbs and company. Pass protection was a little more up-and-down, but still pretty darn good. PFF only credited the Lions’ offensive line as responsible for four total pressures, and no single player allowed more than one (Tate Ratledge had a clean sheet). Compared to expectation, I don’t think there was a unit who performed better on Sunday. Defensive line: B There were so many moving parts on the Lions’ defensive lineup that I’m not entirely confident in my live-watch assessment of how the defensive line played. I do know this: Aidan Hutchinson was still disruptive, I am continuing to be impressed by Skyler Gill-Howard, and the run defense looks about as good as it was in 2024. I’m not as confident in Detroit having an edge defender who can win one-on-ones opposite Hutchinson, and I’d like to see what happened toward the end of the game, when Tyler Shough appeared to have more time. But more often than not, I thought the Lions played pretty well up front, and when it came to the game-deciding play, it was Tyleik Williams’ pressure that forced Shough into a low-percentage throw: Defended for the dub pic.twitter.com/Pe3KG4GQUE — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 13, 2026 Linebackers: A- Let’s start with the only bad play that I can remember from the game from the linebacker unit: Jack Campbell got beat pretty handily on Saints tight end Juwan Johnson’s touchdown catch. Other than that, I thought it was a pretty clean day from the linebacking corps. Campbell tallied seven tackles, including one tackle for loss in a strong run game performance. But perhaps the best defender on the field was Derrick Barnes. He had a teach-tape rep in pass coverage, perfectly dropping into a zone, reading Shough’s eyes, and breaking on the ball for the interception. He also tallied a sack, and his coverage on the final play of the game caused Shough to go through his progressions and hesitate. And while he didn’t jump off the tape initially, Malcolm Rodriguez actually came out as the second highest-graded defender on the Lions, per PFF. Defensive backs: D What a different tale of halves. In the first half, the Lions defensive backs tallied five pass breakups, an interception, and held Shough to: 10-of-22 passing for 85 yards, 0 TDs, 1 INT and a 37.1 passer rating In the second half and overtime, the Lions DBs had zero pass breakups, and Shough went: 25-of-34 passing for 325 yards, 3 TDs, 1 INT, and a 120.3 passer rating We can’t discount either half, so you do take some good with the bad here, but the biggest frustration was the same from last year: big plays. Detroit allowed six passing plays of 20+ yards, more than all but one team in Week 1. That was a huge focus this offseason after allowing the fourth-most last year. But they only averaged 3.4 passing plays of 20+ yards last year, so they actually took a step back. Special teams: D+ Jake Bates was fine on his field goals and extra points, but his kickoffs were an issue. He landed one more than 10 yards in front of the landing zone, and sent another a few yards deep for a touchback. That may not seem like much, but it gave the Saints field position at the 40 and 35-yard line, respectively. Admittedly, Bates made up for it with a great kickoff in overtime that put New Orleans at the 20. Jack Fox, too, had an up-and-down day. While he technically pinned three of his seven punts inside the 20-yard line, he missed on his two easiest opportunities. One punt from Detroit’s 44-yard line went straight into the end zone. Another punt from Detroit’s’ 45-yard line traveled just 31 yards, coming to a rest at the Saint’s 24-yard line. Fox is typically money in those situations, so it was disappointing to see him struggle there. Elsewhere, Tom Kennedy shook off the opening kickoff muff and had at least one decent punt return. And Tay Martin was such a beast on the coverage teams that he earned a game ball from Dan Campbell . Coaching: C- I don’t have any real problems with the way Dan Campbell managed that game. You could nitpick about his decision to punt on the last possession of regulation—facing a fourth-and-long-1 from his own 44-yard line. That was a complete toss up to me, because a missed conversion almost certainly means a loss. And while Campbell doesn’t get official credit for a successful challenge, his throwing of the red flag gave the league time to review and overturn a clear incomplete pass. As for the coordinators, I thought it was a relatively promising debut from…
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions not worried about heavy workload for Jahmyr Gibbs
summary: This offseason, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell promised that Jahmyr Gibbs was taking the next step this year and becoming the team’s bell-cow back. The Lions followed by putting their money where their mouth is, making Gibbs the highest-paid running back in football. On Sunday, with former RB2 David Montgomery in Houston and current RB2 […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) is tackled by. New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker (7) during the fourth quarter at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect This offseason, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell promised that Jahmyr Gibbs was taking the next step this year and becoming the team’s bell-cow back. The Lions followed by putting their money where their mouth is, making Gibbs the highest-paid running back in football. On Sunday, with former RB2 David Montgomery in Houston and current RB2 Isiah Pacheco on injured reserve, Campbell and new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing followed through on that promise. Gibbs played 57 of 77 offensive snaps (74%, fifth-highest percentage in his career), rushed the ball 29 times (career high), and added five catches for 34 total touches (career high). Gibbs made the most of those opportunities, creating 186 yards of offense, two touchdowns, and 12 missed tackles forced. Jahmyr Gibbs forced 12 missed tackles in the Lions' Week 1 overtime win over the Saints, the most in any game of his career. Gibbs carried the ball a career-high 24 times on plays with motion, gaining 131 yards and two TDs (including six explosive runs). #NOvsDET | #OnePride pic.twitter.com/9j1TBuNYkp — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) September 13, 2026 While some were just able to enjoy that performance, others showed concern that the Lions were in danger of overusing their biggest offensive weapon. But when Campbell was faced with that criticism, he wasn’t hearing it. “You know what I like? Winning the game, man, and we were going to win this game. That guy’s our hot hand,” Campbell said. He quickly followed that up, noting that Gibbs’ workload will be something they continue to monitor this season. But on Sunday, he was the right player to ride. That may not be the case every week. “Ultimately, do I want to set records with how many carries? No, that’s not something I want to do,” Campbell said. “When you look at a guy, and you feel like, ‘Alright, man.’ He’s in good shape. I mean, he had a really good camp, and he is in phenomenal shape. He’s in the best shape I’ve seen since he’s been here. Now that doesn’t mean we’re not going to monitor, and we’re going to keep an eye on this guy because we understand that too, but we did what we had to do today.” To the surprise of no one, Gibbs didn’t mind the extra workload . He even suggested he could’ve taken more. “I feel fine,” Gibbs said, per Detroit Football Network. “I could have taken 40 today.” Gibbs was valuable all game, but he really came alive in what would be Detroit’s game-winning drive in overtime. He touched the ball six times for 35 yards, including rushes of 11 and 10 yards. “He’s a beast,” Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown said. “You watch what he does—that whole last drive, he damn-near took us down all the way. It was Jahmyr, Jahmyr, Jahmyr, Jahmyr, Jamo, me.” There are not many who can outwork, outlast, or outcome St. Brown on the field. But even he was in awe of Gibbs’ endurance on Sunday. “He never gets tired. I don’t know how he does it,” St. Brown said. “He’s running the ball every play, catching it out of the backfield. He still—I’m looking at him in the huddle and he’s not even breathing hard. I don’t know how he does it. But we’re lucky, I’m so lucky to play with him. We’re lucky to have him on our team, and we’re going to need him throughout this whole year.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions road underdogs at Buffalo Bills in Week 2
summary: The Detroit Lions (1-0) are on the road in Week 2, heading to Buffalo to take on the Bills (1-0) on “Thursday Night Football.” This looks like it will be one of the most exciting games of the week in the NFL, as not only is it a nationally televised game, but it marks the […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 15: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions shakes hands with Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills after the Bills 48-42 win at Ford Field on December 15, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (1-0) are on the road in Week 2, heading to Buffalo to take on the Bills (1-0) on “Thursday Night Football.” This looks like it will be one of the most exciting games of the week in the NFL, as not only is it a nationally televised game, but it marks the opening of the Bills’ new $2.2 billion Highmark Stadium. Both teams opened their seasons with a win, as the Lions beat the Saints 31-30 in overtime and the Bills knocked off the Texans 36-31 in a back-and-forth battle in Houston. The folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions +3.5 points . Despite having a winning record and making the playoffs in eight of his nine seasons with the Bills, Sean McDermott was fired after the Bills lost in the AFC Divisional round in 2025. With ownership liking where the team was, but also feeling McDermott couldn’t get them to the Super Bowl, the Bills elected to stay in-house for their new hire, promoting offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach. The Bills offense stayed intact and was arguably upgraded following the trade for wide receiver D.J. Moore, who was with Brady in Carolina, while the defense went through an offseason shakeup as new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard installed a 3-4 defense. To help with the transition, the Bills targeted edge rushers Bradley Chubb in free agency and TJ Parker in the NFL Draft, while also adding veterans to their secondary, putting safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson and nickel corner Dee Alford in starting roles. In Week 1, the Bills were able to win a shootout behind the arm and legs of quarterback Josh Allen. The defense gave up more ground (and points) than they’d prefer, but the Bills have a lot of firepower on offense that should help them stay in every game. With the Lions coming to town, they’ll need to keep the offense rolling, as even in an off game, the Lions have shown they can put up points. The Lions and Bills will square off on Thursday at 8:15 p.m. ET at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York. The game is nationally televised on Amazon Prime.
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Discussion: Do you feel better or worse after the Detroit Lions’ win over the New Orleans Saints?
summary: Week 1 of the 2026 season is in the books for the Detroit Lions, and it was a mixed bag. At the end of the day, all you care about is getting in the win column, and the Lions did exactly that, even if it took a tense overtime period to decide it. It was […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell, left, talks to quarterback Jared Goff (16) after a play against New Orleans Saints during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Week 1 of the 2026 season is in the books for the Detroit Lions, and it was a mixed bag. At the end of the day, all you care about is getting in the win column, and the Lions did exactly that, even if it took a tense overtime period to decide it. It was a roller coaster for the team, looking dominant and times then clueless the next. For a team with Super Bowl aspirations, inconsistencies like these need to be fixed sooner rather than later. That being said, there were good and bad performances against the Saints, and with 16 more games to play, this will be a vital early-season lesson for the team. How can they make wins easier down the road? The Lions will need to assess that going forward—in the NFL, every week is a learning experience. What did you learn about the Lions—are you feeling more or less confident in the team? Today’s Question of the Day is: Do you feel better or worse after the Detroit Lions’ win over the New Orleans Saints? My answer: Slightly worse. I think that there were encouraging signs from the team, but the second half collapse really dampened what was a stellar start to the game. Up 21-0, the Lions were in complete control—Ford Field was rocking, the defense was formidable, and the offense had woken up. Yet that quickly evaporated, turning a sure-fire win into a nail-biter in overtime. First, let’s start with the positives: I was happy with the offensive line, even with Ben Bartch stepping in for an injured Christian Mahogany. It is unfortunate that Bartch’s goal line holding penalty overshadows what was otherwise a great outing for him. Elsewhere on offense, Jahmyr Gibbs totally like he is completely capable of handling a full workload. He had 29 carries and looked quick on each of them, never losing a step as the game progressed. The defensive line showed up. Aidan Hutchinson led the way with two sacks, but the efforts of himself, DJ Wonnum, Alim McNeill, and Skyler Gill-Howard made for an unexpectedly potent pass rush. Coupled with great run defense (only allowing 91 yards on 25 carries), it was difficult to pinpoint a lineman that underperformed. Unfortunately for me, the negatives outweigh the positives. I simply have little faith in this secondary going forward. I think that D.J. Reed’s day was better than the numbers indicate, but that secondary nonetheless allowed over 400 passing yards from a Tyler Shough-led offense. Sure, I think Shough is quietly becoming an underrated passer in this league, but giving up 182 yards to Chris Olave and making the likes of Devaughn Vele and Juwan Johnson look elite is inexcusable, even for Week 1. What’s arguably worse is that for the first two-and-a-half quarters, the secondary looked good, if not great. Yet somehow, the wheels came off and it led to New Orleans mounting a massive comeback. Part of the reason why the Saints got back in this game was the faltering of the Lions offense. It’s hard to describe exactly what went wrong for the offense. Jared Goff did not have his sharpest day, but he was far from terrible. Gibbs was dominant as mentioned. Amon-Ra St. Brown had two touchdowns, while Sam LaPorta was impactful as a receiver and blocker. The elephant in the room is Jameson Williams’ nightmarish game, but he alone is not responsible. I was hoping to come out of this game impressed with offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, and sadly, that did not happen. The Lions did score 31 points and rallied for an overtime touchdown when it counted, but I would not say that anything from the offensive scheme stood out. Detroit was rarely airing it out, so a majority of their plays were happening short of the first down mark. Without having re-watched the game, I am assuming that the Saints were trying to eliminate anything over the top, but carving up defenses with short passes should be the Lions’ bread and butter—yet for some reason, it was not on Sunday. The Lions officially finished with 97 yards after the catch per PFF, but almost 40 of those yards came on their final two drives. Before then, it was a historically poor output: The Detroit Lions offense has combined for just 58 yards after the catch against the Saints. As it stands, that would be the lowest YAC output in Jared Goff’s 83 career starts with the franchise. Only four of those games have featured fewer than 80 YAC. • 64 games (77%) with… — Al Karsten (@FootballGuy_Al) September 13, 2026 The Lions thrive on getting their star players open in space, but that was seemingly absent against the Saints. I was shocked to see that Gibbs averaged more yards on the ground than Goff was through the air. Do a few catches from Williams change the course of the game? Certainly. Is that the cure-all for any stagnation on offense? I do not think so. I am far from pressing the panic button on these Lions—they won, after all—but I was hoping to see a more complete performance from the team. We saw flashes this week, but we will need to see consistency in the weeks to come.
author: John Whiticar

title: Why Jared Goff’s fumble-turned-incomplete was the correct call vs. Saints
summary: In the second quarter of the Detroit Lions’ win over the New Orleans Saints, they appeared to catch a significant break. Quarterback Jared Goff was sacked by Chase Young, jarring the ball loose, and the Saints recovered it in the end zone to potentially tie up the game at 7. However, officials stopped the play […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) throws an incomplete pass as New Orleans Saints defensive end Chase Young (99) applies the pressure during the second quarter at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect In the second quarter of the Detroit Lions’ win over the New Orleans Saints, they appeared to catch a significant break. Quarterback Jared Goff was sacked by Chase Young, jarring the ball loose, and the Saints recovered it in the end zone to potentially tie up the game at 7. However, officials stopped the play before the extra point and opted to review the play. Goff’s arm was clearly moving forward when he released the ball, but the football traveled backward. Did it still count as a lateral, or was it an incomplete pass? Take a look yourself: If this is the rule, then why have we spent literally decades obsessing over whether the guy's hand was coming forward or not? pic.twitter.com/Jk2mT5XqJX — Sam Monson (@SamMonsonNFL) September 13, 2026 Officials determined that it was an incomplete pass, offering the Lions new life. Though they punted the ball away on that possession, they would hold the Saints scoreless until they built up a 21-point lead. Vice president of instant replay Mark Butterworth explained the call in the post-game pool report: “If the defender contacts the passer prior to the passer starting his throwing motion, then it can be ruled as a backward pass. Because Goff already started his throwing motion and then the defender contacted him, it is therefore a forward pass.” He explained further: “If the defender contacts the passer prior to the passer starting his throwing motion, then it can be ruled as a backward pass. Because Goff already started his throwing motion and then the defender contacted him, it is therefore a forward pass.” And he’s right. What is defined as a forward pass is laid out pretty clearly in the rulebook. Here is the relevant part, as laid out in the official NFL rulebook —Rule 3, Section 21, Article 3, item 1: Item 1. Contact by Team B Player. If contact by an opponent materially affects a passer after the passer begins his throwing motion, it is a forward pass if he passes the ball, regardless of where the ball strikes the ground, a player, an official, or anything else. Goff joked after the game that he thought it was a good call, but then he immediately admitted he didn’t know of the rule. It’s certainly an odd ruling, but it appears to be by the book.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: 5 winners, 3 losers from Detroit Lions’ win over the New Orleans Saints
summary: Winning in the NFL is never easy, and the Detroit Lions learned why in Week 1. After taking a dominant 21-0 lead over the New Orleans Saints, the Lions failed to close out the game as the Saints rallied back. If not for a failed two-point conversion in overtime, the Lions would have walked away […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jameson Williams #1 of the Detroit Lions drops a pass during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Winning in the NFL is never easy, and the Detroit Lions learned why in Week 1. After taking a dominant 21-0 lead over the New Orleans Saints, the Lions failed to close out the game as the Saints rallied back. If not for a failed two-point conversion in overtime, the Lions would have walked away with a stunning loss. Instead, it is a humbling victory: the Lions have talent up and down the roster, but there are kinks to iron out soon. Which players walked away as winners and losers from the Lions’ first game of the 2026 season? Winner: Jahmyr Gibbs, RB In his first game as the official bell cow of the Lions backfield, Gibbs did not disappoint. With an inconsistent passing attack, Gibbs largely led the offense. He rattled off 156 yards on 29 carries (a new career-high), yet perhaps the most impressive part of that stat line is that his longest was just 21 yards. No breakaway runs inflated his average of 5.4 yards per attempt; it was just consistent gains throughout the game—aside from a few losses where he tried to make something out of nothing. In fact, Gibbs averaged more yards on the ground than Jared Goff did through the air (5.3 yards per attempt). We all know Gibbs is an elite weapon on offense, so these stats aren’t new for him. What impressed me the most is that he held up all game. The Lions are going to lean on Gibbs early and often this season, and if he can consistently handle carrying the ball over 25 times in a game without sacrificing efficiency, that is a recipe for success. Winner: Derrick Barnes, LB Spider-Man Barnes played this game with web-shooters of his own. After a tough 2025 campaign, Barnes needed a rebound this season to not only justify his contract, but justify a spot on the team long-term. If this is what we are getting in 2026, the Lions are in a good spot. Barnes was a force on Sunday. After missing a tackle early in the game, Barnes locked in the rest of the way. As a run defender, he was stout, racking up a tackle for loss and multiple run stops. In coverage, Barnes looked surprisingly stellar. He reeled in an interception on the first play of the second half, with the Lions promptly turning that into a touchdown. He also added two critical pass breakups, one of which broke up a touchdown in overtime (although the Saints scored on the very next play). Oh, and he had a sack too—a complete game for Barnes. If the Lions can get Barnes playing at a high level with Jack Campbell, you have to be optimistic about this linebacking duo. Dan Campbell was a fan: #Lions coach Dan Campbell: Derrick Barnes was all over the field. You could feel that. — Nolan Bianchi (@nolanbianchi) September 13, 2026 Loser: Jameson Williams, WR On a day when the Lions offense was quiet through the air, they needed a playmaker like Williams to step up. Instead, he had a rough season debut. He finished the game with four catches for 45 yards, but it should have been far more than that. Late in the first quarter, Goff threw a perfect deep ball to Williams, but it bounced off both hands. On that same drive, he had another near-catch, but it was broken up at the last second by a defender—hard to say if it should have been caught, but I’m still waiting for a good replay, FOX. In the second quarter, he bobbled a reverse pitch (although Goff said it was a “crappy pitch” from himself). In the third quarter, Williams failed to corral a third-down pass, ending the drive. With under a minute left in the game, another ball went off the fingertips of Williams, forcing a punt. We all know how explosive he can be, and despite a 1,117-yard season last year, his ceiling could be even higher. However, if you are a dynamic playmaker with the ball in your hands, you need to keep the ball in your hands. Winner: Juice Scruggs, C The whole offensive line deserves props for a solid outing ( as Goff said himself ). Penei Sewell looked like a natural at left tackle, while Tate Ratledge and Blake Miller were stout on the right side of the line. Ben Bartch, filling in for an injured Christian Mahogany, had some positive moments. However, I want to give attention to Scruggs in particular. Scruggs was already penciled in as the starting center due to Cade Mays’ injury back in training camp, but there was some concern about how he would perform. The Lions’ run game had thrived under Frank Ragnow’s command, but when they had to pivot to Graham Glasgow in 2025, the offensive line regressed—they could not afford a repeat in 2026. Thankfully, Scruggs showed up. A lot of Gibbs’ success on the ground can be attributed to Scruggs blocking open lanes for him. As for pass protection, Goff was kept clean for most of the game, with Scruggs in particular rarely allowing pressure up the middle. Scruggs looked like a starter, which is something that most teams cannot say about their backup center. Mays will surely regain that spot when he is healthy, but Scruggs profiles as a top-tier reserve—and he could perhaps challenge for the left guard spot as was originally planned. Loser: Rock Ya-Sin, CB For as good as the defense looked on Sunday, Ya-Sin was unfortunately an outlier. The Lions’ CB2 is an asset in run defense, but he had a tough performance in coverage. He was flagged for illegal contact in the second quarter, albeit on a very iffy call. His next penalty, a pass interference call late in the third, gave the Saints life on third down. On the very next goal line play, Ya-Sin was beat badly by Devaugh Vele for an easy touchdown grab. D.J. Reed had a decent outing (though he allowed a 43-yarder to Chris Olave late), but that second cornerback spot looks like a glaring weakness. Remember, the Lions play in a division with receiving duos Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, and Rome Odunze and Luther Burden. Do we trust both Reed and Ya-Sin to hold up? Ya-Sin redeemed himself by breaking up a game-winning two-point attempt in overtime, but he was beat in coverage too often for me to feel comfortable. Unless the Lions can get a rebound from Ya-Sin, you have to wonder what the solution to this problem could be. Do you give Roger McCreary, Keith Abney, or Ennis Rakestraw some looks outside? Do you go shopping for a player like Joey Porter Jr. and his contract demands? I expect Ya-Sin to be the starter going forward, but I need some more encouraging play. Winner: Defensive line I was very impressed with the defensive line. Five total sacks looks good on paper, but there was more to this performance than just sacks. Each member of that unit was clogging running lanes and bringing heat on a consistent basis. Aidan Hutchinson got two of the sacks, one of which came against a running back—a staggering mismatch for the Saints. Alim McNeill had a crucial sack in overtime, a play that would normally win you the game. Barnes had his aforementioned sack, but you have to credit Hutchinson, Skyler-Gill Howard, and DJ Wonnum for collapsing the pocket and forcing Tyler Shough to step into Barnes. Even on Roger McCreary’s strip sack, it was the defensive line eating up blockers that allowed McCreary to slip by unopposed. Gill-Howard in particular stood out. He had his moments, sure, but what really surprised me was the sheer volume of snaps. Per PFF, he played 47 snaps on defense, more than Chuck Clark, Roger McCreary, and even fellow defensive tackle Tyleik Williams. The Lions clearly love him in that pass rushing role, and if the Lions continue to jump out to early leads, expect him to stay busy. The promising thing is that the Lions still have room to improve—Gill-Howard, Williams, and Derrick Moore are still growing. This could be a great defensive line before too long. Loser: Sione Vaki, RB…

title: Christian Mahogany injury update: Detroit Lions get good initial news
summary: The Detroit Lions entered the 2026 season with a competition still brewing at left guard between Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch. The Lions, as Dan Campbell hinted at, opted to start Mahogany in the season opener, but he wouldn’t last long. On Detroit’s second offensive possession of the game, Mahogany fell to the turf on […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Christian Mahogany #73 of the Detroit Lions goes down with an injury against the New Orleans Saints during the first half of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions entered the 2026 season with a competition still brewing at left guard between Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch. The Lions, as Dan Campbell hinted at, opted to start Mahogany in the season opener, but he wouldn’t last long. On Detroit’s second offensive possession of the game, Mahogany fell to the turf on a big Jahmyr Gibbs run. He would stay down for a few minutes before walking off under his own power. After being examined on the sideline, Mahogany was carted to the locker room. The Lions officially announced him as questionable to return with a knee injury. Bartch took over for Mahogany, as expected, and the Lions were able to close out the rest of the drive with a touchdown to take an early lead over the New Orleans Saints. We will update this post with any news on Mahogany’s condition, including any change in his status or an update from coach Dan Campbell. UPDATE : Mahogany was downgraded to out in the second half. UPDATE 2: The Lions appeared to have gotten good news on Mahogany’s injury, despite it looking bad. Lions coach Dan Campbell told reporters after the game that initial tests were negative, but he’s still being cautiously optimistic. “We did do a scan that ended up being negative, so that’s good news, but that doesn’t mean we’re out of the woods,” Campbell said. “Sounds like it could be more hip-ish maybe, but we’ll see.”

title: 5 takeaways from Detroit Lions’  overtime win against New Orleans Saints
summary: The Detroit Lions kicked off their 2026 season at home, taking on the New Orleans Saints, an up-and-coming team in the NFC. Expectations are raised for Detroit this season after a disappointing 2025 campaign, and with an easy schedule, this could be the team’s best chance at reaching the Super Bowl. It was a quiet […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Derrick Barnes #55 of the Detroit Lions celebrates sack against the New Orleans Saints during the third quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions kicked off their 2026 season at home, taking on the New Orleans Saints, an up-and-coming team in the NFC. Expectations are raised for Detroit this season after a disappointing 2025 campaign, and with an easy schedule, this could be the team’s best chance at reaching the Super Bowl. It was a quiet start for the Lions offense, scoring on their second drive of the game, but it wasn’t until the third quarter that they scored again. The defense and special teams kept Detroit in the game despite the sluggish start, holding the Saints scoreless until just past the halfway mark of the third quarter. Once the Saints found the end zone, the game flipped on its head and needed overtime to decide a winner. After the Lions offense moved down the field and scored, the game was decided on a two-point conversion that the Saints couldn’t complete, with Detroit winning 31-30 Here are my five takeaways from the Lions’ win against the Saints in Week 1. Gibbs continues to be the lifeblood of the offense With Detroit trading away former running back David Montgomery, the backfield was handed solely to Jahmyr Gibbs. Gibbs did more than run the ball today, catching multiple passes. While his biggest play was for 21 yards, he made the most of every chance he got the ball. Gibbs also saw more playing time with his new backup, Isiah Pacheco, starting off on IR. . @Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs produces his 50th-career TD. He is the 6th player in @NFL history to accumulate 50+ TDs in 50-career games. #OnePride pic.twitter.com/N4q5y8JeQo — Detroit Lions PR (@LionsPR) September 13, 2026 Gibbs finished the game with 29 carries for 156 yards, finding the end zone twice, and five catches for 30 yards. With Pacheco out, expect Gibbs to continue to get the bulk of touches. The depth at the position has little in-game experience, with Sione Vaki getting just two carries for 7 yards and a catch for 11. This offense had a rough game; even Gibbs fumbled at one point, but he was their most consistent player. He moved the chains, wasn’t afraid of contact, and did whatever he could to help the team win. He’s the lifeblood of this offense, and they’ll need him to keep up with the heavy workload if this team can succeed this season. Lions run defense returns to form After being a dominant run defense for the past few seasons, the Lions struggled to stop the run in 2025. The team wanted to get back to that identity on defense, and they answered the call against the Saints. Saints running back Travis Etienne Jr. led the team with nine carries for 46 yards, followed by Kendre Miller with nine carries for 30 yards and a touchdown. The Lions also did a good job in limiting Saints quarterback Tyler Shough from making plays with his legs, containing him to eight yards on four carries. When Shough tried to move around and make a play, he faced pressure from all over and was sacked five times. Detroit held the Saints to 91 rushing yards, averaging 3.6 yards per carry. If the run defense and pass rush can hold their own, it’ll be the main reason the defense can stop opposing offenses. Secondary woes are blaring Heading into this game, the Saints rostered four wide receivers, with Chris Olave as the biggest threat. Behind him, the Saints have a bunch of players who are either rookies or lack experience. The Lions secondary held its own in the first half, getting an interception and making it difficult for Shough to complete passes. In the second half, the Saints found success repeatedly and picked apart the Lions’ pass defense. Receivers like Devaughn Vele and Bryce Lance were making big catches on fourth down or diving for the ball. Lions cornerbacks Rock Ya-Sin and D.J. Reed couldn’t cover whoever they were matched up against, allowing Olave to finish with a career-high 182 yards on 10 catches. Vele had seven catches for 69 yards and a touchdown. If the Lions secondary is struggling against a team’s lackluster receiving core, it will only get worse when they face a better group. They allowed a total of 410 passing yards and three touchdowns, an awful way to start the year for them. Turnovers and special teams come up big It wasn’t just the run defense that shined for the Lions on Sunday; it was the playmaking ability as well. In the first half, the defense made big pass breakups, tackles for loss, and came away with only one turnover. To start the second half, Detroit’s defense made massive plays to give them momentum. ACTIVATE: SPIDEY-SENSE pic.twitter.com/BU0F9yVUIv — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 13, 2026 It started on the first play of the second half with linebacker Derrick Barnes picking off Shough. Detroit capitalized on that turnover and scored to make it 14-0. On the next drive, Barnes would get a sack, and cornerback Roger McCreary came in for a strip sack, recovered by Detroit. McCreary with the strip-sack, Wonnum with the recovery!! pic.twitter.com/IYTU59YpVk — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 13, 2026 The Lions scored on that drive too, making it 21-0 early in the third quarter and quickly putting the Saints in a hole. Without those turnovers, Detroit doesn’t win this game. You also got to give a shoutout to special teams, as the coverage on punts and kickoffs was excellent, and punter Jack Fox had a solid game, punting it seven times for 336 yards, three of them landing inside the 20 and one touchback. With the Saints repeatedly backed up, the defense had plenty of cushion and chances to be aggressive. Guard rotation happened, but not the way anyone expected One of the biggest storylines entering the game was who would start at left guard for the Lions. The battle between Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch was supposed to happen all training camp, but Bartch dealt with injuries. When Bartch returned, Lions head coach Dan Campbell mentioned the starting job wasn’t locked yet, and the two could even rotate in the game. Mahogany appeared to win the job, but he left the game in the first half with an injury and didn’t return. He walked off the field with help from the trainers, but later left the game on the cart. If Mahogany is out for a while, I think Bartch will be the starting left guard, with Miles Frazier backing him up and right guard Tate Ratledge. After the game, Campbell said that initial tests on Mahogany’s knee were negative, but “they’re not out of the woods with that injury.” He also revealed it could be more of a hip injury.
author: Brandon Knapp

title: You cannot overstate how bad the Packers’ offensive line was on Sunday
summary: I just had the misfortune of watching the Green Bay Packers’ offense on All-22, the third (and final) time I’ve watched the Minnesota Vikings game so far. To make this short: The Packers’ offensive line looked like a second-rate high school team, passing stunts off to no one, turning guys loose when they had to […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images I just had the misfortune of watching the Green Bay Packers’ offense on All-22, the third (and final) time I’ve watched the Minnesota Vikings game so far. To make this short: The Packers’ offensive line looked like a second-rate high school team, passing stunts off to no one, turning guys loose when they had to and getting edged in pass protection left and right. These guards are going to get Jordan killed pic.twitter.com/YmHgGUDNnk — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 14, 2026 Jordan Love deserves a medal of honor for this game. He will not last 17 games if they continue to play like this. Every single offensive lineman disappointed, with the guards disappointing the most and Jordan Morgan disappointing the least. Pass-rush win rate leaders through Sunday's action (min. 20 pass-rush snaps) pic.twitter.com/7s27wEq0ak — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) September 14, 2026 For the most part, the tackles held up decently, aside from their matchups against Dallas Turner. Turner, who had not done great in his first two years in the NFL after being drafted in the first round, had the best game of his career on Sunday. Maybe this is a breakout year for him. Maybe the Packers’ offensive line is just bad. Either way, everyone expected better out of Green Bay’s front, who, despite their shortcomings over the years, were arguably the best team in the league in terms of giving their players extra help, preventing one player from taking over a game and developing a pass protection plan. In this game, Love was hit 15 times, officially, and more than that unofficially. Every NFL defensive play caller ranked by blitz rate in Week 1: Brian Flores: 82.1% Dan Quinn: 50.9% Aaron Glenn: 44.9% Jesse Minter: 43.4% Kelvin Sheppard: 43.0% Todd Bowles: 42.9% Lou Anarumo: 39.1% Mike Macdonald: 35.8% Vic Fangio: 35.8% Christian Parker: 35.3% Zak Kuhr:… — Ryan Paganetti (@RyanPaganetti) September 14, 2026 Yes, Brian Flores blitzed like crazy, even for Flores’ standards. I would have, too, considering how the line played. Even when the Packers were max protecting and running bootlegs, it didn’t look like the team knew the rules they were supposed to be playing, resulting in players being turned loose. According to NFL Pro, Love dropped back 46 times on Sunday, the second-most of any quarterback in Week 1 — only behind the Saints’ Tyler Shough. As a reminder, New Orleans played in an OVERTIME GAME yesterday. NFL Pro has the Packers down for 176 routes run in the game, meaning that Green Bay had 54 extra blockers over Love’s 46 dropbacks in the game, 1.2 per play. At some point, it doesn’t matter if you have extra blockers if the offensive line is performing poorly and guys are getting loose anyway. Both the Lions and Vikings were top 3 in Week 1 in rush/coverage disguise rate, based on pre-snap alignment. pic.twitter.com/3nkiAKsrEC — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 Does Flores drop guys who look like they’re blitzing and blitz guys who look like they’re dropping? Yes! You know who else does that? The New York Jets, the Packers’ next opponent, and the Detroit Lions, who they’ll play twice in divisional play this year. They need to get this issue figured out. Brian Flores is insane pic.twitter.com/HnfEPV3Dvi — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) September 14, 2026 What the Vikings did was a complete and total pantsing of the Packers’ pass protection unit on Sunday. If it doesn’t get better (maybe Aaron Banks’ return will help — hell, there are no bad ideas right now), it’s going to be a long season.

title: Packers Film Room: Christian Watson doubles-up
summary: We’ll be dissecting the film on the overall Green Bay Packers offense & passing game later (we already did a little of it with numbers), but, for now, I just wanted to take a few minutes and talk about the game Christian Watson had. With only the Monday Night game left to play, Watson currently […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’ll be dissecting the film on the overall Green Bay Packers offense & passing game later (we already did a little of it with numbers ), but, for now, I just wanted to take a few minutes and talk about the game Christian Watson had. With only the Monday Night game left to play, Watson currently has the 3rd highest EPA of the week at 13.98 (behind Chris Olave’s 15.42 and Zay Flowers’ 14.06). Per SumerSports , he primarily aligned as the outside receiver (75% of his snaps were outside), and 100% of his targets came when he was the outside receiver. He had an ADOT (Average Depth of Target) of 15.9 yards and had 73 yards of YAC (Yards After Catch). He is currently tied with Zay Flowers for the lead in YACOE (Yards After Catch Over Expectation) with +49 (per NFL Pro ). If you want to talk just regular stats, he caught 6 of his 8 targets for 147 yards (18.4 YPA) and 2 TDs. With those numbers, Jordan Love posted a QB Rating of 156.3 when targeting Watson. Let’s take a look at his two TD receptions. Play 1: 2nd & 10, 7:54 remaining in the 1st quarter The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR), starting in a 2×2 shotgun spread look. Tucker Kraft [85] is initially wide on the right, but he slow-motions pre-snap and ends up under the left tackle, leaving Christian Watson [9] as the lone skill player on the right side of the field. The Vikings have 7 bodies at the line and are showing a completely open middle of the field. With Brian Flores calling the defense, you can’t be sure if he’s blitzing everyone at the line or dropping some back into coverage. At the snap, Watson is running a deep in-cutter. On the other side of the field, Jayden Reed [11] is running a flat route while Matthew Golden [0] is running a big post route over the top. That works effectively to clear out some space on the left. Theo Jackson [26] – one of the Vikings’ safeties – starts this play on the edge, opposite of Watson. Blake Cashman [51] is the linebacker who is originally walked-up over the center. At the snap, both of them drop back to the middle. Cashman is more of a straight drop, while Jackson is buzzing back at an angle. Love takes a quick glance at Jackson off the edge and sees the drop. He then moves his eyes back to the middle and sees Cashman. He holds Cashman in place long enough to pry the window open. Love hits Watson just in front of the buzzing Jackson, and Watson does the rest, erasing angles all the way to the end zone. Play 2: 2nd & 2, 00:18 remaining in the 2nd quarter With 18 seconds left in the first half, the Packers trot out 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) at the 2 yard line. They’re in an under center, YY Wing formation (both TEs in-line on the same side). Watson is in a condensed split on the right, while Golden is split wide to the left. Watson motions pre-snap into an insert position. In this YY Wing formation, that puts him under the line between the two TEs. This is something the Packers do a lot as part of their run game, and Watson’s strengths as a blocker put him in that position quite a bit. It’s a way to give the offense an extra blocker at the point of attack. As we’ll see here, it’s also a useful tool in the passing game. The Packers play action to the Wing side, then Love continues with a sprint-out to the right. The Vikings are biting on the play action, so the defender over Watson is expecting to meet him in the hole for a block. Instead, Watson slips right by him and finds a ton of open space. Love flips it out for the easy TD. I love this playcall. I’m always a huge fan of releasing the insert blocker through the line, especially when you can sell the play action. Albums listened to: Karina Rykman – Joyride ; Beach House – Depression Cherry

title: Packers Discussion: 1st impressions of Jonathan Gannon’s defense
summary: I’m sure that we’re going to talk about the offensive line a lot this week, so I just want to give this space for people to fire off their thoughts on another major subject: the first game that Jonathan Gannon called on the defensive side of the ball. For the most part, I thought the […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is shown during the third quarter of their game Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026 at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Minnesota Vikings beat the Green Bay Packers 39-22. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co I’m sure that we’re going to talk about the offensive line a lot this week, so I just want to give this space for people to fire off their thoughts on another major subject: the first game that Jonathan Gannon called on the defensive side of the ball. For the most part, I thought the defense did fine on Sunday. The defense gave up 3.1 yards per attempt in the run game and 4.9 yards per dropback. It’s amazing how the Minnesota Vikings were able to get 39 points with those numbers. They scored 29 points straight with only one drive over 28 yards, because the offense not only was getting off the field quickly but also giving the defense short fields to defend. What really hurt Green Bay at the end was that Carrington Valentine was playing snaps at cornerback, as he was run at directly for a touchdown and gave up another score to Justin Jefferson on a catch-and-run opportunity. In general, the Packers pretty much played their base 3-4 defense and nickel defenses, as the Penny defense was sort of shelved. I thought Gannon put Lukas Van Ness and Edgerrin Cooper in really good positions to succeed, leading to some of their best games as pros. Keisean Nixon had a good game, too. Zaire Franklin didn’t get exposed in coverage, outside of the touchdown where he was the runner in Tampa 2 (a changeup play that Green Bay just got caught in). title: Packers open Week 2 as favorites against Jets
summary: The Green Bay Packers may have made history with their collapse against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 1, but that does not mean that they are going to be underdogs in Week 2. Indeed, the opening lines at FanDuel sportsbook have the Packers installed as 4.5-point favorites for their road trip to play the New […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 09: Matthew Golden #22 of the Green Bay Packers is tackled by Brandon Stephens #21 of the New York Jets during the NFL Preseason 2025 game between New York Jets and Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on August 09, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers may have made history with their collapse against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 1, but that does not mean that they are going to be underdogs in Week 2. Indeed, the opening lines at FanDuel sportsbook have the Packers installed as 4.5-point favorites for their road trip to play the New York Jets next Sunday. Green Bay’s 0-1 start was due, in large part, to the team’s struggles on the offensive line. Facing a Vikings defense that blitzed over 75 percent of the time, the interior of the line struggled massively, leading to four 4th-quarter sacks and a pair of turnovers. Those giveaways gifted the Vikings great field position, leading to multiple scores as they ran away with a 39-22 victory. The Jets, on the other hand, started the season 1-0 with a road victory. However, theirs comes with a caveat: it came against the Tennessee Titans, who might well be in line to earn the #1 overall pick in the NFL Draft for the second time in three years. The Jets won 23-10 on Sunday afternoon, sacking Cam Ward three times and getting a 100-yard day on the ground from running back Breece Hall. The Packers’ defense actually held up largely well for most of the game in Minnesota when not dealing with a short field. They also largely bottled up the Vikings’ running game, allowing 3.1 yards per carry for the game, a number that is even inflated due to a single 28-yard run by Jordan Mason. Compared to late last year, this unit looks improved through one game, though they started to struggle late in the game with wide zone and stretch runs, including that long gain. The Packers and Jets combined to score 45 points in their week one games, which is right on the books’ expectation. The over/under total points line for the matchup comes in at 44.5, which combined with the point spread suggests that they expect about a 24-20 victory for the Packers.

title: Green Bay Packers News: The Matt LaFleur discourse has only just begun
summary: When Matt LaFleur took three points off the board on Sunday afternoon in Minneapolis, the goal was clear: he wanted his Green Bay Packers to go score a touchdown and take a commanding two-possession lead over the Minnesota Vikings. Instead, wiping out a field goal meant his offense needed convert a 4th-and-1 to keep the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers calls a play during the fourth quarter of the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Matt LaFleur took three points off the board on Sunday afternoon in Minneapolis, the goal was clear: he wanted his Green Bay Packers to go score a touchdown and take a commanding two-possession lead over the Minnesota Vikings. Instead, wiping out a field goal meant his offense needed convert a 4th-and-1 to keep the drive alive, which they didn’t do, and from that point on the whole team fell apart. There’s a process vs. results aspect to the analysis of this decision. If Love picks up the yard he needed on a quarterback sneak and the Packers go punch the ball into the end zone, we might be having a different discussion. Then again, the Vikings’ blitz might have gotten to Love later on that drive and forced a turnover — like they did on the Packers’ next two possessions — making the whole thing moot. Ultimately, another blown double-digit second-half lead will only further inflame the discourse around LaFleur and whether he’s the right coach to lead the Packers in the future. Unfortunately for those who believe otherwise, he just signed a new contract extension in January. In all likelihood, he’s not going anywhere; at least not unless the Packers completely bottom out this season. Still, this collapse came about in a rather different way than those of the last few years. It wasn’t just the offense stalling out and the defense hemorrhaging yards on long drives; instead, the defense was put in terrible positions all second half, first by a long kickoff return, then by garbage penalties, then by multiple turnovers by an offense that looked like it couldn’t block a Pop Warner squad. To that end, three of the Vikings’ last four touchdown drives saw them take over inside the Packers’ 30, with two inside the 15 and one at the one-yard line. The way the collapse happened raises new questions, and yet the same old questions will swirl around LaFleur until this team figures out how to close. Rapid reaction: It’s up to the Packers to change the narrative | Packers.com One of LaFleur’s common lines after the game yesterday was “You’ve got to answer.” Hopefully that’s directed at himself and his offensive staff as much as his players, as the coaches had no answer for a Vikings pass rush that finally opened the floodgates in the second half. Offensive line struggles continue to haunt Green Bay Packers offense | Packersnews.com That said, this team has enormous questions at guard, and it was rapidly clear on Sunday that Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk were in over their heads. In Search for Finishing Touch, LaFleur’s Aggressive Approach Finishes Packers | SI.com Your mileage may vary on how much blame you put on the decision to eschew points in favor of a 4th down attempt. Personally, I don’t know that the final result would have actually changed whether they took the points or if they had converted on Love’s sneak attempt. Packers lost to Vikings in a uniquely terrible way to open season | Packers Wire Isn’t it great to make history right out of the gate? Apparently this was the first time in NFL history that a team led by 12 or more points with 20 minutes to go and ended up losing by at least 17. LISTEN: The Repack, Week 1 — Here We Go Again | Frozen Tundra Frequencies Normally, there’s a silver lining to a loss. It sure is tough to find one coming out of this game, though, but at least one APC commenter is trying: Snoop Dogg wants to pay someone US$10K a month to taste ice cream | Globalnews.ca Sure, why not. Nothing they can make you try will be worse than the taste in Packers fans’ mouths after that game. Download the SB Nation app today! title: Packers Snap Counts, Week 1: Kaleb Johnson absent on offense
summary: Below are the snap counts from the Green Bay Packers’ season-opening loss to the Minnesota Vikings, position-by-position. These numbers only count contributions to the offensive and defensive sides of the ball. Let’s dig into what the Packers showed in Week 1. Quarterback Jordan Love played every single snap of the game, but if the offensive […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Below are the snap counts from the Green Bay Packers’ season-opening loss to the Minnesota Vikings, position-by-position. These numbers only count contributions to the offensive and defensive sides of the ball. Let’s dig into what the Packers showed in Week 1. Quarterback Jordan Love: 67 snaps Tyrod Taylor: 0 Jordan Love played every single snap of the game, but if the offensive line continues to play as they did on Sunday , we’ll see Tyrod Taylor sooner rather than later. Running Back Chris Brooks: 37 MarShawn Lloyd: 30 Kaleb Johnson: 0 The Packers sent a pick to the Pittsburgh Steelers for second-year running back Kaleb Johnson at the cutdown deadline, and despite Johnson having prior experience with offensive coordinator Tim Lester (a former Matt LaFleur analyst) and offensive coordinator Arthur Smith (a former LaFleur assistant), Johnson did not play a single snap of offense against the Vikings. Chris Brooks was Green Bay’s “top” back, though MarShawn Lloyd carried the ball more (13 carries for 37 yards) than Brooks (seven carries for 29 yards). Reciever Matthew Golden: 55 Christian Watson: 52 Jayden Reed: 38 Bo Melton: 7 Skyy Moore: 4 The receiver rotation is dead. Long gone are the days when the Packers tried to get five players involved in the game equally. Right now, Matthew Golden and Christian Watson are the clear starters at outside receiver, and Jayden Reed is the team’s slot receiver. Watson (six receptions, 147 yards and two touchdowns) and Golden (six receptions and 95 yards) led the team through the air. Tight End Tucker Kraft: 44 Jonnu Smith: 32 Mark Redman: 21 Josh Whyle: 11 Both Tucker Kraft and Jonnu Smith were involved in the passing game, bringing in a total of five receptions for 115 yards. Third-tight end Mark Redman was used mostly as a blocking tight end from in-line positions, while Josh Whyle was fourth in the pecking order at the position. Eventually, the team won’t be able to carry these four tight ends because they’ll need numbers elsewhere, on top of the fact that tight end Luke Musgrave (neck) is expected to return to the 53-man roster at some point during 2026. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 67 (LT) Donovan Jennings: 67 (LG) Sean Rhyan: 67 (C) Jacob Monk: 67 (RG) Zach Bako-Bewele: 67 (RT) Anthony Belton: 4 Jager Burton: 0 John Williams: 0 The Packers’ offensive line played so poorly by the end of the game that the Vikings scored 29 consecutive points while only posting one drive of more than 28 yards. Not only was Green Bay’s line playing to a level where the offense was giving up the ball, but they were giving up the ball quickly and on short fields. In the fourth quarter, here was the Packers’ drive chart: turnover on downs, fumble, interception and turnover on downs. Aaron Banks (knee tendinitis) wasn’t able to suit up at left guard, so Donovan Jennings stepped in as the starter there. Both Jennings and Jacob Monk (right guard) had tough goes at it. I’m guessing we’ll see rookie Jager Burton at some point this month. Defensive Line Karl Brooks: 35 Devonte Wyatt: 33 Jonathan Ford: 28 Javon Hargrave: 27 Chris McClellan: 26 The Packers treated Karl Brooks and Devonte Wyatt as true starters this preseason, so it shouldn’t be too surprising that they led the team in snaps played on the defensive line. Jonathan Ford played 3-4 nose tackle (with Brooks and Wyatt at 3-4 ends), while Javon Hargrave and Chris McClellan rotated in from the bench. Whenever Warren Brinson, who was inactive in this game with a calf injury, comes back, there’s a question of whether he or McClellan, a third-round rookie, will be scratched. Anthony Campbell was also a healthy scratch in this game. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness: 39 Barryn Sorrell: 36 Brenton Cox Jr.: 27 Dani Dennis-Sutton: 21 Nothing is surprising here, as Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell have been the starters on the edge throughout the summer. When Micah Parsons comes back from his ACL tear, everyone will move down a spot in the pecking order. Van Ness continued the strong end of his 2025 campaign and had one of his better games in his NFL career. Off-Ball Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper: 61 Zaire Franklin: 61 Isaiah McDuffie: 1 Nick Niemann: 0 Kristian Welch: 0 The three-linebacker defense in Green Bay is dead, which was expected under defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. It’s the Zaire Franklin (Mike) and Edgerrin Cooper (Will) show moving forward. Outside of that, opportunities for playing time will be limited to short-yardage looks and snaps for injury replacements. Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 61 Brandon Cisse: 48 Carrington Valentine: 13 Benjamin St-Juste: 1 Kamal Hadden: 0 Keisean Nixona and Brandon Cisse started this game, but for whatever reason, Cisse was benched at the end of the game for Carrington Valentine. Valentine gave up two touchdowns in the fourth quarter, one on a play where he was run at and one on a play where he allowed Justin Jefferson to catch a ball and hit the pylon. Update: Cisse had cramps. https://t.co/IekW4CkXAr — Peter Bukowski (@Peter_Bukowski) September 14, 2026 Cisse had cramps at the end of the game. I missed that piece of information. Safety Evan Williams: 61 Xavier McKinney: 61 Javon Bullard: 32 Kitan Oladapo: 0 Nothing shocking here, as Evan Williams and Xavier McKinney are the starting safeties, while Javon Bullard is the starting slot defender on the team. This is pretty much what should be expected moving forward. If there’s anything to take from this, it’s that the Packers were about a 50/50 split between playing their base 3-4 defense and subpackages (mostly nickel) in Week 1.
