title: Packers Week 1: Stats from Green Bay’s season-opening loss
summary: Recently, SumerSports rolled out SumerLive, which tracks a lot of tremendous data live for each game. It’s something I’ve enjoyed clicking around, and I did a test drive for the third preseason game. It seemed to go well, so we’re keeping it rolling into the regular season. Is this a game anyone on this site […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers throws a pass during the third quarter of the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Recently, SumerSports rolled out SumerLive , which tracks a lot of tremendous data live for each game. It’s something I’ve enjoyed clicking around, and I did a test drive for the third preseason game . It seemed to go well, so we’re keeping it rolling into the regular season. Is this a game anyone on this site currently wants to relive? Probably not! But we’re taking a look, anyway. Offense As you might expect, the full game numbers aren’t great. Those are mainly due to an absolutely wretched second half. For the game, the Packers posted a negative EPA in both the pass game (-0.07) and run game (-0.37). They posted a 41.3% Success Rate in the passing game and a 33.3% Success Rate in the running game. Not a great showing there. The first half was good from a passing game perspective, with a +0.39 EPA per Play. Their pass game Success Rate of 36.8% was bad. The difference between those numbers shows an offense that was hitting on some explosive plays, but didn’t have great down-to-down consistency. Part of that was the pressure. For the game, Brian Flores had the Vikings bringing an insane amount of heat. They blitzed on 73.91% of defensive snaps (50.79% above the NFL average), with a pressure rate of 56.52% (17.97% above the NFL average). For the game, Love had an average time to pressure of 2.3 seconds and an average time to throw of 2.45 seconds. For a bit of perspective on that, Aaron Rodgers was the QB with the fastest time to throw in 2025, and he averaged 2.59 seconds. Love was throwing the ball 0.14 seconds faster and was targeting deep (Love’s Average Depth of Target was 11.35 yards). Digging into the larger game, the Packers were much more pass-heavy in this game. For the game, they had a pass rate of 68.7%. That holds more-or-less true by half (70.4% pass rate in the 1st half, 67.5% in the 2nd half), but the quarter breakdown is interesting. Here is the pass rate by quarter: 1st: 58.3% 2nd: 80% 3rd: 47.4% 4th: 85.7% That 3rd quarter is the interesting one. Being a bit more balanced in the 1st quarter tracks: you’re in the script so there’s an information-gathering aspect to it. The run wasn’t working, and you like what you’re seeing in the pass game, so you lean into the pass game. Then the 3rd quarter hits and you think you can try to slow it down and establish the run. The problem is that the running game was bad overall, and that didn’t change in the 3rd quarter. They had an EPA per Play of -0.21 and a Success Rate of 40%. With the way the Vikings were blitzing, I understand the approach to some extent, but you’re banging your head against the wall a bit. As far as personnel usage, the Packers were in 11 personnel 47.8% of the time, 12 personnel 31.3% of the time, 13 personnel 14.9% of the time and “Other” 6% of the time (I assume that’s a 6OL package, but I can’t confirm that at the moment). (For the personnel numbering, the first number is the number of running backs on the field, the second number is the number of tight ends on the field and the number of wide receivers is assumed based on there being 5 potential skill position players. So 11 personnel is 1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR.) Their run game mix wasn’t all that different than what we saw last year in terms of % of concepts called. They were 52.3% zone, 47.7% man/power. Their Inside Zone run was only called 4 times, but it was their best run by EPA (+0.06 EPA per Play). Defense From a personnel perspective, the Packers were split right down the middle: 49.2% Base, 49.2% Nickel, 1.6% Dime. They were primarily in Zone, with a rate of 83.3%. I mentioned this in my preseason post, but all Zone coverage is not just “drop back and cover this square of grass with your eyes on the QB.” Gannon runs a Quarters-based Match system, which means a lot of his coverages are zone coverages that can look like Man coverage, with the responsibilities of the defenders changing depending on the route distribution. SumerSports tracks the different types of zone coverages and I was able to get that breakdown through their SumerBrain option. Here’s that breakdown of types of zone coverage: Cover 3: 32% Cover 6: 24% Cover 2: 24% Cover 4: 20% The Packers had a blitz rate of 30% and a pressure rate of 40%. Last year, the Cardinals had a blitz rate of 25.1% and a pressure rate of 32.7% with Rich Gannon as the head coach. The pressure game overall was better than I expected, so I’m curious how those numbers will look over the next few weeks. Albums listened to: Ed O’Brien – Blue Morpho ; Spanish Love Songs – Brave Faces Everyone
author: Dusty Evely

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Week 1 vs. the Vikings
summary: Week 1 is officially over for the Green Bay Packers, and I don’t ever want to speak of it again. The team traveled to Minnesota to face off against the Vikings on Sunday, and things were going well for the Packers until The Spiral™ began. After leading for most of the game, things fell apart, […]
full_text: (Photo by Nick Wosika/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Week 1 is officially over for the Green Bay Packers, and I don’t ever want to speak of it again. The team traveled to Minnesota to face off against the Vikings on Sunday, and things were going well for the Packers until The Spiral™ began. After leading for most of the game, things fell apart, and the Packers left the stadium with an 0-1 record after a 39-22 loss. You know the drill. Let’s dive in. Winner: Christian Watson WR Christian Watson finished the game first half with 5 catches for 131 yards and 2 TDs. The entire Minnesota offense had 136 yards at halftime. With the departures of Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks in the offseason, and a contract extension signed this June, it was pretty evident Watson would be cemented as the Packers #1 receiver this year. And, like a moth to a flame, QB Jordan Love found him again and again during Sunday’s game. Watson is tough to beat downfield, and his hands have become extremely reliable. The receiver finished the game with 6 catches on 8 targets for 147 yards, and 2 TDs. I think we’re going to be seeing a lot more of this in 2026, unless the offensive line continues to exist in its current form. Christian Watson 81-yard catch-and-run! GBvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SVOKajdaok — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Another long connection between Love and Watson 🎯 GBvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jFylZSxW2q — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Winner: Keisean Nixon The always-chirpy DB faced a ton of scrutiny and criticism after the 2025 season ended, as well as throughout preseason. He’s never been one to humble himself, and this week, he backed it all up. On the very first play of the game, Nixon stopped RB Aaron Jones for a 1 yard loss. The next play? An interception with an 11 yard return. He combined for a sack with Jonathan Ford in the second quarter. And, in the third quarter, he applied heavy pressure on QB Carson Wentz, forcing a very quick incomplete pass. In total, Nixon had 5 tackles, including 1 for a loss, with 2 QB hits and 1 PD. Sounds good to me! Keisean Nixon intercepts the first pass of the game GBvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rV7m8xe3TQ — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Winner: Jordan Love Don’t let the stat line fool you: QB Jordan Love had just about as good a game as I’ve ever seen from him, and it came in spite of the offensive line actively trying to get him killed. In the first quarter, he threw the longest TD pass of his career, an 81 yard bomb to Christian Watson. Later, he had a 30 yarder to TE Tucker Kraft. As the second quarter wound down, he made another massive heave to Watson to get the offense close to the endzone. This was all while he was forced to get the ball out quickly, and getting hit in the middle of doing so. Escapes the sack, makes the off-balance throw, gets the first down. Jordan Love making it look easy. GBvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dDufriCdLl — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 In the second half, while escaping heavy pressure, he had the above great pass to Kraft for a first down. There was also a 44 yard bomb to TE Jonnu Smith. Matthew Golden got in on the action with a beautiful 42 yard play. Can you imagine how great he would’ve looked without the world crashing down around him? GOODNESS. Love finished the game 21 of 42 for 387 yards, 2 TDs, 1 INT, and 2 fumbles, while taking 4 sacks. A wide open Jonnu Smith gets inside the 10 😤 GBvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/mNammn1Htl — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Winner: Edgerrin Cooper LB Edgerrin Cooper had probably the best game of anyone on the defense. He was all over the field, and he was disruptive. There was a massive stop at the point of catch which forced the Vikings to punt during the first half. He also had a couple TFLs, including a massive sack on 2nd and 6 in the third quarter. He would’ve been credited with another game-changing sack on the very next play, had the refs not gotten involved. Cooper finished the game with 7 tackles (2 TFLs) and 1 sack. COWBOY COOP OH MY GOODNESS 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/glcTL3l4vX — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 13, 2026 Loser: The Offensive Line I don’t know that I can fully express myself here without losing the opportunity to write about this team on a weekly basis, so I’ll try to be as eloquent as I can. The Packers have an offensive line problem, and they need to solve it, immediately. They were lucky things went well as long as they did today. For Love to go into halftime having not taken a single sack against a Brian Flores-led defense feels miraculous. Love was constantly taking hits, both to the helmet and to the legs. The plays in which he fumbled were when the line completely abandoned him, and he was getting hit from all angles. I am genuinely astonished he made it to the end of the game uninjured, let alone with nearly 400 passing yards. Long gone are the days when the Packers QB1 had a reliable front five. The team need to figure this out quickly, or we are in for a very long, disappointing season. What we saw Sunday afternoon is not sustainable. Loser: Matt LaFleur Offensive line isn’t holding up. RB1 isn’t available. Let’s give the ball to Chris Brooks on 3rd and 11. IT’LL BE FINE. We can talk about the refs and their impact on the game all day (WILL SOMEONE PLEASE DO SOMETHING ABOUT THE REFS), but the fact of the matter is, this team was not well-enough equipped to win. The game was theirs, until it wasn’t anymore. It seemed like things started going downhill when LaFleur opted to take a Trey Smack FG off of the board, and instead attempt to go for it on 4th and 1 with an uninspired QB sneak, which failed. After this, the team just kept getting punched in the mouth, and they spiraled. It’s hard to get that momentum back when it feels like things are just not going your way, but LaFleur’s decision making did the Packers no favors. Add this 12 point blown lead to the list, and consider that seat hot. The team has another away game in Week 2 as they head to MetLife Stadium to take on the New York Jets, this time in the early slate of games. Can the offensive line keep it together as they face a defensive-minded coach in Aaron Glenn? I won’t hold my breath.
author: Sam Kallien

title: The Vikings laid out the blueprint for the Packers’ offensive line
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ offensive line performed extremely poorly on Sunday, as quarterback Jordan Love dropped back 46 times and completed only 21 passes (46 percent), getting hit on virtually every true dropback of the game. While the Packers posted 22 points through the first three quarters of the game, they averaged just 3.8 yards […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ offensive line performed extremely poorly on Sunday, as quarterback Jordan Love dropped back 46 times and completed only 21 passes (46 percent), getting hit on virtually every true dropback of the game. While the Packers posted 22 points through the first three quarters of the game, they averaged just 3.8 yards per play in the fourth quarter, which included two series where the team turned the ball over on downs and two more where the offense coughed up the ball to the Vikings outright. If you can believe it, Minnesota scored 29 consecutive points to end the game, and they only had one drive where they moved the ball more than 30 yards. It was an all-time collapse, assisted by the fact that Green Bay continued to give the Vikings the ball with short fields. Defensively, Minnesota’s game plan was simple: Blitz the hell out of Jordan Love and hit him. Early on in the game, the Packers took advantage of this by throwing the ball to receiver Christian Watson, but as the game unfolded, more pressure started to get through to Love, who was now getting hit before he could release the ball, instead of while he was releasing the ball. Pro Football Focus has the Vikings’ blitz rate listed as 93 percent for the game. Next Gen Stats has it at 78 percent, the most for any quarterback in any game since 2023 . NGS also credited Minnesota with a 53 percent pressure rate. Whatever the true number is, here are the facts: The Vikings showed that if you blitz the Packers, they don’t have the ability to protect their quarterback right now. Their guard situation was very bad on Sunday, which should have been expected when left guard Donovan Jennings and right guard Jacob Monk made their first starts together at the NFL level. Unfortunately, there’s a chance that might be the team’s best tandem this year, too. There’s no promise the unit will get any better under Aaron Banks, who struggled himself in 2025 and is currently inactive with knee tendinitis, or Anthony Belton, who was drafted to play under a different running scheme and is now sort of lost in the mix. NGS had four of the five starters for Green Bay’s offensive line allowing pressure within 2.5 seconds of the play . Generally, when the Packers faced an all-out pressure look pre-snap, Green Bay chose to allow a free rusher from Love’s blindside, the player who was least likely to impact the ball coming out of Love’s hand upon the release. There just has to be a better way to handle things moving forward. Clearly, what happened on Sunday wasn’t good enough. Defenses will try to copy the Vikings’ blueprint, and if the Packers return to the field with the same answers, Love won’t be healthy enough to suit up for 17 games this regular season.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers-Vikings Final Score: Green Bay collapses again in 39-22 loss
summary: Matt LaFleur talked during the offseason about his team needing to be better in closing down games. Whatever he did to try to make that happen didn’t seem to work, at least not for the first week of the 2026 season. The Green Bay Packers led the Minnesota Vikings 22-10 early in the third quarter. […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Aaron Jones Sr. #33 of the Minnesota Vikings carries the ball during the second quarter as Keisean Nixon #25 of the Green Bay Packers pursues at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Matt LaFleur talked during the offseason about his team needing to be better in closing down games. Whatever he did to try to make that happen didn’t seem to work, at least not for the first week of the 2026 season. The Green Bay Packers led the Minnesota Vikings 22-10 early in the third quarter. When the final buzzer sounded, Minnesota had scored 29 unanswered points, dominating the second half in a 39-22 come-from-behind victory. The Packers’ offense, which had scored on each of the team’s first three drives of the game, fell apart, led by its offensive line; the defense committed penalties on three straight would-be third down stops on the Vikings’ go-ahead drive. The special teams gaveth — Trey Smack hit a 59-yard field goal early and Bo Melton had a 59-yard kickoff return — and tooketh away (Smack missed a PAT and the team allowed a 69-yard kickoff return). Ultimately, the team that couldn’t close out a game without Micah Parsons late last season couldn’t do it without him to start 2026. To make matters worse, it happened against a backup quarterback, Carson Wentz, who came in for a concussed Kyler Murray in the first quarter. Jordan Love’s good start was marred by back-to-back late fumbles, brought about by poor protection by his offensive line against Brian Flores’ sellout blitzes, as well as by a late interception partly caused by the same. The running game was practically nonexistent, with the team gaining just 66 yards on the ground. And the performance on 3rd downs was abysmal — Green Bay’s offense went just 3-of-12, compared to Minnesota going 8-for-15, plus getting multiple conversions via penalty as well. Love ended the day with his second-highest passing yardage total ever, going 21/42 for 387 yards and two scores to Christian Watson. But too much of that had to come late with the team bleeding out and trying to gather itself after Minnesota scored two touchdowns in less than two minutes. The Packers will now have to lick their wounds for a few days before they head to New Jersey next week to play the 1-0 New York Jets. Jonathan Gannon’s defense got off to an incredible start with a pair of big plays from Keisean Nixon. He made a tackle for loss on an Aaron Jones run on the first play from scrimmage, then hauled in a prayer from Kyler Murray on the second. Gannon brought a six-man pressure, with linebackers Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper joining the rush, and Franklin came unblocked right into Kyler Murray’s face to force the interception. Trey Smack delivered the next Packers highlight, continuing his strong performance from the preseason. Green Bay’s offense picked up one first down on a run by Chris Brooks, then was held to a stop at the very edge of field goal range. Smack stepped up for his first official NFL field goal attempt just ahead of midfield, and he drilled a perfect ball through the uprights from 59 yards out for the Packers’ first points of the season. Their next points came courtesy of Christian Watson. After a Vikings punt, Jordan Love hit Watson perfectly on a crossing route over the middle of the field and Watson turned on the jets, cruising up the left sideline. He picked up a big block from Matthew Golden — which was initially flagged, but eventually ruled legal — and cruised into the end zone for an 81-yard score. Smack pushed the PAT wide right, keeping the Packers’ lead at 9-0. WATSON TD! 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/NVEU4ikenf — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 13, 2026 The next Vikings drive saw Kyler Murray leave with an apparent concussion. He took a big hit from Javon Bullard and Lukas Van Ness while going to the ground on a scramble and remained down on the field for several minutes. Bullard was flagged on the play — arguably he made helmet-to-helmet contact, though it did not appear to be a late hit — and Carson Wentz came into the game in relief. Wentz helped the Vikings work into field goal range, largely via the handoff, but missed a third-down throw to Jordan Addison to bring on Will Reichard to make the score 9-3. After a 59-yard kickoff return by Bo Melton that set the Packers up at the Vikings’ 40, the offense had to settle for another Smack field goal, this one from 43 yards out. The two teams traded punts for a while, with the Packers getting a sack from Lukas Van Ness to force the Vikings to kick out of their own end one. Skyy Moore’s return then set the Packers up at the Minnesota 36-yard line, but the offense went in reverse with the line getting beaten like a drum up front, leading to another Whelan punt. This time, Minnesota drove the length of the field, even after a sack by Keisean Nixon and Jonathan Ford on the first play of the drive. An unnecessary roughness call on safety Evan Williams and a couple of third down conversions by Wentz set up the Vikings in Packers territory. From the 39, he got a free play with Van Ness jumping offsides, heaving a deep ball to Justin Jefferson, who shook rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse and hauled in a touchdown. That left the Packers with 1:55 on the clock and three timeouts to try to expand upon their 12-10 lead before halftime. Jordan Love drove them down the field in chunks. First it was a 23-yarder to Tucker Kraft, then 10 yards to Bo Melton, then 32 to Watson to get to the 7-yard line with 30 seconds left. A 5-yard run by Chris Brooks set up Watson’s second touchdown, which came off a brilliant play design where he motioned inside and faked an insert block, only to release to the corner of the end zone. WATSON! 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/F3ZxQnWgHd — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 13, 2026 That sent the Packers into the half up 19-10 and set to receive the second-half kickoff, but they were unable to move the ball and had to settle for a punt. Minnesota did the same, setting up the Packers back inside their own 20. Love went to work. He connected with Matthew Golden for a gain of 13 while under extreme duress, then converted a 3rd down to Jayden Reed before finding Jonnu Smith wide open for a big gain of 43 yards to get inside the 10-yard line. Another drive bogged down close to the goal line, though, and Smack hit a short field goal to make the score 22-10. Minnesota responded quickly, however, with a 69-yard kickoff return from Myles Price. After getting one first down on the ground, Wentz found T.J. Hockenson open over the middle for a 16-yard touchdown, pulling the Vikings back to within five points. Love converted a 2nd and 20 on the next series after a sack, hanging in the pocket and finding Matthew Golden again for a huge 43-yard gain to set the team up in field goal range. Another failed 3rd down led to a Smack field goal attempt, but the Vikings were flagged for a penalty and the Packers preferred to keep the offense on the field on 4th and 1 instead. Jordan Love tried a QB sneak, but a questionable spot ruled him just short of the line to gain, leaving the Packers without a score after having had the opportunity to take an 8-point lead. Wentz came out firing for Minnesota, finding Josh Oliver for 13 yards, but then Edgerrin Cooper came up with back-to-back sacks. Unfortunately, the second one, on third down, was wiped out by an illegal contact penalty on Javon Bullard, handing the Vikings a free first down. Shawn Hochuli’s officiating crew made their presence known once again on an apparent third-down stop, flagging Chris McClellan for roughing the passer despite him bracing his body weight to ensure that it did not actually fall on Wentz. Hochuli bailed out the Vikings a third time on third down inside the red zone. Evan Williams picked off Wentz in the end zone, but Xavier McKinney drew a holding penalty, and one play later…
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Week one is finally in the books. It is time for that feature that everyone knows and loves. This is where we look at the basic numbers from the game to determine if we can see any patterns in winning and losing. Obviously, there are no patterns with a sample size of one, but as […]
full_text: Week one is finally in the books. It is time for that feature that everyone knows and loves. This is where we look at the basic numbers from the game to determine if we can see any patterns in winning and losing. Obviously, there are no patterns with a sample size of one, but as we move forward we will start to see them. As you know, the Texans lost a nail biter 36-31, but the final score hardly ever indicates how close it was. The Texans drove it down to the nine for a go ahead score, but fizzled out when pass protection broke down two plays in a row. There is no way in a million years that anyone that watches this team could have predicted how this game would play out. Close game? Sure. Texans loss? The Bills were favored in the game. 67 total points scored? Not a chance in hell. That’s why they play the games as they say. So, let’s see what the basic statistics say about how this one turned out. Key Statistics Total Yards: Texans 73/381, Bills 52/409 Rushing Yards: Texans 32/124, Bills 21/86 Passing Yards: Texans 41/257, Bills 31/323 Sacks: Texans 2, Bills 3 Penalties: Texans 7/106, Bills 10/85 Turnovers; Texans 2, Bills 0 Time of Possession: Texans 36:17, Billa 23:43 It’s amazing how one or two plays can change the whole complexion of a game. Kamari Lassiter dropped a sure interception in the end zone that looked more like a wounded duck then a throw from Josh Allen. If he gets that interception then the Texans simply kneel on the ball and win the game 31-30. I won’t harp on one plays in terms of going good, bad, and ugly, but that one play is indicative of how close these games come. The Texans don’t have a second turnover, so the turnover battle ends in a draw. Take away the turnover battle and the Texans have the slight edge across the board. The Good It is safe to say that every football game has positives. Even when you lose 59-0 you can usually find something small to hang your hat on. There is nothing small about David Montgomery. Sure, he gained “only” 60 yards, but many of those were tough yards and he did score three of the four offensive touchdowns in the game. He added three more catches for 19 yards with one of those coming for a score. No one is going to call Canton for 79 yards for scrimmage, but clearly the Texans have found something there. Woody Marks gained 42 yards on the ground in nine carries in the kind of role the Texans envisioned last season for him. If the team gains an average of 124 yards every week they will be much improved offensively. In particular, while the turnovers hurt, this ball control offense is what they are looking for. If you control the ball for 35+ minutes and generate 31 points on offense then you win nine times out of ten. The Bad There are a lot of things on defense that did not go well. In particular, only getting to Josh Allen twice has to be a disappointment. Meanwhile, the secondary in general probably played their worst game in well over a season. Allen carved up the Texans defense and generated more big plays then we would expect in a month. I mentioned the Lassiter drop earlier. That is a play he would love to have back, but the bigger sins were the numerous chunk plays that made life easy for the Bills. The Ugly There is bad play and then there is alarmingly bad play. Anyone that looked at PFF and other sources had to express some concern when the Texans brought in Reed Blankenship. We were told they would use him differently, so a lot of us bought into the hype and hoped a return to his glory days were in the offing. It’s only one game, so that’s still possible, but this one is one where you want to burn the tape. Dalton Kincaid is a good tight end, but he turned into the reincarnation of Rob Gronkowski out there. If they continue to use him to cover tight ends it could be a long season. Focus on Stroud Since C.J. Stroud is angling for a new contract worth more money than 100 of us will make in a lifetime, it probably is a good idea to look at this week to week. The official stats say he had 274 yards passing with two touchdowns and zero interceptions. I’m not good at the math, but 17 weeks of that seems like it would be career highs (and lows) in every single category. The 106.7 rating is also something that would bode well for him at the end of the season. I’m not one to overly criticize because there are any number of reasons why the Texans lost the game. However, he needs to take better care of the football under pressure. Two key fumbles resulted in three Bills points and took points off the board at the end of the game. The Texans win the game without those fumbles. So, as much as I would love to give him an A, I can’t because key errors played a part in them losing. A solid B performance kicks the can down the road. It was a very Dak Prescotty kind of performance. Good numbers. Some great moments, but not quite enough. Let’s see if that trend continues.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Texans lose heartbreaker to Bills 36-31
summary: It’s one game. It is really easy to overreact to the Texans’ performance on Sunday after losing a nailbiter. There was a lot to love about the game (the offense looked downright competent until the fourth quarter), there was a lot to hate (the secondary and Reed Blankenship in particular were hideous), and there was […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Xavier Hutchinson #19 and Nico Collins #12 of the Houston Texans celebrate after Collins' receiving touchdown against the Buffalo Bills in the second quarter of a game of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s one game. It is really easy to overreact to the Texans’ performance on Sunday after losing a nailbiter. There was a lot to love about the game (the offense looked downright competent until the fourth quarter), there was a lot to hate (the secondary and Reed Blankenship in particular were hideous), and there was a lot of “what the hell did I just watch?” (the rest of the game). It’s one game. There are no data points to connect here. We don’t know what the Texans are yet. The secondary gave up 334 yards and two passing touchdowns to Josh Allen, much of which came from explosive plays which the Texans simply didn’t have an answer for. The defense gave up more points in the season opener than they did all of last season. But we don’t know if this is what we should expect from the Texans defense or if it was a blip. If it wasn’t a blip, however, this team is in much bigger trouble than any of us thought. It’s one game. The offense looked sharp through most of the game and aside from the bad plays by Stroud to bookend the game, there was a lot of encouraging signs from them. David Montgomery ran for 60 yards and two touchdowns (and hauled in a third through the air). They got the hard yardage that they failed, consistently, to get last season. There’s some good news in this. It’s one game. We will know more about this team in the next 2-3 weeks. Until then, just remember: it’s one game. We’ll wash this game off and move on to a home game against the Bengals on Sunday. See y’all then!

title: Colts start the season on sour note, with “clunker” home loss to Baltimore
summary: It’s one game, but if the Indianapolis Colts lay a few more consecutive “clunkers” like that, and the already hot seats of both longtime general manager Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen will only get hotter in-season. The Colts got off to an early start on Sunday afternoon with an offensive touchdown (with a […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens scores rushing touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s one game, but if the Indianapolis Colts lay a few more consecutive “clunkers” like that, and the already hot seats of both longtime general manager Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen will only get hotter in-season. The Colts got off to an early start on Sunday afternoon with an offensive touchdown (with a missed PAT) on their opening offensive drive, but after that, it was all Baltimore beating and bruising up the Colts—to the tune of Indianapolis surrendering 500+ total offensive yards defensively. The final score may have read 41-23, but this one was already over at halftime with the Ravens up 31-13. In particular, the Ravens top offensive playmaker duo of Derrick Henry and Zay Flowers had huge afternoons against the Colts. Henry looked like he in the middle of his playing career prime as an All-Pro running back for the Tennessee Titans again, crushing the Colts to the tune of 144 total rushing yards and 3 rushing touchdowns, while debuting slot Justin Walley was no match for Flowers, who went off with 5 receptions for 150 total receiving yards and a touchdown reception. Let’s just be glad that Henry isn’t in the AFC South anymore! Colts team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has already stated this early offseason that there’s never been a greater sense of urgency regarding this team and her top football lieutenants, but their Week 1 ‘laugher’ of a showing against the Ravens didn’t do much to instill confidence that this regime remains the right recipe for success for the franchise going forward. It’s early, and the Colts still have the next few weeks to “round into better form,” albeit against a very tough early season schedule by virtue of playing both the Kansas City Chiefs and Houston Texans next up in back-to-back weeks. I agree that with NFL teams playing starters very little in preseason games these days, it takes at least a few weeks to know who your team really is from a talent, execution, and identity standpoint, but Indianapolis doesn’t have the luxury of a soft initial schedule to ease into finding that best version of themselves. The offense and field position battle also didn’t do the Colts any favors, as a Daniel Jones interception and Jonathan Taylor fumble lost swayed the scales in favor of Baltimore. The Colts were constantly behind the 8-ball regarding beginning their offensive drives, only adding to their ineptitude. If they aren’t careful, they could very well dig themselves into an initial hole and begin the 2026 campaign at 0-3, and given the results on Sunday, they may not be good enough to dig themselves out of as far as future AFC playoff contention is concerned. They need to put themselves in position to be successful later on this season, when their schedule thankfully lightens up a bit. That opener showing at Lucas Oil Stadium in front of their own home fans left A LOT to be desired. I wouldn’t say that NFL opening day carries the same significance as within the MLB among diehard fans, but at the same time, they’ve got to come out more prepared than that. That was flat out embarrassing. As veteran former Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner eloquently stated post-game , “Plain and simple. We got our ass whooped.” Which fine, every NFL team can lay an egg here and there, especially when you’re shaking off initial offseason rust, but there’s real concern right now, that this could be less of an aberration and more of the Colts’ new norm.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: What went wrong on defense against the Ravens?
summary: The Colts spent the offseason talking about urgency, change and a defense that was supposed to look better under Lou Anarumo in Year 2. Then they opened the season by giving up 41 points and 506 yards at home. There is some obvious context here as Baltimore is a difficult offense to defend. Lamar Jackson […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Moore #17 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates a first down against the Indianapolis Colts during the third quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts spent the offseason talking about urgency, change and a defense that was supposed to look better under Lou Anarumo in Year 2. Then they opened the season by giving up 41 points and 506 yards at home. There is some obvious context here as Baltimore is a difficult offense to defend. Lamar Jackson is a two-time MVP, Derrick Henry is still one of the hardest backs in football to bring down and Zay Flowers is a tough cover for any cornerback, especially one making his first start after missing all of last season. That can all be true, and Sunday can still be unacceptable. The Ravens have eight explosive plays (runs of 12+, passes of 16+) in the first half against the Colts. The last game in which they had at least eight first-half explosives was Week 17 in 2023. 987 days ago. — Benjamin Solak (@BenjaminSolak) September 13, 2026 The Ravens did not need a perfect game to move the ball. They had eight explosive plays in the first half alone, according to Ben Solak. Josh Wilson noted that 506 yards allowed were the most the Colts have ever given up in a season opener in the Indianapolis era. He also noted that this was the first time since 2015 that Indianapolis allowed 40-plus points and 500-plus yards in any game. The Colts had their worst season opener in decades – which is saying a lot, for this team. Allowed 41 points, t-3rd-most in opener in Indy era. Allowed 506 yards, most in opener in Indy. Lost by 18, 6th-worst defeat in opener in Indy. And it could have been much worse. — Josh Wilson (@JoshWilsonSB) September 13, 2026 That is not the kind of performance a team can explain away by pointing to the opponent. The pass rush was fine overall. It was not dominant, but it was not the main reason the defense fell apart. The bigger problems were behind it. The Colts struggled in man coverage, lost too often against Baltimore’s heavier run looks, got almost nothing from their linebackers and looked disorganized far too often for a unit that entered the year with this much pressure on it. Justin Walley and man coverage Colts played man in between the 20s at a 61.5% rate today, per @NextGenStats They allowed 13.4 yards per pass on those plays… — Brett Kollmann (@BrettKollmann) September 13, 2026 Justin Walley’s first start could not have gone much worse. That does not mean the Colts should give up on him. It does not mean he cannot become a good player. It does not even mean the team was wrong to trust him going into the season. It does mean that Sunday was a bad introduction to the NFL. Walley was picked on early, and the Ravens kept going back to him. Flowers beat him on the Ravens’ first play of the game for a 49-yard gain, and that set the tone for the rest of the afternoon. Walley looked late reacting to cuts, struggled to stay attached across the field and had a difficult time dealing with the type of movement Baltimore used to attack man coverage. Things have not started well for the Indianapolis defense. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Ravens #BALvsIND pic.twitter.com/vZhUszvDQd — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) September 13, 2026 Zay Flowers is a really brutal matchup for Walley's first career start. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Ravens #BALvsIND pic.twitter.com/39poOJASvN — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) September 13, 2026 Flowers was a brutal first assignment. He is quick, sudden and extremely difficult to cover when an offense is using motion, crossing routes and condensed formations to create traffic. The Ravens knew what they were doing. They put Walley in conflict and forced him to chase one of the league’s shiftier receivers through space. Still, that is the job. If the Colts are going to play this much man coverage, the corners have to hold up better than they did Sunday. Brett Kollmann posted that Indianapolis played man coverage between the 20s at a 61.5 percent rate, per Next Gen Stats. The Colts allowed 13.4 yards per pass on those plays. That is a defensive plan getting punished. Walley was the main target, but he was not the only problem. A.J. Haulcy was at fault on one of the Flowers plays. The Colts also failed to properly recognize Flowers when he was aligned in the backfield, which should not happen against a player who is clearly one of Baltimore’s most dangerous weapons. Charvarius Ward had a rough rep on a deep ball where his feet looked stuck in the ground, and instead of reacting cleanly, he ended up grabbing late after getting beaten. The linebackers did not help much underneath either. Baltimore hit crossing routes and man-beaters, and the Colts too often looked late sorting through it. That is the danger of playing man coverage against a team that knows how to manipulate matchups. If one defender is late, the ball comes out. If the linebackers are unsure underneath, the middle of the field opens up. If the safety help is late or the corner loses leverage, a modest gain can turn into a field-flipping play. The Colts wanted to be more aggressive defensively this season, which is fine but Anarumo’s defense was always going to ask more of the secondary. What Sunday showed is that playing man at that rate comes with a price if the corners are not winning and the rest of the defense is not connected. Run defense The run defense was not much better. Baltimore leaned into bigger personnel and jumbo looks, forcing the Colts to answer with heavier fronts. That brought Jerry Tillery onto the field more often, and he had a rough game. When teams go big-on-big, there is nowhere to hide up front. Every defensive lineman has to hold his gap, especially when the Colts are using five-man fronts with three interior defenders. Can't wait to post a Colts highlight again. What is Jerry Tillery doing? #Colts #ForTheShoe #Ravens #BALvsIND pic.twitter.com/l25t179V7o — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) September 13, 2026 Tillery did not do that well enough. Baltimore moved him too easily, and once the Ravens started creating movement inside, the linebackers had to clean up the mess… and they didn’t. Most rush yards after contact on Sunday so far Derrick Henry 104 Jahmyr Gibbs 82 Saquon Barkley 82 D'Andre Swift 79 Kyle Monangai 79 pic.twitter.com/I0Cuzf0ZSk — PFF (@PFF) September 14, 2026 Derrick Henry finished with 104 rushing yards after contact, according to PFF. Some of that is Henry being Henry. He is going to break tackles, fall forward and turn ordinary runs into bruising gains; that is part of playing Baltimore. The problem is that the Colts were not just losing to a great back as they were failing to finish plays they had chances to stop. #Colts starting LB Jaylon Carlies did not record a single stat in 42 snaps played, according to PFF. — Noah Compton (@nerlens_) September 14, 2026 The linebacker play was especially concerning. Jaylon Carlies played 42 snaps and did not record a single stat, according to PFF. That’s horrible… A linebacker can do some things that do not show up in the box score, but when the defense is giving up 41 points and getting pushed around in the run game, 42 snaps with no recorded production is a major problem. Akeem Davis-Gaither did not look comfortable either. He looked late diagnosing plays and just looking lost in space. There was a play where he completely followed his man all the way down the field without realizing Lamar Jackson was right behind him running the whole time. Baltimore makes linebackers think, and that is part of what makes the Ravens so hard to defend. They use Lamar, Henry, motion, tight ends and misdirection to stretch every rule. Still, the Colts needed their linebackers to settle things down, and instead they looked like part of the problem. The CJ Allen usage also deserves scrutiny. Chris Ballard called Allen a green dot…
author: Andrew Aziz

title: The Colts shouldn’t panic…just yet
summary: How can something so beautiful turn so ugly so quickly? The Indianapolis Colts began their home opener in the most positive and convincing fashion imaginable by marching down the field and punching it in for six. Missing the first extra point felt as if it could cause problems later but in reality, missing out on […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates after a touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images How can something so beautiful turn so ugly so quickly? The Indianapolis Colts began their home opener in the most positive and convincing fashion imaginable by marching down the field and punching it in for six. Missing the first extra point felt as if it could cause problems later but in reality, missing out on the 19 additional points needed to beat the Ravens proved bigger. It’s early though. The Colts shouldn’t panic. At least not yet. The old adage in football is that half the league is 0-1 to start the year. With only one game, 50% are losers, but that doesn’t mean that is where they will stand when the dust settles. The Ravens are good, maybe really good. They have Super Bowl aspirations. A backfield of Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry is always going to be upper crust. They showed Sunday just how “upper” it is. The only saving grace is that the second coming of Jerry Rice, Zay Flowers, couldn’t play the second half. Otherwise, he might have broken 300 yards of offense by himself. The offense stalled and turned the ball over too much, and the defense was a sieve. All hope isn’t lost, however. The start of the schedule is brutal. We knew that coming in. It doesn’t get easier traveling to Kansas City, but the Colts fare well against Patrick Mahomes. Do they have to play much better? Absolutely. They can clean things up and work to provide better resistance on defense. The Chiefs are good, but they are a different style of play. There is plenty of time to get back on track. It isn’t a time to throw in the towel. Some teams match up poorly. Some teams have great games while others can’t find their footing. Championship contenders, and even those that go on to win it all, have games that are rough. It happens. The Colts had a bad one. They just can’t make it a habit. The Colts are 0-1. So is the rest of the league. Save that panic for another day.

title: Colts land first punch, Ravens respond with TKO in 41-23 season opener loss
summary: INDIANAPOLIS — The losing streak reared its ugly head once again inside Lucas Oil Stadium as the Baltimore Ravens roughed up the Indianapolis Colts 41-23 in the 2026 season opener. For a team that spent the offseason preaching a fresh start with a revamped defensive unit, the opening act instead looked painfully familiar. Indianapolis has lost […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images INDIANAPOLIS — The losing streak reared its ugly head once again inside Lucas Oil Stadium as the Baltimore Ravens roughed up the Indianapolis Colts 41-23 in the 2026 season opener. For a team that spent the offseason preaching a fresh start with a revamped defensive unit, the opening act instead looked painfully familiar. Indianapolis has lost 11 of its last 13 season openers, which includes a tie during that stretch. Most opponents would expect the Colts gameplan is to emphasize running the football, but quarterback Daniel Jones dropped back seven times on the nine-play opening drive in his first start back from the Achilles injury that ended his 2025 season. Indianapolis came out with an aerial attack as the opening script worked according to plan. Jones found receiver Josh Downs on a slant for 25 yards, then later sent him in motion to recognize the man coverage and beat it with another slant to Downs for 12 more yards. After receiver Alec Pierce caught a 13-yard pass to set up 1st-and-goal, Jonathan Taylor punctuated the opening drive with a 1-yard plunge into the end zone to give the Colts their lone lead of the game. JONATHAN TAYLOR TOUCHDOWN #BALvsIND on CBS pic.twitter.com/goOwTIjzID — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 13, 2026 Baltimore needed no time to answer and scored four touchdowns on its first five drives, with the only defensive stop being a goal line stand from Indy’s 3-yard-line. The Ravens racked up 506 total yards of offense, including 202 rushing yards and 324 passing yards. It took just three plays for the Ravens to seize the lead, for good. Two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson ran play action and found receiver Zay Flowers on a corner down the left sideline for an explosive 49-yard gain, with Flowers beating cornerback Justin Walley on his very first NFL snap in a regular season game. Two plays later, Jackson kept the read option himself to scamper seven yards into the end zone. Just like that, the Ravens were ahead 7-6 and never looked back. The Colts’ next possession lasted just two plays. After Taylor was stuffed in the backfield for a 2-yard loss, Jones’ next pass was intercepted by linebacker Roquan Smith to give the Ravens possession inside Colts territory. The Ravens made the Colts pay by turning the early mistake into the go-ahead touchdown. After a chop block penalty pushed Baltimore from 3rd-and-1 back to 3rd-and-16, Jackson showcased exactly why he’s perhaps the most dangerous dual threat weapon in league history. It seemed like Jackson was surrendering at a dead end on the midfield horseshoe, but somehow he ducked underneath the grasp of both Arden Key and DeForest Buckner, escaped the pocket, then tucked it himself for an astonishing 16-yard run to move the chains. Even from inside the stadium, it felt like the game-defining play. Three plays later, Henry powered into the end zone from 4-yards out to extend the lead to 14-6. LAMAR JACKSON, THE MAGICIAN YOU ARE 🤯🎩 (via: @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/BAOpJgeayW — B/R Gridiron (@brgridiron) September 13, 2026 Flowers tormented the Colts secondary with five catches for 150 receiving yards, including a 54-yard touchdown, all in the first half before he exited with a hamstring injury. Henry later broke loose for a 32-yard touchdown as the Ravens turned a 6-0 deficit into a 28-6 lead in just 20 minutes of action. The lone bright spot for Indy’s defense created a spark late in the second quarter as edge rushers Arden Key and Laiatu Latu corralled Jackson, forcing a fumble that Buckner recovered to give Indy possession inside the red zone. Turnover to touchdown. pic.twitter.com/hhvrKPTRQ6 — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 13, 2026 The Colts were able to capitalize on the takeaway as Taylor ripped off a 10-yard run, then finished the short drive with a 3-yard touchdown run to cut the deficit to 28-13. The league’s leading scorer last season finished with 98 rushing yards on 19 carries and two touchdowns, averaging 5.2 yards per carry. Baltimore controlled the opening half with 326 total yards compared to Indy’s 112. Mind you, the Colts started the new campaign by receiving the opening kickoff. While the Colts settled for a 58-yard field goal from Spencer Shrader on their first drive of the second half, Henry kept up his phenomenal performance and delivered his third touchdown for the eighth time in his career. Henry finished with 144 rushing yards on 24 carries and three touchdowns, moving into third on the NFL’s all-time career rushing touchdowns list. Jones eventually connected with tight end Tyler Warren for a 9-yard touchdown late in the fourth quarter to make the final score a little more digestible. Jones finished 19-of-31 for 166 passing yards, one touchdown and one interception. After the opening script however, Jones was limited to 14-of-24 for just 107 yards. Pierce led the Colts with four catches for 61 yards, but exited the game after the opening quarter with a wrist injury. Indianapolis went just 3-for-10 on third down and managed 251 total yards of offense, less than half of Baltimore’s 506. For the opening drive, the new season looked exactly like the fresh beginning Indianapolis had envisioned. The Colts landed the first punch, but then the Ravens responded with four touchdowns for a decisive technical knockout on the road. The Colts visit the Kansas City Chiefs for a Sunday Night Football primetime matchup at Arrowhead Stadium. Dating back to last season, the Colts losing streak has reached eight consecutive games. With just three primetime games scheduled this season, the Colts have to make sure they don’t dig themselves too deep into a hole that heads start rolling.

title: Alec Pierce expected to be on snap count vs. Ravens
summary: Alec Pierce will play for the Colts against the Ravens, but he will not be a full-go in Week 1. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reported Sunday morning that Pierce will be on a snap count in Indianapolis’ season opener against Baltimore. Garafolo said he does not expect Pierce to handle a full workload and added […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - JANUARY 04: Alec Pierce #14 of the Indianapolis Colts runs the ball during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Alec Pierce will play for the Colts against the Ravens, but he will not be a full-go in Week 1. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reported Sunday morning that Pierce will be on a snap count in Indianapolis’ season opener against Baltimore. Garafolo said he does not expect Pierce to handle a full workload and added that one source estimated Pierce would play roughly 20 to 30 snaps. That would put Pierce below his normal usage, especially for a player expected to have a major role in the Colts’ passing game this season. It also lines up with where things have been trending after Pierce missed most of training camp while recovering from ankle surgery. Pierce was activated off the physically unable to perform list late in camp, giving him a chance to be available for the opener. That was the first important step, but being active and being ready for a full workload are two different things, though, and the Colts appear prepared to manage him carefully in his first game back. From a football standpoint, Pierce’s presence still helps. Even on a limited snap count, his vertical speed forces Baltimore to respect the deep ball and gives Daniel Jones another outside option. Still, the limited workload is worth watching. Pierce is expected to be one of the Colts’ top offensive weapons after a breakout 2025 season, and Indianapolis needs him healthy for the long run. Pushing him too hard in Week 1 would not make much sense if the team believes he is still ramping back up. For now, the main takeaway is simple: Pierce is available to play against the Ravens, but he isn’t 100% yet.

title: 5 Bold Predictions for Ravens at Colts Regular Season Opener
summary: The Indianapolis Colts kick off their regular season at home against the Baltimore Ravens this afternoon, and here are five bold predictions ahead of today’s matchup: 1. Sauce Gardner locks down Zay Flowers earlyFlowers is dealing with a hamstring issue and drew a hefty target share expectation, but he’ll be seeing plenty of Sauce Gardner […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts scores a touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens during the first quarter at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2020 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Bobby Ellis/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts kick off their regular season at home against the Baltimore Ravens this afternoon, and here are five bold predictions ahead of today’s matchup: 1. Sauce Gardner locks down Zay Flowers early Flowers is dealing with a hamstring issue and drew a hefty target share expectation, but he’ll be seeing plenty of Sauce Gardner in man coverage. If Gardner wins that matchup in the first half, it takes away Baltimore’s easiest answer when the offensive line struggles — and that line is the year’s biggest question mark for the Ravens. 2. Colts RB Jonathan Taylor exploits Ravens head coach Jesse Minter’s defense again Taylor torched Minter’s Los Angeles Chargers defense for 94 total rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns last October, as head coach Jim Harbaugh’s former defensive coordinator. Minter’s scheme hasn’t fundamentally changed, and the Ravens are breaking in new pass rushers up front (with starting Pro Bowl defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike out). Expect Taylor to be the tone-setter often that keeps Indy’s offense ahead of schedule, especially with starting quarterback Daniel Jones working his way back from a torn Achilles early on. 3. The Colts win the pressure battle without blitzing much Minter’s defenses have historically blitzed at a low rate (19% last year), which means the Colts’ front — led by DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart — gets to win with four rushers against a Ravens line PFF ranks 24th in the league, including a center making his first career start. Clean pocket push, not exotic pressure packages, is how Indy and Colts veteran defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo gets to Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson. 4. Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones avoids the big mistake Jones enters surprisingly healthy after last year’s late Achilles injury, and Indy’s offense was historically explosive by EPA/play under Colts head coach Shane Steichen. If he protects the ball against a Baltimore defense that’s also breaking in new pieces, field position swings the Colts’ way in a game expected to be low-scoring and close. 5. Colts win a tight one at home, something like 24-20 Baltimore is favored by 3.5 with a 47.5 total , but a lot of that leans on unknowns — new OC Declan Doyle calling his first regular-season game, a shaky interior line, and Jackson playing behind a center with zero career starts. The Colts faithful’s rapid noise, plus a battle-tested Colts offensive identity tips a close one to Indianapolis.

title: Jacksonville Jaguars Winners and Losers From Week 1: Jags Stomp Lowly Browns In All Three Phases
summary: I truly don’t know of a much better way to start a season than what the Jaguars did on Sunday. Against the god-awful Cleveland Browns, the Jacksonville Jaguars did far more than handle business in their 34-10 season-opener win. It’s now 2-0 in season openers in Duval County for Liam Coen and the vibes couldn’t […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: Travon Walker #44 of the Jacksonville Jaguars reacts with teammates after a play against the Cleveland Browns during the first half of the game at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images I truly don’t know of a much better way to start a season than what the Jaguars did on Sunday. Against the god-awful Cleveland Browns, the Jacksonville Jaguars did far more than handle business in their 34-10 season-opener win. It’s now 2-0 in season openers in Duval County for Liam Coen and the vibes couldn’t be higher. When you have a win where arguably the worst play for your team is allowing a long kickoff return that didn’t go for a touchdown, resulting in just three points, you probably played pretty well. That’s how it seemed on Sunday. No real losers this week as the Jaguars ride high as the only AFC South team to win their opener, starting the season 1-0. WINNERS The Jaguars Everyone’s a winner collectively from yesterday’s game. Sometimes you just need to handle business, not play with your food and win a game outright. The Jags did that in all three phases. The offense scored on its first four drives, not having to punt until the final drive of the first half. The defense grabbed a pick on Cleveland’s first drive and forced about two dozen more fumbles throughout the game to go along with five sacks. Special teams did its job with a pair of long field goals from Cam Little and got some nice returns from Ameer Abdullah and Parker Washington. Handle business and move on. The decreased stadium capacity was a little strange and the heat definitely impacted the crowd, but the Jags fans showed up like they always do to see the team off right to start the season. We can’t play the Browns every week but it’s a start. On to Denver. THAT'S A TEAM WIN pic.twitter.com/D4BKU7lAiX — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) September 13, 2026 Trevor Lawrence Coen was asked postgame about the importance of starting Trevor Lawrence fast this season in the second season of this offense. The head coach said he and his staff were more intentional about working earlier in the week on the script. It paid off big time. Had it not been for some mammoth games by Caleb Williams (the Chicago variant) or Tyler Shough, Lawrence might have had the best quarterbacking day in the league on Sunday. Lawrence went a solid 18-23 for 245 yards and four touchdowns. He was sacked just once and was turnover free. The offense moved at will with Lawrence slinging it. It was smooth, his throws were layered beautifully and it just looked all around clean. Juxtaposed to whatever the hell Deshaun Watson was doing, it made Lawrence look even that much better. Trevor Lawrence looked completely in control to open the season for Jacksonville 🔥 18/23, 245 PYDS, 4 PTD, 0 INT, 150.6 Rating pic.twitter.com/IDJ4r51BcF — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) September 13, 2026 The quarterback has a clear trust in every offensive weapon he has, with nine different guys catching at least one pass. The most catches on that list though did belong to… Parker Washington Hey look, Parker Washington is actually good and it wasn’t just a one season thing. Maybe they should have paid him. In all seriousness, Washington was perhaps the best non-Lawrence player on the field yesterday with five catches for 83 yards and his leaping opening drive touchdown. He looks like a legit WR1 after just a game. Maybe the best part about Washington is that his newfound superstardom finds guys like Jakobi Meyers (two catches, 40 yards, one score) and Brian Thomas Jr. (three catches, 40 yards) that much more open. It all works in tandem. Sunday was a testament to that. Chop Wood. Carry Water. Catch touchdowns. Parker Washington with the DIVING CATCH for his first TD of the season 😱 CLEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FzpS0RbR6u — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Rookies Another guy who benefitted from the Washington hype train was rookie wide receiver Josh Cameron, who caught a touchdown in his first NFL game. Cameron looks the part through one game: a two catch, 20 yard and a score performance. His big frame is clearly something Jacksonville wants to take advantage of early and often. Nate Boerkircher hauled in a pass as well, highlighting another rookie who flashed in spurts Sunday. Brenton Strange led the tight end room in “moments” so to speak, but the rookie Boerkircher did his job. As did rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon, who got the start up front. At least offensively, the early returns look just fine for the rooks. Defense It probably doesn’t need to be stated just how horrific the Browns are, but the Jags defense had a lot to do with that. Travon Walker AND Josh Hines-Allen each walked away with 1.5 sacks. Foye Oluokun had a pick that resulted in a touchdown drive. Ventrell Miller looked like prime Brian Urlacher, leading the team with 10 tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack. Travis Hunter played both sides and played well. Those are your cornerstone guys who made the big plays all day long. You cannot ask for anything more. There is something to be said that Anthony Campanile stayed in Jacksonville and got another season with what was a good defense last year. All three levels of the defense played well all day long and coach Camp should be getting a lot of praise for that fact. Josh Hines-Allen told me he thought Ventrell Miller would lead the league in punch-outs. Miller just got his first punch-out of the season, and Hines-Allen got the fumble recovery 🔮🔮 pic.twitter.com/5kr0XqK8O9 https://t.co/mqgliUdBXe — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) September 13, 2026 Obligatory Cam Little Mention Little was solid again Sunday, connecting on his two kicks of 47 yards and 40 yards. I would’ve loved to see him actually make a tackle on that long kick return but oh well. Ross Matiscik laid the boom in his place later anyway. Ameer Abdullah I would’ve guessed that if I was mentioning Abdullah in any capacity after a Jags game, it would be because everyone else played so badly and I was grasping at straws. But not so fast. The Jags RB3-ish actually looked really good in his limited time. He had four carries for 32 yards and amassed 59 total kick return yards. He’s a veteran player and for what the Jags seemingly are going to use him for, he should be great. Credit to him. LOSERS Deshaun Watson This dude flat out sucks, holy mother of Mary. The demons that follow Watson around and speak ancient phrases into his ears were working overtime Sunday. That first interception he threw was perfect timing for the defense. See ya next week. Deshaun Watson trying to wipe off whatever is in his visor that's making him throw the ball repeatedly to Jaguars players pic.twitter.com/Iy271MUtzO — Sam Monson (@SamMonsonNFL) September 13, 2026 Who do you think was the big winner from the Jags Week 1 win? Want to talk more on how well Lawrence played? Comment down below and we will see you right back here for the team’s Week 2 matchup next Sunday at the Denver Broncos.

title: 3 Reasons Why the Jaguars Beat the Browns
summary: There were plenty of questions surrounding the Jacksonville Jaguars heading into the 2026 season. Could Trevor Lawrence take another step forward? Could Liam Coen’s offense maintain the momentum it built during last year’s AFC South-winning campaign? And, perhaps most importantly, could the Jaguars turn all that promise into the sort of convincing performances expected from […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars high fives Jakobi Meyers #3 against the Cleveland Browns during the first quarter of the game at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images There were plenty of questions surrounding the Jacksonville Jaguars heading into the 2026 season. Could Trevor Lawrence take another step forward? Could Liam Coen’s offense maintain the momentum it built during last year’s AFC South-winning campaign? And, perhaps most importantly, could the Jaguars turn all that promise into the sort of convincing performances expected from a team with genuine postseason ambitions? Consider the first test passed. Jacksonville dismantled the Cleveland Browns 34-10 at EverBank Stadium on Sunday, racing into a 24-0 half-time lead before extending the advantage to 31-0 early in the third quarter. Cleveland eventually found a couple of consolation scores, but by then the Jaguars’ starters were already in cruise control. So, what were the biggest reasons behind such a comprehensive opening-day victory? Trevor Lawrence was simply outstanding Trevor Lawrence with his 4TH TD pass of the game 🔥 PUTTING ON A SHOW CLEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/77IDTz3gOw — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 There isn’t really anywhere else to start. Trevor Lawrence was magnificent. The Jaguars quarterback completed 18 of his 23 attempts for 245 yards and four touchdowns, without throwing an interception, finishing with a career-best 150.6 passer rating. More importantly, he looked completely in command of an offense that made Cleveland’s defense look lost for long stretches. And this wasn’t a case of Lawrence piling up empty numbers after the game was already won. He did his damage immediately. Jacksonville scored touchdowns on each of its first two possessions, with Lawrence finding Parker Washington for 30 yards before connecting with rookie Josh Cameron for a four-yard score. He then added a third touchdown to Brenton Strange in the second quarter before finding Jakobi Meyers for a 32-yard score on the opening drive of the second half. The particularly encouraging part for Jacksonville was how easy Lawrence made it look. Cleveland couldn’t consistently pressure him, couldn’t disguise enough to confuse him and, crucially, couldn’t keep the Jaguars’ receivers covered. Seven different Jacksonville players caught a pass in the first half alone. This is the version of Lawrence Jacksonville needs if it is serious about making noise in January. He finished 2025 playing some of the best football of his career. On Sunday, he looked less like a quarterback hoping to prove last season was sustainable and more like one who knows exactly what he is now. That is a frightening prospect for the rest of the AFC. The Jaguars’ defense completely suffocated Cleveland Foyesade Oluokun with an INT on the Jaguars first drive on the season pic.twitter.com/CtsoWsw89f — Fitz (@LaurieFitzptrck) September 13, 2026 If Lawrence provided the fireworks, Jacksonville’s defense provided the foundation. The Browns finished with 272 total yards, but that number is somewhat misleading given that they did much of their damage after the Jaguars had already established a 34-0 lead. For the first half, Cleveland managed just 95 net yards and five first downs. And it started immediately. Deshaun Watson’s first regular-season start since 2024 lasted just five plays before Foyesade Oluokun intercepted him, ending a promising Browns drive inside the Jacksonville 20-yard line. Then the pressure kept coming. Cleveland punted on each of its next three possessions, before K.C. Concepcion Jr. fumbled in the second quarter. Josh Hines-Allen recovered, and Jacksonville promptly turned the mistake into another touchdown. By half-time, the Browns weren’t just behind; they were completely out of the game. The pass rush deserves particular credit. Hines-Allen finished with two sacks, while Travon Walker, Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs added one apiece. Jacksonville also forced two turnovers and held Cleveland to just one conversion on eight third-down attempts. There will be much tougher offenses coming down the road. But if Jacksonville’s defense can consistently generate that sort of pressure while forcing opponents to play from behind, it gives the Jaguars a remarkably high floor. Jacksonville’s offense was far more than Trevor Lawrence Parker Washington with the DIVING CATCH for his first TD of the season 😱 CLEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FzpS0RbR6u — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 It would be easy to look at the score and simply conclude that Lawrence won the game. And he certainly played the starring role. But Jacksonville’s offensive performance was impressive precisely because Cleveland couldn’t simply focus on stopping its quarterback. The Jaguars scored on six of their first seven possessions, and Lawrence spread the ball around beautifully. Parker Washington led the way with five catches for 83 yards and a touchdown, while Brian Thomas Jr., Jakobi Meyers, Brenton Strange and Josh Cameron all made significant contributions. The variety was what stood out: Deep shots. Quick completions. Play-action. Screens. Throws outside the numbers. Throws over the middle. Jacksonville kept giving Cleveland different problems to solve, and the Browns never found the answer. Even when the running game wasn’t spectacular statistically, the Jaguars remained committed to it. Bhayshul Tuten carried 15 times for 66 yards, while Jacksonville ran the ball 32 times overall. That balance helped keep Cleveland from simply turning the game into a pass-rush contest every time Lawrence dropped back. And that might ultimately be the most encouraging takeaway of all. The Jaguars didn’t need one player to carry them; Lawrence was outstanding, but Liam Coen’s offense produced a genuinely complete performance. The Verdict It’s only Week 1, and nobody should be booking Jacksonville’s Super Bowl parade just yet. But this was about as emphatic an opening statement as Liam Coen could have asked for. The Jaguars scored touchdowns on their first four possessions, led 24-0 at half-time and had the luxury of taking Lawrence out of the game with the score at 34-0. Cleveland’s late points did little to change the overall picture. The quarterback looked elite. The defense was ferocious. And the offense had enough variety to make life miserable for Cleveland. There will be considerably tougher tests ahead, but if this is what the 2026 Jaguars look like when they are only getting started, the rest of the AFC should probably be paying attention. Jags fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!
