title: Mike Vrabel defends Patriots’ offensive game plan against Seahawks
summary: After struggling in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots offense was hopeful to turn things around in its rematch with the Seattle Seahawks defense in Week 1. While the game as a whole was much more competitive, the end result was still disappointing. The Patriots finished with just 10 points on the day, turned […]
full_text: After struggling in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots offense was hopeful to turn things around in its rematch with the Seattle Seahawks defense in Week 1. While the game as a whole was much more competitive, the end result was still disappointing . The Patriots finished with just 10 points on the day, turned the ball over three times, and were plagued by some of the same issues that already haunted them back on Super Sunday. The game was there for the taking, but Drake Maye’s third interception of the day sealed it in the home team’s favor, which came away with a 13-10 victory over the reigning AFC champions. In the aftermath of the loss and New England’s disappointing outing, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels found himself the subject of criticism for what was seen as a fairly conservative game plan. However, head coach Mike Vrabel defended the plan on Monday. “I don’t look at things as conservative. That’s what we felt like was best against this defense,” Vrabel said during an appearance on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show . “We didn’t hit some things and you have to be able to run the football against split safety defense. That’s no secret. You don’t play split safety defense to stop the run; they play it to not give up big plays. We tried to hit some shots down the field. We threw it to the running backs a couple times for 12 or 15 yards when they were all off there, and on the interception should have thrown it to the back again for a third time. You just can’t get bored doing things right. If it’s not there it’s not there.” Through three quarters, the Patriots had performed decently against one of the NFL’s best defenses. They were up 10-3 and managed to move the ball even after losing star wide receiver A.J. Brown to what was later diagnosed as a high-ankle sprain . New England took its first snap of the fourth quarter — a 1-yard Corey Kiner run — in Seattle territory and with a chance of adding to its lead. From that point on, however, things went downhill. Drake Maye threw an interception on the very next play while attempting to hit Romeo Doubs deep on the play Vrabel was referencing; this turnover was a turning point in the contest and opened the floodgates. The Seahawks scored the game-tying touchdown five plays later, while Maye threw another pick on the next possession. Seattle added three more points off of that giveaway, which was then followed by the Patriots driving deep into their opponent’s territory only to be denied on another, game-ending INT. Could a different game plan have changed things and let the Patriots offense perform at the same level as others around the NFL in Week 1? Not in Vrabel’s estimation. “Every game is different, every defense is different,” he said. “We all sit down, we game-plan. Josh game-plans with his staff; each guy has an area. I’ll sit in with those. I think to look and say, ‘Well, this guy, this team put up number…’ — we didn’t win the game.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: A.J. Brown injury: Patriots receiver to miss more than 4 games on IR
summary: The New England Patriots did not just lose their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks last Wednesday, they also lost wide receiver A.J. Brown to injury. The high-prized offseason trade acquisition suffered a high-ankle sprain and was since placed on injured reserve. While that means he will miss at least four games, the expectation is […]
full_text: The New England Patriots did not just lose their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks last Wednesday, they also lost wide receiver A.J. Brown to injury. The high-prized offseason trade acquisition suffered a high-ankle sprain and was since placed on injured reserve . While that means he will miss at least four games, the expectation is that his absence will be longer than that. “My understanding is the expectation is he misses six weeks,” NFL Network insider Rapoport said on the air on Sunday. “Generally, it is four to six. This is a little more serious. Six weeks, no surgery planned.” From @NFLGameDay Morning: Injury updates from this week, as #Seaahawks QB Sam Darnold actually has a glute injury, #Patriots WR AJ Brown is out about six weeks, and #49ers WR De'Zhaun Stribling (deltoid ligament) is out at least a month. pic.twitter.com/0VlHlIzgw7 — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 13, 2026 Brown caught three passes for 26 yards in his Patriots debut, but hurt his ankle in the early third quarter while diving for an under-thrown Drake Maye third-down pass. He remained on the ground before gingerly walking to the blue medical tent on the sidelines; he subsequently reemerged and headed to the locker room for further testing, where he was then ruled out for the remainder of the game. The Patriots did score three more points with Brown sidelined, to cap the very series he departed with a 50-yard Andy Borregales field goal. Afterward, however, the team was shut out and ended up losing 13-10. Now on injured reserve, Brown will not be available against the Steelers, Jaguars and Bills. If indeed held out for six weeks, he would also miss games against the Raiders and Jets. In his place, the Patriots’ outside wide receiver group will be headed by Romeo Doubs, Mack Hollins and Kyle Williams. The group will see its first extended action without Brown on Sunday against Pittsburgh. Kickoff for the Patriots’ home opener at Gillette Stadium is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET.

title: Patriots position grades from Seahawks loss in Week 1
summary: The New England Patriots started their 2026 season the way they ended their 2025 campaign, with a loss to the Seattle Seahawks. The 13-10 game was as tightly-contested as the final score indicated, meaning that the visiting Patriots were not as bad as their minus-3 turnover differential or current 0-1 record would suggest. We already […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WA - SEPTEMBER 09: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on September 9, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots started their 2026 season the way they ended their 2025 campaign, with a loss to the Seattle Seahawks. The 13-10 game was as tightly-contested as the final score indicated, meaning that the visiting Patriots were not as bad as their minus-3 turnover differential or current 0-1 record would suggest. We already spoke about the standout performances from the game . Now, after rewatching it through broadcast copy and coach’s film, here are our final position grades from the Patriots’ defeat. Patriots position grades from NFL Week 1 Quarterback: For three quarters, Drake Maye played the game he needed to play for the Patriots to win. He took what the defense gave him, showed good accuracy in the short and intermediate parts of the field, and most importantly did not make any back-breaking mistakes. Then came the fourth quarter and a dramatic flipping of the switch. The patience he showed earlier disappeared as he launched a deep ball toward a double-covered Romeo Doubs that ended up as the first of three interceptions. That pick was a turning point for New England and its young QB, who still made some positive plays but ultimately crumbled while trying his version of “hero ball.” | Grade: D+ Running back: No TreVeyon Henderson meant a heavy workload for Rhamondre Stevenson, and he did what he could. Ultimately, however, he found little room to run en route to gaining just 51 yards on 18 carries for an underwhelming 2.8-yard average. He was more effective as a receiver, finishing with 44 yards on five catches, but did give up one hit against Drake Maye. The only other backs to see action — Corey Kiner and Lan Larison — combined to play 11 snaps, with the former carrying the ball six times for 11 yards and the latter working exclusively as a receiver and gaining 9 yards on a pair of receptions. | Grade: B- Wide receiver: The Patriots’ new-look receiver group had a challenging first day. A.J. Brown was lost to a high-ankle sprain after catching three passes for 26 yards, while fellow offseason pickup Romeo Doubs was held without a reception on three targets — one of them an interception, the other a rough drop. The player most consistently open against the Seahawks was DeMario Douglas, who finished with five catches for 20 yards. Mack Hollins was a go-to-guy for Drake Maye on the final drive and actually finished the game with a team-high 51 receiving yards. He also was involved on the game-losing interception, failing to properly clean out space underneath for Hunter Henry. Kyle Williams was largely a non-factor even after Brown departed in the early second half. | Grade: C- Tight end: It was a mixed bag for New England’s tight ends, only two of whom actually saw the field on offense. Hunter Henry caught all three of his passes for 26 combined yards, but also did not come off the line quickly enough on the final Drake Maye interception. Eli Raridon, meanwhile, caught the first touchdown of the season and threw a key block on Rhamondre Stevenson’s longest run of the day, a 12-yarder on the final drive. However, he also was responsible for two stuffed runs. | Grade: B Offensive line: No statistic from Wednesday’s game might be as damning for the offensive line as this one: Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner combined to gain 62 yards on the ground, with 59 of those coming after contact. Frankly, the running game had almost no room to operate, and looked the part. To the line’s credit, though, it did show some improvement in pass protection since the Super Bowl. However, Drake Maye was still pressured on 38.1% of his dropbacks even though he ended up taking just three sacks. As for individual efforts, Alijah Vera-Tucker had a rough Patriots debut, while Jared Wilson — who hurt his hand in the early second half — also struggled with consistency. Will Campbell, meanwhile, looked good outside of two penalties. | Grade: C – Defensive line: The Seahawks found some room to run early on and ended up with 97 yards on 22 carries, an average of 4.4 yards per attempt. Still, there were some solid moments both inside — such as Milton Williams’ 3rd-and-1 stuff in the fourth quarter — and on the edge. The latter was particularly encouraging after it was a major concern during joint practices with the Colts and Eagles. The pass rush from that part of the line was somewhat inconsistent outside of Dre’Mont Jones, with both of the group’s sacks of the clean-up variety. Inside, Christian Barmore gave Seattle’s interior line all it could handle even though his pressure total (4) does not quite reflect his impact. | Grade: B – Linebacker: Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss were the only off-ball linebackers to play on the defensive side of the ball. They were unsurprisingly actively involved, registering a combined 12 tackles but also missing three takedown attempts. Spillane also struggled to run with quarterback Drew Lock on one outside scramble. All in all, they had an adequate debut but were unable to provide any impact plays from the second level. | Grade: C Cornerback: Christian Gonzalez posted a shutout in 10 coverage matchups with Jaxon Smith-Njigba and looked every bit like the highest-paid cornerback in football he is. He did drop an interception and appeared a bit overeager on a run blitz on what ultimately ended as a 45-yard catch-and-run touchdown from the NFL Offensive Player of the Year, but overall looked like the shutdown cornerback is being paid to be. The other cornerbacks, meanwhile, performed at a high level as well. The only real blemish was Marcus Jones giving up a 24-yard catch to convert a third down before the Seahawks’ first field goal, but even that play was more due to Cooper Kupp’s concentration and ball skills rather than some bad coverage. | Grade: B + Safety: Craig Woodson had one of the best games of his young career against the Seahawks in the Super Bowl, but was less effective in the rematch on Wednesday. He missed a pair of tackles, including when he came in too hot on Jaxon Smith-Njiba’s long touchdown, and would have given up a touchdown to Cooper Kupp if not for an unrelated offensive infraction. Kevin Byard was solid in his Patriots debut, while the heavily-involved Dell Pettus had an up-and-down day as well. | Grade: C – Special teams: New England’s kicking game operation performed well. Andy Borregales made his lone field goal try from 50 yards out and split the uprights on an extra point. New punter Mitch Wishnowsky averaged 44.3 yards on four kicks, and pinned Seattle inside the 20 on three of them. Rashid Shaheed did have one 30-yard kickoff return but otherwise was held in check. Meanwhile, Kyle Williams averaged a solid 29.0 yards per kickoff return. Marcus Jones, on the other hand, was a non-factor in large part due to some excellent punting from Seattle’s Michael Dickson. | Grade: A- How would you grade the Patriots’ performance against the Seahawks? Do you agree with our assessment? Please head down to the comment section to discuss with the rest of the community. Download the SB Nation app today! title: Jaylen Reed’s Patriots debut was quiet. So was Kayshon Boutte’s first Texans game.
summary: Months of speculation finally their conclusion in late August, when the New England Patriots decided to indeed trade wide receiver Kayshon Boutte. The fourth-year man, who had been an integral part of their offense the past two seasons, was sent to the Houston Texans in exchange for safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round draft […]
full_text: Months of speculation finally their conclusion in late August, when the New England Patriots decided to indeed trade wide receiver Kayshon Boutte. The fourth-year man, who had been an integral part of their offense the past two seasons, was sent to the Houston Texans in exchange for safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round draft pick that was later repurposed to bring aboard running back Corey Kiner from the Cardinals. All three of the players either directly or indirectly involved in the original Boutte-to-Houston trade made their debuts for their respective new teams in Week 1. And all of them were relatively quiet. S Jaylen Reed The third member of the Patriots’ safety pecking order behind Craig Woodson, Kevin Byard and Dell Pettus, Reed did not see any playing time on the defensive side of the ball on Wednesday night in Seattle. Even though the Patriots used three-safety sets on 20 of 50 snaps (40%), the team clearly — and unsurprisingly, given Reed’s relatively late arrival to the team — trusted Pettus in that role. The second-year man did see the field on special teams, though. Playing eight of 22 possible snaps (36%), he played five snaps on punt return and three on the field goal and extra point blocking unit without registering any statistics. RB Corey Kiner Even though the Patriots were without RB2 TreVeyon Henderson, Kiner played only eight of 71 snaps (11%) versus the Seahawks. Only occasionally subbing in for workhorse Rhamondre Stevenson, he received six handoffs but gained a mere 11 yards for an underwhelming average of 1.8 yards per carry. He was not used in any different capacity, including on special teams. WR Kayshon Boutte The Texans opened their season at home against the Bills, and came close to a victory before ultimately fumbling the ball away while deep in Buffalo’s red zone on what potentially could have been a game-winning series. Boutte, however, did not have too active a hand in his team’s fortunes on Sunday. While the ex-Patriot was on the field for 36 of 79 snaps (46%), he finished with only one catch: in the third quarter, Boutte gained 21 yards on a C.J. Stroud pass to help set up a Houston touchdown. He had another catch for 6 yards taken off the board due to a chop-block penalty against teammate David Montgomery, and was unsuccessfully targeted a third time by Stroud. Just like in New England, Boutte did not play special teams.

title: Patriots rooting guide for NFL Week 1

Between Sunday and Monday a total of 14 games are […]
full_text: The New England Patriots opened their 2026 regular season with a disappointing 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks. While they enjoy a mini-bye before starting preparation for their Week 2 home opener versus Pittsburgh, the rest of the league will enter the action as well. Between Sunday and Monday a total of 14 games are on the menu. Here’s who to root for in each one of them. Sunday 1 p.m. ET Chicago Bears (0-0) at Carolina Panthers (0-0) : Go Bears! title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints loss to the Lions
summary: The Good: Resilience The Saints nearly matched the largest comeback in team history after falling behind 21-0 in the 3rd quarter. Instead of folding after a terrible half of football. the offense responded in crunch time. The Saints clawed their way back to force overtime and were a two point conversion away from stealing a […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints throws a pass during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Good: Resilience The Saints nearly matched the largest comeback in team history after falling behind 21-0 in the 3rd quarter. Instead of folding after a terrible half of football. the offense responded in crunch time. The Saints clawed their way back to force overtime and were a two point conversion away from stealing a win on the road against a team with Super Bowl aspirations. They easily could have gone the way of the Cleveland Browns on Sunday and stayed on the mat and lost by 20, but they didn’t. Chris Olave fought through pain to put up a career high 182 yards and Devaughn Vele looked like the solid WR2 we hoped he would be when the team acquired him last year. Tyler Shough responded after the half to finish with 410 yards and 3 TDs. The Saints ultimately came up short, but if the first half was just shaking off some rust that they weren’t able to shake off in the preseason due to the starters not playing then we should expect more of what we saw in the second half in Detroit. The Bad: Officiating Simply put, the officials stole 7 points from the Saints in this game. Don’t let anyone tell you different but Jared Goff fumbled the football and Jonas Sanker took it back for a touchdown, but the refs once again stole a game from the Saints. Why this keeps happening to them I do not know, but the NFL has had an officiating problem for many years that isn’t just exclusive to the Saints and it seems they have no interest in fixing. The incompetence of the officials is costing teams games and people their jobs, and the NFL has no accountability or oversight for their own officials who are supposed to be impartially judging these games with incredibly high stakes. This isn’t a problem that only the Saints suffer from, as I am sure they have been the beneficiaries of a bad call here and there in the past, but the fact is with how advanced the replay system is now, there shouldn’t be this many obviously bad calls anymore. The Saints would have won this game if it was officiated correctly, but there is no use dwelling on it as there is nothing they can do about it but expect more of the same going forward and work to make it not matter. The Ugly: The first half (and the first three minutes of the 3rd quarter) The Saints looked absolutely awful to start the game. Their first eight drives ended in five punts and three turnovers which resulted in them falling in a 21-0 hole. Despite the valiant comeback attempt, it is hard to win games in the NFL after falling behind by 21 points in the second half. If they had been able to manage just a field goal in the first half they would have won, but they couldn’t do that. Let’s hope this was just a fluke and that what we saw on their last five drives of the game is what we will see going forward.

title: Game Recap: Saints visit Lions in season opener
summary: The New Orleans Saints were looking to pull off a road upset against the Detroit Lions on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter The hosts got the ball to begin the game and went three-and-out. But the Saints didn’t fare much better on their opening series, with a 9-yard pass […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Devaughn Vele #14 of the New Orleans Saints attempts to make a catch against Rock Ya-Sin #23 of the Detroit Lions during the fourth quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints were looking to pull off a road upset against the Detroit Lions on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter The hosts got the ball to begin the game and went three-and-out. But the Saints didn’t fare much better on their opening series, with a 9-yard pass from Tyler Shough to Devaughn Vele marking the only first-down gain of the drive. Jared Goff and the Lions offense proceeded to get going on their second possession. A 19-yard connection with Sam LaPorta preceded a pair of big bursting runs from Jahmyr Gibbs to put Detroit in the red zone. From there, the Lions capitalised, with a 1-yard score from Gibbs capping off an 89-yard touchdown drive. Second Quarter The teams then exchanged a number of punts as the game moved into the second quarter. Shough did find Chris Olave on a few big throws, though the Saints never moved into scoring position. Detroit would then turn it over through a Gibbs fumble after a successful Saints challenge, but the visitors returned the favor when Shough threw an interception a few plays later. The Lions went three-and-out again, pinning New Orleans deep in their own half. Shough was able to move the drive past midfield with a 19-yard throw to Bryce Lance, but a sack a few plays later from Aidan Hutchinson forced a Saints punt just before the half. Third Quarter Trailing 7-0, Shough threw another interception on the first play of the second half. Detroit took advantage of the short field as Gibbs continued to punish the Saints defense, breaking off for an 18-yard run before eventually running in another 1-yard score to push the lead to 14-0. Shough proceeded to fumble early on the ensuing possession to give the Lions yet another short field. Goff connected with Amon-Ra St Brown for a 19-yard touchdown pass to give Detroit a 21-0 advantage. Then, at last, the Saints offense burst into life. A 47-yard pass to Olave and a 9-yard throw to Noah Fant put the black and gold on the edge of the red zone. A few plays later, including a third-down scramble from Shough for a first down, Kendre Miller ran in an 8-yard touchdown to get the visitors on the board. The Saints defense responded with a perfect series of their own, forcing a three-and-out. Shough picked up where he left off, completing his first three throws of the ensuing drive for 31 yards. A defensive pass interference call put the Saints down at the 1-yard line, before Shough found Vele for his first touchdown pass of the season to cut into the lead again. Fourth Quarter Now leading just 21-14, Goff and the Lions were forced into another quick punt. The Saints offense continued their momentum, as Travis Etienne ran for 14 yards to begin another scoring series. Shough’s 31-yard connection with Vele put the visitors in the red zone, though this time they were held to a field goal attempt. Daniel Carlson’s 28-yard chip shot put the score at 21-17. Having nearly blown their lead entirely, the Lions at last found some life. A facemask penalty against Tyree Wilson meant they began their drive at midfield. Gibbs continued to have success running the football, but the Saints defense did manage to hold Detroit to a field goal. Jake Bates’ 23-yard kick put the lead back to seven, at 24-17. Needing a touchdown to tie the game, the Saints quickly found themselves on 4th-and-12 with the game on the line. Shough delivered, finding Lance for 15 yards. He connected with Vele on the next play for another first down, and then connected with Olave on another bomb for a 42-yard gain. Juwan Johnson caught the 9-yard touchdown pass a play later, and the extra point tied the game at 24-24. With just over a minute remaining, Detroit would go three-and-out, giving New Orleans a slim chance at winning the game in regulation after an Etienne run and an 18-yard catch from Johnson gave Shough time to spike the ball for a long field goal. But Carlson’s 62-yard effort went wide right as the clock expired. Overtime The Saints deferred to Detroit, who put together a 70-yard touchdown drive highlighted by a 22-yard pass from Goff to Jameson Williams to set up 1st-and-goal. St Brown caught the touchdown pass to put the Lions up 31-24. Needing a touchdown of their own, Shough threw for 20 yards to Olave on another fourth-down conversion as the Saints moved past midfield. He found Fant for 10 yards amidst short runs from Miller and Etienne, before finding Johnson for 27 yards to set up 1st-and-goal. It was Fant again who caught the 8-yard touchdown pass to put New Orleans down by just a point. Kellen Moore elected to go for two and the win, as opposed to tying the game and giving Detroit a chance to score again. But the Lions defense prevailed, as Shough’s pass intended for Lance had almost no chance. Despite a resilient comeback effort from the black and gold, the Lions emerged victorious, 31-30. If it’s any consolation, all three NFC South rivals dropped their opening game on Sunday. Next up for the Saints is a visit to the Baltimore Ravens on September 20.

title: What are the odds? Saints open as 8.5-point underdogs for Week 2 at the Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints will continue their 2026 season on the road Sunday when they take on the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2. What initially looked like a likely loss on the Saints’ schedule has suddenly become a much more fascinating matchup after Week 1. After falling behind 21-0 in Detroit, New Orleans battled back […]
full_text: Sep 1, 2016; New Orleans, LA, USA; Baltimore Ravens quarterback Josh Johnson (2) runs the ball during the fourth quarter against the New Orleans Saints at the Mercedes-Benz Superdome. The Ravens won 23-14. Mandatory Credit: Matt Bush-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints will continue their 2026 season on the road Sunday when they take on the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2. What initially looked like a likely loss on the Saints’ schedule has suddenly become a much more fascinating matchup after Week 1. After falling behind 21-0 in Detroit, New Orleans battled back to force overtime before ultimately losing 31-30 to the Lions. Despite three turnovers, quarterback Tyler Shough delivered an impressive performance, throwing for 410 yards and three touchdowns, while wide receiver Chris Olave hauled in 10 passes for 182 yards. Baltimore, meanwhile, opened its season with an impressive 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. Derrick Henry rushed for 144 yards and three touchdowns, Lamar Jackson threw for 324 yards, and the Ravens piled up 506 yards of total offense. Zay Flowers racked up 150 receiving yards before leaving the game with a hamstring injury, making his status something to monitor throughout this week. That presents another challenge for a Saints defense that struggled early against Detroit before settling in as the game progressed. Slowing down Jackson is difficult enough, but New Orleans will also have to find a way to contain Henry and prevent Baltimore from controlling the game on the ground. For the Saints, however, Week 1 showed that this offense may be capable of keeping them in games many expected them to lose. Shough showed poise in leading the comeback, Olave looked every bit like a No. 1 receiver, and New Orleans refused to fold after falling behind by three touchdowns. Now comes another difficult road test. The Saints may be 0-1, but if what they showed in Detroit was any indication, Sunday’s matchup in Baltimore could be a lot more interesting than it looked when the schedule was first released. According to FanDuel, the Saints are currently 8.5-point underdogs against the Ravens, with an over/under of 48.5 points. However, those odds could move as kickoff approaches. title: Malik Nabers on his NY Giants comeback: ‘Yeah, it’s time’
summary: Hope season for the New York Giants lasted longer than most teams this year, and so too did the questions that hung over their offseason. With the second-to-last kick-off of opening weekend, Giants fans had to wait, and wait… and wait to find out what their team would look like in 2026. Likewise, they also […]
full_text: New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers celebrates after beating the Dallas Cowboys | Getty Images Hope season for the New York Giants lasted longer than most teams this year, and so too did the questions that hung over their offseason. With the second-to-last kick-off of opening weekend, Giants fans had to wait, and wait… and wait to find out what their team would look like in 2026. Likewise, they also had to wait until the last minute to find out whether star receiver Malik Nabers would even play against the Dallas Cowboys. Nabers’ status remained unclear even into Sunday afternoon, and reports eventually emerged that Nabers would be a true game-time decision. Even Nabers himself wasn’t sure if he’d be ready to go against the Cowboys. He even told his family to not come to the game, in case he wouldn’t be able to play. “I really didn’t know; my family didn’t even come to this game because it’s a one-on-one battle that you have go through. You have to do it for yourself,” he said after the game. “I didn’t want everybody here, I didn’t want my family here and I feel like I let them down by not playing, so I had to do it for myself first. I had to go out there, feel it out, feel like I was doing it and I felt good.” It was ultimately decided that Nabers would test his surgically repaired knee prior to the game against the Cowboys and make his decision based on how it felt. And even then, Nabers was nowhere to be seen when the media arrived at the press box, at least not until he came out for a dynamic warmup prior to the game. Malik Nabers stretches on the field pic.twitter.com/YWW33tXVf7 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 13, 2026 Then the announcement was made: Malik Nabers wasn’t among the inactive players. The Giants’ star receiver would make his return against the Cowboys. “The deciding factor was when I got out there, I just felt good.” Nabers said. “I felt good, I got a little chill through my body. I was like ‘Yeah, it’s time, it’s time’.” “I got a sense about three hours before the game, maybe two and a half, somewhere in there, when he went out and tested it and he felt ready and that’s when the decision was made,” Giants head coach John Harbaugh said. “It was his call. He had been cleared medically, but he had to feel right. He had to feel like he was ready to go and he could protect himself and perform the way he wanted, and he did. Malik played a great game. He played a heck of a game.” “I decided in warmups; really during warmups I felt really good, I felt good running around,” Nabers added. “I was catching really (well), I stretched really (well), warmup went pretty well. I just felt like it was time to go.” Even quarterback Jaxson Dart wasn’t sure whether his top target would be able to play or not. At least not until he was able to see Nabers’ body language during warm-ups. “I didn’t really want to ask for a while” Dart said. “So, I was just watching him during the warm-ups, and I was trying to keep my distance and I was able to see this from his, like, you know, his communication, I guess. And then I saw him give one little nod before he came in and did routes on air, and then I went over and told (Giants quarterback) Jameis (Winston) that I think Uno’s (Malik Nabers) playing, and I was just ecstatic from that point on.” Ecstatic for good reason. While it was the Giants’ punishing running game that ground the Cowboys down, Nabers was invaluable for Dart. He was targeted on a team-high 9 of Dart’s 29 pass attempts, catching 6 for 69 yards, including several key gains. “He’s just a guy where, no matter what the coverage is, no matter who they put out there on him, you have all the confidence in the world that he’s going to make a play,” Dart said of Nabers. “And I think that we were all not 100 percent sure what was going to happen. So, I was just super stoked. I think that once he was able to feel those lights and feel the game-day environment, maybe he had a little bit of adrenaline, and then he’s just a guy who wants to play for this team, loves the game. And I’m so happy that he was able to come back and have a game like this where he was just able to play really, really efficient and good football.” In other words, Nabers played winning football, and his play helped the rest of the team play winning football. Which is exactly what they set out to do from the start. “We got guys in here that expect to win,” Nabers said. “During the walk-through I looked at everybody’s eyes, and I could tell from everybody’s eyes that they were ready to play. There was no doubt in anybody’s mind that we weren’t coming out here giving our best foot forward and winning this game. Harbs’ (Giants Head Coach John Harbaugh) speech before the game yesterday, I (saw) it in his eyes that he knew we were coming out to play. We were coming out to play hard and that gave me all the confidence I needed.”
author: Chris Pflum

title: ‘Things I think’ about Giants-Cowboys: ‘Unbelievable environment’ best sign of all
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — That was different. Yes, the simple fact that the New York Giants won a season-opener on Sunday night was different. The Giants had lost six of seven season-opening games against the Dallas Cowboys prior to Sunday’s impressive 28-20 victory. They had started 10 of the 13 previous seasons 0-2 or worse. […]
full_text: Isaiah Likely celebrates with fans after the Giants’ victory over Dallas on Sunday night. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — That was different. Yes, the simple fact that the New York Giants won a season-opener on Sunday night was different. The Giants had lost six of seven season-opening games against the Dallas Cowboys prior to Sunday’s impressive 28-20 victory. They had started 10 of the 13 previous seasons 0-2 or worse. So, sure, Sunday was different in that sense. What was really different, though, was the atmosphere inside MetLife Stadium throughout the night. Fans of the Cowboys, Philadelphia Eagles, and other teams have made a habit in recent years of infiltrating and taking over the Giants’ home stadium. Not Sunday night. Maybe it was emotions from the 9/11 commemorations by the Giants. Maybe it was the beginning of the John Harbaugh Era following a summer of optimistic reporting about the state of the team. Maybe it was the introductions of Malik Nabers, who played, and Odell Beckham Jr., who officially returned. Whatever it was, the atmosphere inside MetLife Stadium was electric. From the second the Cowboys stepped on the field things were different. Dallas was booed so vociferously it was impossible to notice that there were thousands of Cowboys fans in the stadium. Long after the game ended, loud “Let’s Go Giants” chants from happy Giants fans reverberated around the building. Harbaugh called it an “unbelievable environment.” “This crowd, I’m telling you, man, the parking lot. The parking lot was off the chain driving in here. It was packed! I’m talking like four and half hours before the game,” Harbaugh said. “I get here early now, and I’m thinking it’s going to be easy to get in here and it wasn’t. And then the stadium was just absolutely electric from beginning to end. The sideline was electric before the game. I mean the whole thing was just quite an environment. It was really great to be a part of it and to see our guys step up in that environment, to handle all that and to focus on the football. “It was more than I expected in all honesty. It was incredible. The stadium was unbelievable. It was everything that you would think, but it was more than I thought. It was really something. I want us to play well enough that we can create that atmosphere every single week here going forward throughout the season. That’s up to us. That’s our job as coaches and players to create a football team good enough to deserve that type of a stadium every time we play.” Sunday was a reminder of what Giants football can look and sound like when the team is going well. Players noticed. “New York likes winning,” Kayvon Thibodeaux said. “When we win, it’s fun.” It certainly was on Sunday. Veteran offensive tackle Jermaine Eleumunor, in the league since 2017, smiled when asked about the atmosphere. “I’ve never seen a crowd like that ever before,” Eluemunor said. “It just gets you going. You don’t want to disappoint that crowd. You want to keep that same crowd the entire season. The fans don’t know how much that means to everyone. It means a lot.” With the release last week of Darius Slayton, star left tackle Andrew Thomas is now the longest-tenured Giant. He has been with the team since 2020. Thomas said the playoff season of 2022 is the only other time he has experience a home crowd like that in MetLife Stadium. “It was great to see,” Thomas said. “It means everything. We play for the fans. We want to give them a good product.” Running back Cam Skattebo has talked in the past about wanting to be part of changing the expectations around a Giants team that has been mostly down-trodden since winning the Super Bowl at the end of the 2011 season. He said Sunday’s atmosphere was “beautiful.” “It was an amazing crowd. It was awesome to have everybody that showed up tonight be as loud as possible,” Skattebo said. “On third down you couldn’t hear anything. It’s been awesome to be able to be a part of this. “We’re gonna build on this. We want every home game to be like this. This is how every home game should be, whether it’s Sunday Night Football, Monday Night Football or if it’s just a regular game. They all should be this big. They all should be this wild.” Quarterback Jaxson Dart, who put together a spectacular 23 of 29, 230-yard, 3 touchdown performance, also lauded the atmosphere. “Seeing the crowd out there tonight, they had a huge impact in the game, just the energy and momentum. That stuff’s huge,” Dart said. “So, just everybody showing up, showing out on a big night like tonight, where it was bigger than even just the game itself, was just a really special environment to be in.” The Giants, of course, hope it was the start of something that will become a regular occurrence and not just an aberration. Here are more ‘things I think’ after Sunday’s game. Malik Nabers made a difference Nabers said he didn’t decided until he was on the field two hours before the game that he would play. He didn’t even have family in attendance because he didn’t want to be pressured to play if he didn’t feel right. “During warmups I felt really good, I felt good running around,” Nabers said. I was catching really (well), I stretched really (well), warmup went pretty well. I just felt like it was time to go.“ Nabers went, and went well. He finished with six catches for 69 yards. Give an assist to Harbaugh for helping Nabers realize he was ready for game action. Harbaugh, 63, apparently tackled Nabers during a walk-through at the end of the week. “We were all just chilling on the sideline. It was right before we were supposed to start our walkthrough, and things were just up in the air. We didn’t know exactly what was going to happen,” Dart said. “And me and Coach Harbs kind of had some conversations. He’s like, ‘You know what, like, I think that once he gets hit for the first time and realizes that he’s okay, then he’s going to feel confident.’ So I think in his mind that triggered, ‘Oh, maybe I should tackle him right then and there.’ So, we’re all just standing there, and then all of a sudden Leek goes down on the ground, and our team’s super protective of him. So we all turned to look, and it’s Coach Harbs tackling Leek, and then he pops up and he goes, ‘See, you’re all good.’” Jaxson Dart How good was the Giants’ second-year quarterback on Sunday? This good: Jaxson Dart with the best QB performance in Week 1. • EPA/Play: +0.73 (1st) • WPA/Play: +2.2% (1st) Every 5 plays, Dart added 3.5 expected points and 11% win probability for the Giants. pic.twitter.com/01OTeikQyu — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 Dart was in control throughout. He was on target. He forced maybe one pass all night. He used his legs on both designed runs and scrambles. He got out of bounds. He got down. When he took a late hit out of bounds it seemed like the entire Giants sideline jumped to his defense. “I felt very comfortable,” Dart said. “I thought that we just did a really good job of staying in progress throughout the game, whether it was the run game, whether it was the pass game. Thought our O-line just played their ass off, and that just helped everything around. So, I’m really just happy with how the offense executed. I thought Nags (Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy) called an awesome game, and I thought the guys just played really, really hard. So, it made my job a lot easier, and guys all over the place made a ton of plays, so I’m excited about that.” I told you so All summer I kept mentioning the idea that Isaiah Likely had become Dart’s favorite target in “gotta have it” situations. Well, among Likely’s eight catches on Sunday were a pair of touchdowns in the red zone, and four plays that produced first downs. I missed on this one I expected Najee Harris to play and Tyrone Tracy to be inactive vs. the Cowboys. After Tracy fumbled away a scoring opportunity Sunday night, I am pretty certain that is what we will see next week against the Los Angeles Rams.…
author: Ed Valentine

title: 4 things we learned from the Giants’ 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys
summary: The New York Giants had not defeated the Dallas Cowboys in a game that was meaningful to both teams since 2016. That’s pretty impressive (actually, depressive if you’re a Giants fan). Yes, they beat them in the final meaningless game last season to drop the Giants in the draft order; that worked out all right […]
full_text: Isaiah Likely catches a touchdown pass Sunday night. | Getty Images The New York Giants had not defeated the Dallas Cowboys in a game that was meaningful to both teams since 2016. That’s pretty impressive (actually, depressive if you’re a Giants fan). Yes, they beat them in the final meaningless game last season to drop the Giants in the draft order; that worked out all right for the Giants. Yes, they beat them in the final game in 2020 when the Giants were trying to win the NFC Least at 6-10, but that game meant nothing to Dallas and Andy Dalton was the quarterback. In 2022 when the Giants actually had a good team, they couldn’t even beat Dallas at home when Cooper Rush started for them. Dak Prescott has had their number for almost his entire NFL career. The Cowboys put 40+ points on the board against the Giants three times in that span, and 30+ points three other times. Those days are now officially over. The Giants defeated the Cowboys 28-20 in a game you might even say they controlled. How did they do it? Not an explosive offense, but an effective offense If tonight was an indication of what’s to come, the Giants’ offense is going to be annoying for opponents to play against. Jaxson Dart only attempted two passes longer than 20 yards and completed neither. Dart’s longest completion was his 15 yard TD pass to Isaiah Likely. Still, Dart managed to accumulate a respectable 230 yards passing, with 3 TDs and a 134.2 QB rating. What had to be frustrating to the Cowboys was getting their hands on the ball so seldom. The Giants dominated time of possession 36:40 to 23:20. The did it by doing many of the same things over and over again on long drives. A lot of that was Isaiah Likely, who only had 78 yards, but that was on 8 receptions in 8 targets (including the beautiful catch and toes down in the back of the end zone, a key play in the game). For now, he is the linchpin of this offense. Another 54 yards were on keepers by Dart. Three of those carries were scrambles, nine others designed runs, but unlike last year, Dart showed that he has finally learned his lesson by mostly keeping himself out of harm’s way. Little of it was spectacular, but all of it felt like an offense that Dart knows how to run and is in complete control of. The running game is clearly going to be an important part of this possession offense. Cam Skattebo picked up where he left off, as the human bowling ball bounced off tacklers for 81 yards in 18 carries. We also got our first taste of the Patrick Ricard experience. Ricard was on the field for 27 of the Giants’ 35 rushing plays, and pretty much wherever he went was where the ball was going to go behind him. The offense will take a little getting used to for me; I like explosive plays. But dominating time of possession is a winning formula…as long as you convert those possessions into points, as the Giants did tonight. Malik Nabers is back Perhaps the best news of the evening was seeing Malik Nabers back on the field, given that we didn’t know for sure until almost game time that he was going to play. More importantly, Nabers caught 6 balls in 9 targets for 69 yards. Those aren’t the types of stats that made Nabers a rookie sensation, but he was still a valuable component of the offense, and he seemed relieved after the game. We’ll see whether the Giants open up the offense at SoFi Stadium next week against a Rams defense that was diced up by Brock Purdy in Australia and will be without Myles Garrett. Malachi Fields made his debut as well as caught 2 balls for 25 yards. The defense will go as far as the pass rush and run D takes it The Giants’ defense didn’t sack Dak Prescott all night, but they pressured him 9 times and he was 0 for 8 on passes thrown while under pressure. Compare that to his 22 of 26 when he was kept clean. Abdul Carter, Chauncey Golston (nice to see him being used finally), and Kayvon Thibodeaux all pressured Dak multiple times, so even with Brian Burns having a quiet night, Dak couldn’t really get comfortable. I also thought the Giants’ run defense was better tonight than anything I saw last year. Dallas doesn’t live by the run, but Tremaine Edmunds and rookie Arvell Reese seemed very effective against the run. Edmunds in particular had 7 tackles and 1 assist and Reese 5 tackles. Golston also had 2 tackles and 2 assists. Dallas only had 69 yards rushing all night, and we only saw one run of 10 yards, and that was by Prescott. The Dallas OL was not gashing holes up the middle, and we weren’t seeing their backs get outside and turn the corner on the Giants much either. And it’s a good thing, because if tonight was any indication, any time an opposing quarterback does manage to get a clean pocket to pass against the Giants, it may be trouble. After one game, it’s still fair to say that the Giants do not have a single cornerback who can be counted on to defend a pass. Admittedly, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens are a challenge for any secondary. However Dru Phillips continued to show that he can’t be trusted in coverage, drawing three interference penalties (one of them pretty iffy). Deonte Banks surrendered a TD, although he at least seemed more competitive in coverage than he had in the past two years. Paulson Adebo was beaten twice in 3 targets for completions. The one bright spot was Jevon Holland, who had an interception and only allowed one completion. Again, Lamb and Pickens are a tough ask…but next week it’s Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. Will Tyrone Tracy be buried on the depth chart? Skattebo is clearly RB1 on the depth chart despite just returning from a serious season-ending injury. He looked like his rookie self with no ill effects. Unfortunately when Tyrone Tracy entered the game, he fumbled on his second carry and spent the rest of the game on the bench. Fortunately Devin Singletary, although not running the ball much, caught swing pass after swing pass after swing pass without the Dallas defense adjusting to stop it. And of course the Giants have Najee Harris on the bench if needed. But it’s fair to wonder whether/when Tracy is going to get another chance after having similar problems last year. After the game Harbaugh greeted him warmly, so maybe he’ll be back in the rotation in LA.
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: Giants-Cowboys instant grades following New York’s Week 1 victory
summary: The New York Giants pulled off the 28-20 upset of the Dallas Cowboys in Week 1. Dallas has had the Giants’ number for years, but the John Harbaugh era starts off fantastically for New York, who out-gained 394 yards to 244 at MetLife Stadium on Sunday Night Football. The Giants played heavy – old-school – football, and […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants pulled off the 28-20 upset of the Dallas Cowboys in Week 1. Dallas has had the Giants’ number for years, but the John Harbaugh era starts off fantastically for New York, who out-gained 394 yards to 244 at MetLife Stadium on Sunday Night Football. The Giants played heavy – old-school – football, and Jaxson Dart was efficient passing the football. The Giants were 9 of 11 on third-down conversions and averaged 4.5 yards per carry; they ran the football well, and Jaxson Dart rose to the occasion multiple times to ensure the Giants earned the win. Here are the grades from the Giants’ Week 1 victory! Quarterback Jaxson Dart was DIALED in throughout the Week 1 matchup against Dallas. His two-minute drill was near flawless, as he led the Giants 55 yards downfield on six plays and found Malik Nabers for 13 yards on a third-and-nine. He then completed a pair of consecutive passes before finding Isaiah Likely for 15 yards and a touchdown, which gave the Giants a touchdown lead heading into halftime. Dart finished 23/29 for 230 yards with three passing touchdowns and 11 carries for 54 yards on the ground. Not only was he efficient, but he found solutions and worked through his progressions well. It was a very impressive performance by the second-year play caller. Grade: A+ Running Back Cam Skattebo was the lead back for the Giants, but Matt Nagy and Greg Roman did opt to go with a committee. We saw Devin Singletary early and Tyrone Tracy Jr., who fumbled the football on his second touch. Nevertheless, it was Skattebo who scored the Giants’ first touchdown of the season. Skattebo finished with 18 carries for 81 yards with one touchdown. Devin Singletary became a big part of the fourth-quarter offense with Skattebo taking a breather. Singletary touched the football on four consecutive plays, including his nine yard touchdown reception midway through the fourth quarter. Singletary finished with six carries for 16 yards with four catches for 22 yards. Grade: B Wide Receiver It was excellent to see Malik Nabers healthy and dressed for the Giants. A couple plays were designed for him early. Nabers caught six passes for 69 yards on nine targets. Darnell Mooney had two catches for 27 yards and Malachi Fields had a pair of grabs for 25 yards. Those were the only three wide receivers to catch the ball, but the Giants’ receivers were blocking their backside off all game, which was a major plus for the overall offense. Grade: B Tight End Isaiah Likely is a difference-making tight end. He converted two third downs in the first half for the Giants. He took advantage of the blown coverage in the red zone for his first Giants’ touchdown. Likely was clutch for the Giants, finishing with weight catches for 78 yards with two touchdowns. He flashed strong hands and was reliable for the Giants, which helped earn John Harbaugh his first victory as the Giants’ head coach. Theo Johnson also finished with one catch for nine yards, and Chris Manhertz did Chris Manhertz type things – throwing impactful blocks for the Giants’ offense Grade: A+ Offensive Line The entire off-season was full of conversation of the physical nature that John Harbaugh is attempting to instill in the Giants, and that was demonstrated – along with impressive play-calling/design – by the Giants’ offensive line early against Dallas. New York took their opening possession and drove 80+ yards for a score, while running the football on eight of ten plays, including a 22-yard Jaxson Dart read-run to the outside. Francis Mauigoa proved to be an excellent addition to the Giants’ offensive line – a line that dominated up front and rushed for 165 yards (4.5 YPC). The identity of John Harbaugh was felt, and the offensive line held up their end of the deal to ensure that the Giants could operate as they desired against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 1. Grade: A Defensive Line We did not see DJ Reader or Shelby Harris in the preseason, but the Giants’ run defense was DIALED in early. Dallas averaged just 3.2 yards per carry, including Dak Prescott’s scrambles, through their first three offensive drives; Javonte Williams had just eight carries for 20 yards through those first three drives. The Giants held Williams in check through the end of the first-half, and he finished with just 12 carries for 41 yards on the ground. Overall, the defensive line did enough against the run, although they weren’t overly impactful as pass rushers. Grade: B- EDGE The Giants were getting early pressure on Dak Prescott, but the veteran evaded the pocket and picked up valuable yardage with his legs. Abdul Carter’s movement ability just JUMPS out at you when you watch him. Still, New York couldn’t get home against Dak Prescott, and the Cowboys’ offensive line was able to keep New York away for much of the game. I will state, though, that Kayvon Thibodeaux’s pressure against Prescott resulted in the Holland interceptions, which was vital to the victory. Grade: C+ Linebacker Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese are difference makers at linebacker. Edmunds’ play on the goal line against Dallas late in the third quarter showcased his ability to cover outside the numbers. Reese didn’t POP in the game, but he had several plays where he executed his assignment well. I am excited to dive into his tape to give a more comprehensive view of his performance. Reese was fooled on the Javonte Williams receiving touchdown, which resulted in Brandon Aubrey missing the extra point. Watching the duo fly around was a welcome sight. Grade: B Cornerback The Giants’ cornerbacks were tested – that was not a surprise – but on Dallas’ first scoring drive, Dru Phillips and Greg Newsome II both committed third-down penalties that resulted in 57 yards for Dallas. The Giants cornerbacks MUST be more disciplined and locate the football when it is airborne. Also, Tae Banks had two missed tackles on the edge in the first half; he must become more reliable as a tackler. Banks lost his one-on-one in the end zone with CeeDee Lamb for Dallas’ first touchdown. Overall, though, the Giants’ cornerbacks held Lamb and George Pickens in check throughout the game. Both players were sloppy and dropped passes. New York was undisciplined in coverage, which led to several defensive pass interference calls; but, to be fair, some were wildly ticky-tacky. Dru Phillips fell victim to three such calls. Both Banks and Newsome were injured in the fourth quarter, forcing Paulson Adebo and Colton Hood into the game. Both made plays against Pickens and Lamb, but the late personal foul penalty by Holland against Flournoy ( going against Hood ) gave the Cowboys extra life with the passing touchdown to Javonte Williams. Statistically, the Giants held up very well against arguably the best wide receiver duo in football, but DPI penalties don’t show up in player stats. It could have been worse, but it wasn’t excellent either for the Giants’ DBs. Grade: C Safety Jevon Holland made his presence known with less than a minute left in the first half. Kayvon Thibodeaux flushed Prescott out of the pocket, and the veteran quarterback heaved the ball in the air, where Holland closed distance to come away with the pick from a middle-of-the-field closed position. Holland showed great recognition and awareness. I will have more takeaways once I review the film. Grade: B+ Special Teams The Giants had one punt that went 46 yards, and Dominic Zvada made all of his extra points. The coverage teams were fine, and specials were not an issue against the Dallas Cowboys. Grade: B
author: Nick Falato

title: 12 winners, 4 losers for NY Giants in impressive victory over Cowboys
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants (1-0) won by eight points on Sunday night, beating the Dallas Cowboys, 28-20. In reality, though, the Giants put a beating on the Cowboys, dominating them physically. The crowd was electric. The Giants played the way head coach John Harbaugh envisioned. They took advantage of the good […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo and Jaxson Dart celebrate on Sunday night. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants (1-0) won by eight points on Sunday night, beating the Dallas Cowboys, 28-20. In reality, though, the Giants put a beating on the Cowboys, dominating them physically. The crowd was electric. The Giants played the way head coach John Harbaugh envisioned. They took advantage of the good vibes and the preparation that came out of the summer. They mostly did what they wanted to do on offense. Defensively, they controlled one of the NFL’s best offenses. How big was the victory for Harbaugh? “It’s funny, it’s number one. It’s number one because it’s the one right now. My dad always says that. He’ll say this in the car on the way home, he’ll say, John, you’ve never had a better win than that,” Harbaugh said. “He says it every time and I’m going to tell you, I think this time it might be true. But this was really special because these guys, these players, these guys who’ve had belief from the beginning, who don’t bat an eye, who just try to do the right thing every single day. Who try to be on point, and even when they’re not on point, they’re willing to bounce back and make it right. “Maybe there’s a mistake, maybe there’s a false start, but we come back the next play and we find a way to make a play and erase the mistake and make it right and make it better. Buying into that kind of a mindset just in practice and then seeing it happen in the game, that’s what as a coach you feel so good about.” Let’s get to the ‘Kudos and Willies’. Kudos to … Giants fans — I cannot remember the last time the atmosphere in MetLife Stadium was as raucous as it was on Sunday night. There were loud boos when the Cowboys came on the field before the game, ovations for Malik Nabers and Odell Beckham, some ‘Let’s go Giants’ chants, and a constant buzz. This was an awesome environment for the home team. It hinted at the possibilities of what things can be like if the Giants are actually good. “It was more than I expected in all honesty,” Harbaugh said. “It was incredible. The stadium was unbelievable. It was everything that you would think, but it was more than I thought. It was really something. “I want us to play well enough that we can create that atmosphere every single week here going forward throughout the season. That’s up to us. That’s our job as coaches and players to create a football team good enough to deserve that type of a stadium every time we play.” John Harbaugh — The Giants paid off Harbaugh’s strenuous training canp with an impressive victory. There were good vibes entering the game, wildly enthusiastic fans in the stands, and the Giants cashed in with a massive victory. A number of players credited the Giants’ tough training camp with how ready they were to play on Sunday night. Co-owner John Mara gave a game ball to Harbaugh after the victory. #Giants owner John Mara gave HC John Harbaugh a game ball after his first win with the organization. “I was overconfident. I really was. And I was right!” https://t.co/9XK0FvQyFn pic.twitter.com/OkX2rbqrrm — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 14, 2026 Harbaugh celebrated by giving his parents a game ball. The Harbaughs celebrate the victory! John Harbaugh gave his father a game ball from Western Kentucky's 2002 championship pic.twitter.com/yjOnbPdjsO — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 14, 2026 Isaiah Likely — Likely caught eight passes in eight targets for 78 yards and two touchdowns. The numbers are impressive. His contribution was even more impressive. All summer, we saw Dart lean on Likely in “gotta have it” situations. That carried through on Sunday night. Leading 28-20 and trying to close out the victory, Dart found Likely for first downs on third-and-9 and third-and-3 to allow the Giants an opportunity to run the clock out. Likely ended up catching four passes for first downs. In the red zone, Likely was the first option, catching two short TD passes. Malik Nabers — God told Nabers to play against the Cowboys. He did. And, he played exceptionally well. Nabers ended up with six catches on nine targets for 69 yards “No matter what the coverage is, no matter who they put on him, you have all the confidence in the world that he’s going to make a play,” quarterback Jaxson Dart said of Nabers. How did Nabers know he would be able to take a hit on Sunday night after not playing since tearing his ACL in Week 4 of last season? Harbaugh apparently tried to tackle him, that’s how. Giants WR Malik Nabers tells me John Harbaugh tackled him during walk through 🤣 “Everybody was worried if I could tackle. Actually Coach Harbaugh tackled me…” Me: “He tackled you himself?” “Yeah, he wanted to see if I could take a tackle.” Me: “Did you go down?” “Nah I… pic.twitter.com/acHfshAc6e — Simone Eli (@SimoneEli_TV) September 14, 2026 Recovering their own fumbles — The Giants fumbled four times, and that could have dramatically changed the outcome of the game. Fortunately for them, the only one they lost was a Tyrone Tracy fumble in the red zone. They managed to get on top of the other three fumbles. Devin Singletary — In training camp, Harbaugh said Singletary was one of the most consistent players he had been around. Singletary doesn’t do anything spectacular, he simply contributes. He had just six carries for 16 yards on Sunday, but added four catches for 22 yards, including a 9-yard touchdown catch to put the Giants up by two touchdowns midway through the fourth quarter. Jaxson Dart — The second-year quarterback was outstanding against the Cowboys. He completed 23 of 29 passes (79.3%), for 230 yards, and three touchdowns. He ran 11 times for 54 yards. He got down or out of bounds when he needed to. He made big throws when the Giants needed them. He played the way a franchise quarterback is supposed to play. Cam Skattebo — The Giants’ human battering ram of a running back helped the Giants grind down the Cowboys by running 18 times for 81 yards, 4.5 yards per carry. The Giants ran for 165 yards total on 37 attempts, 4.5 per rush. Matt Nagy (and the offensive staff) — Maybe the way the Giants’ offense performed on Sunday, always seeming to be a step ahead of the Dallas defense, will quiet those who aren’t sure about Nagy’s ability to coordinate the Giants’ offense. The Skattebo touchdown run was a beautifully-designed play where Skattebo had no Dallas defenders within 10 yards of him. One of the two Likely touchdowns was a gorgeous play where Likely seemed to appear out of thin air with everyone else going away from him. Giants’ wide receivers were running wide open all night. The Giants ran the ball when they wanted to, and how they wanted to. They passed the ball efficiently, and Dart had to make few tight-window throws. The Giants finished with 394 total yards, 150 more than the supposedly offensive superior Cowboys. They dominated Dallas physically, holding the ball for 36:40 compared to 23:20 for the Cowboys. Third-down offense — Whether it was throwing the ball to Likely, running the tush push, Dart running the ball, Skattebo hammering into the line, it didn’t matter. The Giants went an audacious nine of 11 on third-down conversions. Run defense — The offense wasn’t the only group dominating the Cowboys physically. The Giants allowed just 69 rushing yards on 18 carries, 3.8 yards per attempt. Who needs that Dexter guy? Jevon Holland — Holland had a sliding interception that set up a Giants’ touchdown in the second quarter. Wet Willies to … Tyrone Tracy — After fumbling away a scoring opportunity in the red zone on just his second carry of the game in the second quarter, Tracy did not play again on offense. He was on the kickoff return team after Deonte Banks suffered cramping, but that’s it. Veteran running back Najee Harris was inactive Sunday. I have to think Tracy and Harris will be changing places for the foreseeable future. Dru Phillips — Phillips was called for three defensive pass…
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants at Rams Week 2 opening odds: New York opens as big underdogs
summary: The New York Giants open Week 2 as 8.5-point underdogs on the road against the Los Angeles Rams, per FanDuel Sportsbook. The Giants opened their season by stunning the Dallas Cowboys, but have an uphill battle ahead of them against the Rams in Week 2 on Monday Night Football. This game was widely expected to […]
full_text: The New York Giants before Monday Night Football | Getty Images The New York Giants open Week 2 as 8.5-point underdogs on the road against the Los Angeles Rams, per F anDuel Sportsbook . The Giants opened their season by stunning the Dallas Cowboys, but have an uphill battle ahead of them against the Rams in Week 2 on Monday Night Football. This game was widely expected to be a blowout win for the Rams, but it’s significantly more complicated than it appeared when the schedule first came out. First the Rams decision to travel to Australia shortly before their season opener rather than arrive early seemed to backfire. They appeared gassed from the start against the San Francisco 49ers and were outplayed by their division rival. Then the Rams learned earlier Sunday that star pass rusher Myles Garret would need knee surgery and will spend (at least) the next four weeks on the short-term injured reserve. It remains to be seen in what condition the Rams will be after travelling back from Australia to the The Giants, meanwhile, are riding high after a dominating 28-20 victory over the Cowboys on Sunday Night Football. The Giants utterly controlled the line of scrimmage and time of possession, running the ball down the Cowboys’ throat while Jaxson Dart was surgical with the football. Can the Giants travel across the country and turn their Week 1 win into an actual winning streak?
author: Chris Pflum

title: Malik Nabers will play for Giants vs. Dallas Cowboys
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Malik Nabers will play for the New York Giants on Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. Nabers has not played since tearing the ACL in his right knee in Week 4 of the 2025 season. Nabers worked out under the supervision of return to play coordinator Allison Boudreau before kickoff. Nabers […]
full_text: Malik Nabers | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Malik Nabers will play for the New York Giants on Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. Nabers has not played since tearing the ACL in his right knee in Week 4 of the 2025 season. Nabers worked out under the supervision of return to play coordinator Allison Boudreau before kickoff. Nabers had been clear that the decision would be his. “It’s my career. It’s my body,” Nabers had said on Thursday. “I know when I’m able to play, and I know when I’m able to do what I want to do. So, everybody’s got to live with the decision on what I want to do with my career.” How many snaps Nabers plays remains to be seen, but this is a positive development for the Giants as they open the John Harbaugh era. Nabers playing means Dalen Cambre, signed to the 53-man roster on Saturday, will be inactive. Running back question answered Najee Harris will be inactive. The Giants will have three active backs — Cam Skattebo, Devin Singletary, Tyrone Tracy. Full inactives Giants OT J.C. title: Giants vs. Cowboys: Malik Nabers’ status remains murky
summary: We are, as of this writing, about six hours from kickoff in the New York Giants season opener against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football. And as things stand right now, nobody seems quite sure if Giants’ star receiver Malik Nabers will play. Adam Schefter of ESPN is reporting that Nabers’ status for tonight’s […]
full_text: Malik Nabers | Getty Images We are, as of this writing, about six hours from kickoff in the New York Giants season opener against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football. And as things stand right now, nobody seems quite sure if Giants’ star receiver Malik Nabers will play. Adam Schefter of ESPN is reporting that Nabers’ status for tonight’s game “remains murky at best.” Schefter points to the Giants elevating WRs Dalen Cambre and Braxton Berrios to the active roster. The decision on whether Nabers plays has been left to the player himself, and Schefter adds that Nabers hasn’t given the Giants’ clarity on whether or not he’ll play. Schefter reports that Nabers is “leaving whether or not he [Nabers] plays to God. He wants God to guide him.” Jay Glazer of Fox Sports is reporting that Nabers has been cleared to come back. Glazer says, “They’re [the Giants] are going to bring him out about three hours before the game. It’s his [Nabers’] decision if he plays, how much he plays.” He adds, “From what I’m gathering right now, the sentiment is that they think he’s going to go. But they won’t really know until three hours before.” Three hours before kickoff will be roughly 5 p.m. eastern, and we’ll update throughout the afternoon with more information on Nabers’ status as we get it. If Nabers can’t pay, the Giants will likely be depending on TE Isaiah Likely and WR Darnell Mooney to fill the void, as well as Odell Beckham Jr. in his return to MetLife Stadium.
